meta.title: Simon's Story
meta.description: Play 1 — Pre-Event through Registration. October 2026 to 1 April 2027.

_schema._comment: Self-describing schema for this JSON. Added S167. Authoritative for key names and valid values. Any Claude reading this file must check here before querying.

paragraphObject.notes: A paragraph is an object in turn.paras[]. 't' is the text. 'c' is the class (optional — omit for default prose). 'media' attaches image/video (optional). 's' is inline style string (optional, rare).

paragraphClasses._default: (omit c key — renders as default prose)
paragraphClasses._warning: Engine renders ANY c value as an HTML class attribute with no validation. Unknown values render as default prose with no styling and no error. Always use a value from _valid.
paragraphClasses.inner: Simon's internal voice / self-talk — pale red italic with left border
paragraphClasses.lyric: Song lyrics — muted olive-green italic with left border
paragraphClasses.solo: Single-line beat with breathing room — plain text, 40px margins
paragraphClasses.solo big: Larger standalone line for big reveals
paragraphClasses.subtitle: Named sub-section within a chapter — Crimson Pro 26px italic
paragraphClasses.time: Time-of-day marker within a chapter — Crimson Pro 36px italic
paragraphClasses.break: Scene separator — empty text, renders as thin horizontal line
paragraphClasses.quote: Quoted external text — muted earth-green italic with left border

turnObject.after: Optional array of paragraph objects rendered AFTER the end-of-turn choices. Currently unused in data but supported by engine.

questionModes._comment: Set on turn.questionMode when turn.isQuestion is true. Nine modes in engine as of S167.

signalStructure._location: top-level `signal` object keyed by turn ID string (e.g. '17a', '23')

paras.t: Feeling fresh, invigorated, ready to go. Nine hours of unbroken sleep. Day six without a glass of wine. Herbal infusions before bed. Ginger and turmeric my favourite. Neutralise those free radicals, baby. The morning juice. Spinach (freshly picked from the allotment each morning), apple juice (pressed at the local orchard), a splash of lemon, a handful of spirulina (it ‘might’ help lower blood pressure, it ‘might’ have anti-inflammatory properties). Fifteen quid for a bag of tasteless powder. It better do something.

The late autumn sun is already up. Watery, but still radiating a gentle, comforting warmth. The last of the dewdrops evaporate around my bare feet as I stretch my arms up to the heavens and try and click that annoying knot in my lower neck that I just can’t quite get to. I assess the work planned for the morning. Late-season potatoes to dig up. The last of the tomatoes to pick. Dahlias to cut, they’ve been remarkable this year, the Café au Lait in particular. Plus the least enticing job — the eternal battle with the weeds. Perhaps I should just call them all wild flowers and be done with it?

My phone detox has entered day three. It’s on the kitchen table. Out of sight and all that. Having said that emails don’t check themselves. Well they do, but the AI bot that I didn’t ask for or install (actually quite useful) has an annoying habit of occasionally auto-filling crucial work emails in junk. I did say quite useful.
So, cup of green tea, glass of water (must order a new filter) and the morning dose of ubiquinol, NAC and Taurine. Quick scan of emails. Back out into the garden.
Kettle on. There it is on the table.
My precious.
The automaton takes over. Just a quick scroll of X. To ‘check the news’.

Turns out the news was quite interesting. Reports of military manoeuvres at Royal Air Force Wyton. The ‘top-secret’ (so secret it’s the first thing that comes up on a google for ‘secret military bases UK’) Pathfinder Building is Britain’s premier military spy base. I remember it was mentioned in an article I read a few years ago about D.U.M.B.s (Deep Underground Military Bases). Nuclear fallout bunker that could keep several thousand ‘elites’ alive for two decades. So they say. Maybe they keep the Greys there? And Elvis.
Anyway, the quick check has now ticked over 90 minutes.
Learn your lesson, dickhead.

The cottage garden waits for no man. The military activity is hardly covert though. Front page of BBC, no less. If it’s in the news, it’s likely a ruse. They’re probably planning something though. They’ve always been planning something. Allegedly. According to ‘inside sources’, ‘data leaks’ or ‘whistleblowers’.

I let it wash over me. Control the controllables.
Zen and the art of digging up spuds.

choices.label: Morning
choices.prompt: The garden or the screen. You know which one wins.

opts.text: Stay out. The dahlias need cutting. The Café au Lait especially.
Check the RAF Wyton story properly. Something feels off.
Come in. Those DUMB articles from 2024 are still open in a tab somewhere...

paras.t: Dev is extraordinary. I’ve never met anyone else like him. In fact very few people are like him. Or even quite like him. I met him at school. Christ, nearly forty years ago. He’s been an intermittent constant in my life. You can set a clock by his chaotic timekeeping and unreliability. He goes silent for months at a time. He’s not what you’d call a traditional communicator or responsive to messaging. And I’ve learnt not to push him - if you want to get in touch with him the worst thing you can possibly do is bombard him with texts and calls.
‘Are you OK?’ or ‘Just checking in’ are his Kryptonite.
When he does get in touch it’s a frenzy. He’ll bombard you with months of dense research and be amazed that you don’t have an encyclopaedic knowledge of it twenty four hours later.
‘Have you read it yet?’
‘No, Dev. You sent it at 2.30am and I’ve been at work’
‘This is fire though, Simon. Fuck work, drop everything. Read it’

He also has a habit of just ‘finding you’. You won’t have seen him for months, last you heard he was in Bangkok or Cape Town, then he just appears in a pub you hadn’t told him you were going to, or knocks on the front door, wanders in and nonchalantly puts the kettle on. No ceremony. No chit chat. Just a hug and straight into a deep dive. It wouldn’t surprise me if he’d cut himself a door key and I found him sitting at the kitchen table waiting for me, an open bottle of bourbon in front of him.
Dev just gets away with it. The rascal’s rascal. Nobody has a bad word to say about him, as long as you don’t consider cad, scoundrel, philanderer, rogue or loon to be bad words. Which he doesn’t.

God knows where he gets some of his stuff from. He absorbs information like no one else I’ve ever met. He’s probably a speed reader but he’s never confirmed this. The closest he ever got was a wink and a knowing tap on the nose. His book recommendations have always been a thing of legend. At school he started me on my journey through the sci-fi and dystopian literature landscape. Illuminatus! Trilogy, 1984, Brave New World, Hitchhiker’s, Foundation etc. He once showed me a pre-release handwritten copy of Ready Player One. It had a slightly different ending. Better in my opinion. A bit like Blade Runner Director’s Cut. It wouldn’t surprise me in the least if he’d written it himself.

He’d often just send you a photo of a book. No message. No ‘hi mate’. No emoji. Just a photo and then dark mode for six months. There are plenty of other must-reads he’s sent my way. Let me think. Off the top of my head, Snowcrash (if you haven’t read, read it), Wool, The Road, Children of Time, Cryptonomicon, Daemon, Vurt. Sorry I’m getting carried away, you’re not here for book club.

That’s just books. As I’ve said he occasionally bombards you with his latest ‘data drop’. 4Chan whistleblowers, alleged intelligence agency leaks and his own mind blowing prose that interweaves fact, fiction, psychedelia and science that often goes slightly over my head. A lot of it is quite dark. Keeps you up in the middle of the night sort of dark. Yet when he explains it, he somehow manages to offer you an almost empty glass whilst convincing you it’s nearly full. How he retained such positivity I’ll never know. He’s unflappable. He never looks back. Only Forward. (I’ve unwittingly given you another book recommendation).

We got on like a house on fire since the day we met. I think he liked the fact that I took the piss out of him. I understood some of his obscure references and I got his dark sense of humour. I’d never hassled him. He hates being hassled. We just clicked. I was never in awe of him, at least I gave the impression I wasn’t. Most people were. He was the annoying bastard that most blokes wanted to be and most girls wanted to be with. A lot of boys too for that matter. Don’t tell him I said this, but he does come across as a mixture of Jason Bourne, Mr Spock and the grooviest side of Austin Powers. A sort of all-action, logical Man of Mystery. It was common knowledge that his school fees had been covered by scholarship. It was widely suspected that he’d inherited a rather large Trust Fund. He had pads in London and Miami. That I knew of.
What he actually did was an unknown. Think of something uber-cool, verging on the implausible, and you’ll be on the right lines I imagine.

I’ve mentioned Dev because I had a message exchange with him earlier today. An actual chat-by-text rather than a dump-and-run. It was prompted by Amy showing me a photo from a couple of years ago - her phone had decided to collate a montage to music of ‘In the garden through the years’ or some such - and one stood out. The sky had done something that night that it wasn’t supposed to do in the south of England. Shimmering ribbons of green and violet. We stood in the garden in our dressing gowns at midnight, transfixed. I’d rushed out as Amy had shouted my name in a voice I’d never heard before — not frightened, not excited, not elated. At peace. A peaceful shout, is that a thing?
I’d meant to ask Dev about it at the time but it had slipped my mind. The algorithm does not forget. Better late than never, I sent Dev the photo with ‘Thoughts?’
I knew he’d have a provocative take. He did.

We were five minutes into the drive home from the market. Sam was in the passenger seat doing that thing where he scrolled his phone with one hand and spooned rich, spicy lamb curry and basmati rice into his mouth with the other — a coordination skill I genuinely envied. He was dropping rice all over the car seat, but I didn’t say anything, I didn’t want to be the moaning parent. Olive or Wilf would sort out the debris later with glee.

The curry was from a relatively new street food trader. Authentic home-cooked-style Punjabi cuisine. Creamy butter chicken, handmade parathas coated in ghee, minced lamb samosas, naan bread wraps packed with chicken tikka, raita and tamarind chutney and an ever-changing menu of weekly specials. I had wolfed down two bhajis at the start of the journey — onions, vegetables and whole spices, deep fried until their gram flour batter was perfectly crunchy — I had doubtless dropped some prized nuggets for the dogs too.

Sam had been accompanying me on my trips to the market on Saturdays since he was a young boy. I’d go most weeks, sometimes on my own, often with Amy and sometimes with one or more of the children. We’d been running the market for as long as they could all remember. It was part of the fabric of our lives. Amy and I run a company that organises food-based events in Sussex and the southeast. The market was our flagship event, one of the most vibrant and successful in the country and our bread and butter.
We’d been lucky, we worked predominately from home which had allowed us to both play an active daily part in raising our children and our two dogs. Three dogs at one point.
Freddie, God how I miss you
We’d lost Freddie quite a few years ago, but his memory lives with me everyday. He was the most wonderful chocolate lab, a stubborn bastard with a mind of his own. He lived to a ripe old age.
‘Pa?’
Sam had been calling me Pa for a few years now. It was endearing, it carried a similar tone to daddy but was more age appropriate. An eighteen year old couldn’t use daddy.
‘Yeah’
‘Cheeky range on the way back?’

Sam enjoyed coming with me to the market, solid father-son bonding time. He was the most food-obsessed of the kids and he enjoyed browsing the artisan food stalls, knowing the traders would treat him to a cookie, cake or a coffee. He’d get his pick of some amazing street food for lunch too. Today was curry, but he could’ve had wood-fired pizza, Goulash, jerk chicken, galettes, Bunny chow, Pad Thai, falafel, shawarma, Louisiana chicken, souvlaki, or dim sum.

I knew the main reason he came with me was that we passed the golf course on the way back. Of course I wasn’t going to say no to hitting a few balls on the driving range and our traditional chipping and putting competition. The clubs were in the boot.
‘Go on then. I’m gonna whip you today, Sammy-boy’. I winked at him.
I wouldn’t. He was golf-obsessed and much better than me now. I used to let him win. ‘I beat Daddy’. A couple of years ago I used to narrowly beat him, most of the time. Now he kicks my ass.

‘Any business idea brainwaves?’ I ask him. He’d decided, as had George, to take a gap year. We’d been quite insistent. It was the right decision. We’d had the ‘University is not the same as it was in my day’ chat on many occasions. I’d been lucky. No tuition fees, accommodation paid for, a Student Grant to cover food and travel, a Student Loan to cover E’s and booze. These days you’d graduate with a fifty grand debt you’d take half a lifetime to pay off, and enter a world of AI and unknown career prospects. I’d shown them the online ‘when will I pay off my student debt?’ calculators. They made for horrific reading. I’d asked my mate Andy to have a chat with him. His son Max, lovely lad, good cricketer, got a 2:1 from Exeter and is currently working in Waitrose. Student Loans Company in to him for nearly sixty thousand and he’s scanning Essential Houmous at the one remaining checkout that isn’t self-service.

So we’d come up with a plan. Amy and I had sat down with the boys and Sam’s mum to formulate it. It was perfectly amicable. A bottle of Gavi and some olives. The Gap Year (the capitalisation gives it a sense of formality and gravitas, rather than it simply being an excuse to get up late, doss about and ‘do’ Thailand.
I suggested the year was split into three sections — earning money — entrepreneurial investigations — travel. Earn your keep — dream big — ‘do’ Thailand. We’d agreed this was a solid framework.

So far, Sam has done a few odd jobs, he’s dreamed very big, but without any idea how he can make those dreams real, and he’s talked a lot about ‘doing’ somewhere. Ideally doing somewhere with decent golf courses.
‘Not really’ was his response. ‘Maybe something to do with golf?’
I’m all for him doing something he’s passionate about.
‘How about curated golf and food holidays?’
I wasn’t reinventing the wheel here, but it’s something he (and I) could do well.
‘Google it, see what’s out there’
He typed in foodie trips for golfers. ‘I’ve got no service, can I try your phone, Pa?’
He grabbed it from the magnetic holder on the dashboard.
‘What’s this website?’
I had Biblioteca Pleyades open in my browser.
‘It looks like it was made by a serial killer in 1998?’
1998 seemed like ancient history to Sam. To me it was last week.

‘That is the most comprehensive encyclopaedia of everything that is, might be, or definitely isn’t happening in the world. And it looks a bit like that because it prioritises content over aesthetics.’
‘It looks like it was built by someone who was prioritised for a psychiatric assessment.’
‘Quite possibly.’

Sam scrolled. I glanced across at him, intrigued as to what he’d make of it. He was on the index page. The one that lists about four hundred topics side by side with zero editorial hierarchy. Scalar electromagnetics next to the Illuminati next to nanotechnology next to the Anunnaki.
‘Pa, there’s a section called Reptilians.’
‘Yeah. Read it, it’s quite mental. You know David Icke, don’t you?’
‘Kind of. Next to it there’s a section called Mind Control.’
‘Yeah, that’s worth reading.’
‘Have you read all this?’

‘Some of it. Not the Reptilian stuff for a bit. The thing is about forty percent of it is total bollocks. Hollow Earth and The Galactic Federation. Fun, but absolute bollocks. I think. And about forty percent is true. Well verifiable with links to official documents. Whether that makes it true is another conversation. Declassified government programmes. Patent filings. Institutional white papers. Real shit.’
‘The other twenty percent?’
‘Who knows. That’s the problem. That’s the whole problem. Not just with this website. With everything.’

Sam had the last scrapings of his curry. He could probably eat the whole thing again. He was listening in the way he often listened — with enough attention to make me feel heard but enough distance to make you feel old. At least twenty percent of his brain was thinking about refinements to his golf swing.

‘The thing is’ I said, about to go on a tangent that could last the rest of the drive. ‘Once you start pulling on a thread, it opens into more threads, and more threads. It never ends. Three hours later you realise you’re reading a paper about magnetite in human brain tissue that was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, which is a real journal, and you’re wondering whether the electromagnetic frequencies from the phone mast outside Emilia’s college are doing something to the magnetite in her brain, and then you look up and it’s quarter past three in the morning and you’ve got to be up in four hours.’
‘So don’t start, Pa.’
‘Easier said than done.’
Sam laughed. He knew what I was like. Obsessive. Loved a rabbit hole.
‘Open the Libre App for me’
‘You feel OK?’ Sam asked
‘I’m fine. Just want to check my sugar.’
‘A bit high, those bhajis are full of carbs’
I got my insulin pen out of the compartment in the door and injected 5 units of Fiasp insulin into my tummy as I drove.
You need to get to the gym next week.
‘That website is a bit like the universe.’
‘What do you mean?’

‘The Total Perspective Vortex. From The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy. You know the book I’ve been telling you to read for nearly a decade. You put someone in it and it shows them the entire universe. Its vastness. And their significance. Or lack of it. It destroys them. It’s too much for a human mind.’

That website is the Total Perspective Vortex for conspiracy researchers. You go in thinking you’ll understand how the world really works, and four thousand pages later you understand that the world really works in about four thousand ways simultaneously, most of which contradict each other.
‘So what’s the point?’
‘I don’t know. What’s the point in doing anything?’
‘To enjoy yourself?’
‘Maybe’
It’s what I’d have said at his age. Maybe that is the answer to life, the universe and everything? I somehow doubt it though.
‘But fun doesn’t pay the mortgage, Sammy boy. If it did I’d have owned houses all over the world before you and Emilia were born’
‘Like Uncle Dev’
It was funny that he still called him Uncle. He wasn’t even his Uncle, but it would be weird if he stopped calling him it.
‘Yeah, just like Dev. But Dev doesn’t have a mortgage to pay, does he? Never has.’
Dev seemed to be able to turn fun into money. And he got a pretty good exchange rate. His Trust Fund didn’t hinder the process.
We sat with that for a minute. Well I sat with it. Sam was probably thinking about buying a new utility wedge.

‘The problem with that website is that the real shit — the actual declassified programmes, patents, white papers and all that — are stored in the same warehouse as the Reptilians. On the same shelf. With the same formatting. And if you point someone at the warehouse and say — look, there’s evidence of coordinated global infrastructure that’s being built without democratic consent — they look at the shelf next to it and laugh. Reptilians.’
‘I thought you believed in Reptilians?’
‘Well, in a way. Kind of. Not really. Let’s not go there now. The important thing is they put the truth in plain sight but hide it within a Total Perspective Vortex.’
‘That’s pretty smart.’
‘It’s the cleverest thing they do.’
‘Who’s they?’
Fuck me, if I had a quid every time I’d heard this I’d have definitely paid off the mortgage.
‘Another excellent question’
‘You don’t know, do you.’

‘I know some of it. I can map some of it. The institutional layer — the Bank for International Settlements, the World Economic Forum, the Club of Rome, the Trilateral Commission — that’s all public. The funding flows, the revolving doors between government and private sector, the policy documents. That’s not conspiracy theory. That’s just reading. But above that it gets murky. The Rothschilds. The Illuminati. Ancient Bloodlines. The Committee of 300. It’s all of these, but also none of them. Or no single one at a particular time. No, I don’t really know. Anyone who tells you they do is either lying or selling you a subscription.’
‘So you’ve spent thousands of hours reading four-thousand-page websites to reach the conclusion that you don’t know.’
‘When you put it like that...’
We laughed as I pulled through the gates to the golf course.
‘Ready for pain, Pa?’

There would be no pain. Winning or losing on the putting green is an irrelevance compared to the feeling you get when your son calls you Pa. And there’s no amount of reality that the Total Perspective Vortex could show me that could change that.

The potatoes, dug up last week, were exceptional. Actually tasted like potatoes. Gently boiled, a large knob of butter. Perfection. I feel a long way from self-sufficiency though. Weeks of nurture, toil, turning soil and watering yielded two, maybe three weeks worth. The Marmande tomatoes were very pleasant but there weren’t nearly enough for a family of six Tricolore salad addicts. A labour of love that had to be topped up each week with Isle of Wight selection box reinforcements from Waitrose. I reluctantly admit these were just slightly sweeter, juicier and firmer than our homegrown crop. But they didn’t fill me with such a sense of enormous wellbeing.

The sunshine skies of early-October have turned into an overcast perma-drizzle. It’s certainly not cold yet, but the evenings have a chill. I’ve stubbornly resisted putting the central heating on. The underfloor heating in the bathroom keeps the chill off in there. I’ve yet to light a fire either.
Must organise a firewood delivery.
The logs in the garden remain un-split. The axe bought especially for this purpose remains pristine, as sharp as the day it was delivered.

I sit down for a ‘break’ — a spot of pre-cooking ‘research’ on X. The daily mix of rage-bait, distraction and division. An ‘Islamophobic protest’ against the ‘Boat Invaders’ up north somewhere. Retweeted (the old lingo never dies) by the usual suspects, AI-created British Bulldogs waving St. George flags and ‘Refugees are welcome here’ bots in the replies. Divide and conquer.
KEEP DOOMSCROLLING

I see a sharp comment from Derrick Broze. I haven’t read much of his stuff for ages. Seems a genuine dude. I remember a spat he had with Alison McDowell a few years ago about the use of crypto in the ‘freedom movement’. I never found out how that resolved itself, or if I did I can’t remember.
Seeing his post reminds me that I’ve had Derrick’s ‘The Pyramid of Power’ documentary open in my browser for months, barely skimmed, mentally flagged as ‘Must Read’.

No time like the present.
Down the rabbit hole I go.

choices.label: Tuesday Night
choices.prompt: The tab has been open for months. Today could be different.

opts.text: Actually read the Pyramid of Power. All of it. This time.
Skim the intro, save the rest for later. You always say that.
Close the tab. Cook something. The allotment needs you more than Derrick Broze does.

paras.t: Early starts. 5 days in a row. Working until it’s too dark or I’m too tired. I wouldn’t say I was born to do this sort of thing. Not many people would say ‘Oh yeah, Simon, he’s handy’. But I’m not totally inept.
This time I’d thrown myself in at the deep end with this project. I could’ve got a carpenter in to do the job in half the time, but where’s the satisfaction in that?

Today also marked a capitulation. My first ever use of AI. I needed to work out how far apart I should space the joists. I’d promised myself I wouldn’t jump on to the slippery slope bandwagon of ChatGPT. But I wanted to make the most of the light and do some actual work, rather than using my brain, pen, pad and calculator. So I created an account. My first step into a brave new world. Answer in seconds, with hints and tips I didn’t even ask for, but turned out to be very useful.
Clever. Too clever by half.

I haven’t told you what I’m doing. You may have guessed? Building a deck. In the garden. To put our bell tent on. Long story short, earlier in the summer, Amy suggested we buy a bell tent. Another ‘room’ in the garden. A place to have a late night drink when the nights turn nippier. An extra roof (of sorts) for friends to crash under. Somewhere the kids could party. I still say kids — the girls are both sixteen. Sometimes it's sweet sixteen. The boys eighteen and nineteen. That officially makes me an old bastard.

It wouldn’t surprise anyone that knows me in the slightest to learn that I didn’t buy a 3 or 4m tent — large enough to do the job, small enough to put up and take down with ease. And didn’t cost the earth. Oh no. I bought the premium ‘Bell Tent Plus’ 8m. Half moon coir matting. Wood burning stove. The full monty.

We’d put it up on the grass. Quite straightforward actually, other than the fight to get the central pole upright. Amy dressed it with her usual panache and her eye for getting things just right. The centrepiece — a beautiful king size bed that we’d been storing in the shed, surrounded by ethnic rugs, animal skins, an abundance of cushions (the de rigueur female accessory) and vintage furniture. It looks like something out of a VIP boutique camping area at a bougie festival. I added 100m of festoon lights to add to the glamping vibe.
The dogs were bemused by the gargantuan structure at first, but soon realised it gave them shelter from the summer sun.
George and his girlfriend, Clara were the first to use it. They’ve slept in it twice. We’re planning a proper christening on Bonfire Night.
in the Red Corner…Mother Nature

A few weeks later, Mother Nature landed a one-two of misfortune. The left jab — unbeknown to us a mole had decided to burrow up under the central pole. Structural stability compromised. The right hook to floor us — a storm, violent 70mph gusts. A soggy, collapsed pile of canvas greeted us upon inspection.
Bollocks.

We got knocked down, but not out. We picked ourselves up from the canvas, metaphorically, and picked the canvas off the grass, literally. That was a week or so ago. Excellent progress has been made. We have something that looks very much like a 9x9m deck, just a few more planks to lay.
Screen time down. Pride up. Doomscrolling thumb rested, palm slightly blistered from power tool use. Beer well earned.

choices.label: Evening
choices.prompt: The joists are spaced. The answer came in seconds. You didn't even have to think.

opts.text: Delete the app. You promised yourself you wouldn't. The pen, pad and calculator worked fine for decades.
Keep it. But only for practical stuff. DIY, measurements, that sort of thing. You're not going to start asking it to think for you.
Ask it something else. You've been wondering about that RAF Wyton story. See what it makes of it.

paras.t: The Bonfire celebrations in Sussex are truly remarkable. And this coming from someone who used to be a bit of a fireworks curmudgeon.
They’re a throwback to the England that only exists in village pubs and in the memories of soon-to-be-lost generations.
The spirit is medieval. Raucous. Revolutionary. Anti-authoritarian. If only I could bottle it and unleash it upon the country on a wet Wednesday afternoon.

There’s beer. Proper beer. Brewed with love and served from the barrel. Harvey’s Bonfire Boy, brewed in Lewes. Warming, fruity, tinged with woodsmoke. Dark amber in colour, malty and with more than a hint of caramelised apple on the palate and a longing for days of yore aftertaste.

The soul of the annual celebrations are the Bonfire Societies. Processions around county towns throughout the autumn. Lewes always marks 5th November, The Gunpowder Plot. The effigies burnt on the bonfire are symbols of rebellion. Trump. Boris. Merkel. A rogues gallery.

The Procession, each town identified by their traditional hooped patterned jumpers in their own coloured stripes, is the main event. Some Societies dress as pirates. Some as WW1 infantry. Some as witches and warlocks. All costumes elaborate, handmade and drenched in pride and dedication.

Everyone carries a torch, real fire. Lit with paraffin. The rawness, the heat, the two fingers to health and safety. Hand-painted banners and painstakingly-crafted signs are raised aloft by each Society as they march past the assembled masses.
Newick…Isfield…Hastings…Rye. A roar for each.
The finale. The effigy burnt. The flames of the bonfire licking high into the autumn blackness. No ropes or pedestrian fencing here. The intense heat provides a natural barrier.
The fireworks. Funded by donations. Set off by volunteers to roars of delight and murmurs of ‘this is the best year ever’.
They are good. Astonishing. I’m no longer a firework curmudgeon. Mesmerising. Alluring. Raw and tinged with danger. The scent of sulphur lingers in the air.
Film them on your iPhone if you want. Their magic won’t be replicated. The beauty of the moment, retained forever in the cloud, but never captured by your soul.
Four pints. No food. A delicious buzz. A huge pot of chilli sits warming on the hob to greet us when we get home. The bell tent not quite ready, we’ll eat inside in front of the fire.

‘We burn for good.’
That’s the motto.

‘We wunt be druv.’
We won’t be pushed around. Stubbornness, independence.

That’s the spirit.
More of this, England.
More of this, I beg.

And then tomorrow? Back to compliance. Back to the day jobs.

choices.label: Walking home, midnight
opts: Film the next procession on your phone. The fireworks are extraordinary. Capture it.
Put the phone away. Some things aren’t meant to be saved. Just felt.
Post about it. People should know this still exists. England isn’t dead yet.

paras.t: We’ve been dancing round the issue for months. ‘What are we going to do when we grow up?’ we ask one other. Before we know it we’ll be empty nesters. Four little reprobates will have become none. A house once filled with laughter, tears and chaos will fall silent. I can feel the sadness welling up in me just thinking about it. I am a sentimental old fool. For a bloke, anyway. Amy’s a woman. A soft, tender, highly emotional one. The sense of loss will hit her savagely. Eat her up.

It’s starting already. The relief we thought we’d feel when the children didn’t need 24-hour monitoring, questions needing constant answering, daily lifts to and from school, to dance class, to play dates or football training has instead materialised as a sense of being superfluous, redundant, an annoyance. Freedom reborn trumped by the sadness of not being needed any more.

Did I not give enough? I should have cherished every single second more than I did. I look at pictures of the four of them in the bath together as toddlers or on an Easter egg hunt and my whole world shatters. Oh to look into those young innocent eyes again. Just for a moment. Just one more bedtime story.

But one day the crayons did quit. One day we woke to find that we weren’t going on a bear hunt. One day, I don’t know when, we read them their last tale together. Oh, to cuddle them close, to still be able to offer them protection, safety and reassurance.

Sorry. For a minute there I lost myself. Where was I? Ah yes, making plans. Finding solutions. When all the kids have left home it will really free us up. We can go where we please. Maybe move to Devon. Suffolk. Maybe do what my mum did and escape to a warmer climate. We can be self-sufficient, have our own water supply, power, food. Break away. Can’t beat The System? We’ll see about that.
We’d decided to have a proper chat about it later this evening. Discuss the next phase of our lives together. Follow our dreams, the world once again our oyster.
Find a way of dulling the heartache.
Shit, I didn’t mean to say that out loud. Don’t let Amy hear this, I need to be strong for her.
In preparation, I decided to dip back into the Corbett Report archives and watch an episode that had been in my ‘watch this tomorrow’ list for months.

The Only REAL Solution to Digital ID — #SolutionsWatch
by Corbett | Nov 5, 2025 | Solutions Watch, Videos
Hakeem Anwar of AbovePhone.com returns to the de-program to discuss his latest report: “Life Under Digital ID: A Global Analysis with Solutions.”
I love James Corbett.
‘The Corbett Report is an independent, listener-supported alternative news source’ he states at the top of his website.
Underselling himself. He’s as astute, witty and sharp as they come. The antithesis of the asinine, crazy conspiracy theorist caricature. A New World Order analysis guru.

‘Solutions Watch’ used to be ‘Propaganda Watch’ or ‘Psyop Watch’, but he flipped the script. Instead of continual investigation into the ways in which they control, divide and cattle prod us, he decided to offer us, with the help of a series of freedom-loving guests, insights and ideas about how we can fight back. Take control of our own destiny.
I don’t watch these weekly broadcasts nearly enough.

I dived in. This is good shit. I got through the first eleven minutes and the phone rang. Duty called. Then dinner needing cooking. We cooked together, laughing and joking. Dinner was eaten. Wine was opened.
The happily ever after chat didn’t materialise. Netflix was binged instead.
The remaining 31 minutes of Corbett added to my ‘watch this tomorrow’ list. The chat rescheduled.

choices.label: Evening
opts: Finish the episode. It’s only 31 minutes. You owe it to yourself.
Send it to three people who might actually watch it. Do your bit.
Leave it. You already know enough. Knowing more changes nothing.

paras.t: ‘You know about Palantir, don’t you?’ George asked me.
‘A bit. Why’s that?’
‘There’s this thing on TikTok. They’re offering ten grand a month to eighteen year olds. Engineer interns. Everyone is asking how much you’d sell your soul for. Why would you be selling your soul?’
‘You want the long version or the short version?’
‘I’ll get the long version anyway, so hit me with it’. George sniggers through his cheeky smile.
‘Go and grab two beers, we could be here a while.’ I wink as I reply.
I wish Dev was here. He’d fucking nail this.
I take the caps off two M&S German lagers. Hardly hipster, but bloody lovely.
‘What do you know about them, Georgie?’
‘Not much. They’re a data company. People are saying they’re pure evil.’

You know Peter Thiel? It’s his company. The Paypal founder. Multi-zillionaire. Started Palantir twenty years or so ago with some other transhuman twat. I can’t remember who. He named after those seeing stones in Lord of the Rings that Sauron used to see all of Middle Earth. A company after Sauron’s all-seeing surveillance tech. There’s your first clue.

I say it’s his company — it’s basically CIA. They fund all this sort of shit through In-Q-Tel. Google Earth. Pokemon. I think Facebook too originally. I mean, whatever the exact details, they’re all part of one big surveillance psyop.
‘Pokemon?’ George looked baffled. ‘As in Pikachu Pokemon?’

‘Yeah. It’s basically a 3D spying/mapping network disguised as a game. Clever really. Look it up. I think the company was called Keyhole or something like that. Look up the whole CAPTCHA thing too. A Google Maps data mining operation. Basically anytime you see safety and convenience, read surveillance and control.’
‘So they’re a surveillance company, mining our data, sneaking things in the T’s & C’s that no one reads. Listening to our conversations. Doesn’t every company do that?’
‘Well, yes. But Palantir are the daddies of this shit. Mental AI software that monitors everything that moves, thinks, gives off heat or an electric signal, farts…’
‘Well they’ll be able to track Mum pretty easily’. We laugh, clink bottles and have synchronised glug. ‘Go and get two more, Georgie’.

‘You know when I drone on about digital ID?’ (George gives me a look that says, you? Drone on? Never). Well this is what I’m talking about. Not some digital card. Not something you can use to prove your age to buy a pint. An interoperable database, the backend, that links and cross-references everything. You think your TikTok account is anonymous because you don’t use your name? You think those facial recognition cameras don’t know who every single fucker in the crowd at football is? Your WhatsApp messages are ‘encrypted’? I do that annoying two fingers on each hand air quote.

They’ve got this AI software called Gotham. It was made for intelligence agencies and the police in America. CDC. ICE. Every agency you can think of and undoubtedly some that we don’t even know exist. Probably most of the world. It connects datasets. Everything about a person, pulled into one profile, searchable.

They’re here too. Loads of contracts with NHS. They sold one of their platforms for a quid or something. Foundry I think it was. Drug dealer model. (we chuckle) MOD. Cabinet Office. Local authorities. The Old Bill. Whilst everyone’s arguing about Starmer and Farage, illegal immigrants preying on our girls and rainbow zebra crossings, Palantir and co are mopping up Government contracts. Bringing in The Beast System under our noses. Algorithm Ghettos. No one asked for this shit. And please don’t give me the ‘if you haven’t done anything wrong, you’ve got nothing to worry about’ bollocks.

Thiel says it out loud. On camera. To investors. ‘I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.’ The founder of the company that runs our NHS data said that. Out loud. And no fucker cares. The NHS kept the contract. And I’ve kept my NHS number. Because the other option is…?
Amy came in from the kitchen. ‘You doing the Palantir thing again?’
‘Yes, I’m doing Palantir.’
‘I’m about to tell George who runs the UK branch. Do you know?’
Shit, I’ve gone into condescending mode.
‘Er, no.’
‘Louis Mosley. Grandson of Oswald.’
‘The Fascist MP guy?’ asked Amy. She had entered the chat.
‘Yeah. Gotta laugh.’
‘So what do we do?’ George asked.
And there it was. The question. The one that lands every time like a brick through a window I’ve just spent ten minutes carefully constructing.
‘Nothing. Well, mass non-compliance or nothing. Basically nothing.’

George laughed. It wasn’t a cruel laugh. It was recognition. He’s nineteen. He’s lived his whole life inside a watered-down algo-ghetto. Palantir is furniture to him — another piece of the digital architecture he mindlessly navigates. The same way I drive to work on pothole-ridden roads without thinking about who built them or why they go where they go. The difference between us isn’t that he doesn’t understand. It’s that understanding doesn’t produce the same anger in him. He doesn’t remember The Before Times.

‘They also got a multi-billion dollar US Army contract’ I said, to nobody in particular. Amy was in the room in body only. George was distracted by TikTok notifications. ‘All those targeted killings in Gaza, Iran or wherever. Palantir. AI’s perception of collateral damage is a little different to yours and mine. A five-year-old cancer patient in a hospital sacrificed to take out an evil terrorist group leader?’ (air quotes) ‘Fine. I can’t remember what half their ‘defence solutions’ are called. Maven I think is one. Look them up, they’re all on their website. Presented to the world with pride, like they’re a good thing.’
I’d lost George now. But hopefully he’d absorbed enough to understand why you’d be ‘selling your soul’ to work for these wankers.
I reckon I’d given a pretty good synopsis. Dev would’ve been able to hold court for longer. Probably picked up on numerous inaccuracies.

I hadn’t even got as far as their partnership with Oracle. Oracle’s Cloud infrastructure and Palantir’s AI. ‘Defending western interests.’ Ellison, cut from the same ‘elite’ cloth, telling rooms of ‘investors’ (sorry about all the air quotes) that ‘citizens would be on their best behaviour because we’re constantly recording and reporting everything.’
Just fuck off. Please.

I’ve researched this shit. I remember about ten percent of what I read. Entropy. Entropy and alcohol. The Oasis version was better. Oh for George’s brain plasticity combined with my seasoned rage. I can see what’s coming. Give or take. I’ve read about Palantir’s architecture, their contracts. That Foundry ingests everything and Gotham builds individual profiles searchable by tattoo, immigration status, flagged social media posts and probably our fucking unique biofield.
I rant, I moan. But I basically achieve nothing. I explain the cage from the inside and I close the door behind me with every click, every updated app and every ‘agree all’.

I’ll go to bed tonight and lie there thinking about Palantir and Thiel. That interview when he was asked ‘should the human race survive?’ and he didn’t answer. I’ll think about the NHS and that snide Mosley and his ‘we won’t get involved in digital ID, we’re just involved in the back end.’ I’ll think of the twenty-four UK contracts, the predictive dashboards, the algorithmic regime that’ll sit somewhere between reading our thoughts and programming them. I’ll get angry. We should do something. We must do something.
Then I’ll fall asleep.
And in the morning I’ll drive to work, guided by Google Maps to ensure I miss the traffic.
Twat.

choices.label: Gotham is burning. Which one are you?
opts: Batman. I see the corruption. I fight it. I never win — because the system regenerates faster than I can dismantle it. But I fight anyway.
The Riddler. I see the patterns. I leave the clues. I need people to understand what I’ve understood. The compulsion to explain is the cage.
The Joker. I’ve seen the absurdity. The only sane response to an insane system is laughter. Or madness. The line between them is thinner than anyone admits.

paras.t: It happened.
I’m certain of that. I think. Maybe it was a fever dream?

Nope. The last four hours are inked into the timeline of my life. They’ve changed my relationship with him for good. Correction, they’ve updated the file of our relationship that has been sitting unsaved on the desktop of my life for the past decade.

Giles. I’ve shared some of the best nights of my life with him. Intimate moments. You were there for one another when life got shit. When one of us got dumped by the girl. When we needed a friend, a confidant, a shoulder to cry on, a mate to get mashed up with. We were there for the lows.

And by God we were both there for the highs. I’ll find that picture of us. It’ll save me a thousand words. Post club, still high. Tops off. Bottle of whiskey held up to the camera. Not in the modern, normative narcissistic, look-at-me, timeline-curated, affected, posed, kinda way. Real. Raw. Untainted. You can see it in our eyes, reflected in the dilated pupils.

I think you're the same as me
We see things they'll never see
You and I are gonna live forever

I try to hold those lyrics close to my heart, despite this evening’s heated exchange. I desperately cling on to the memory of the boy I once knew. How things were, not how things are. But right now it feels like our paths, our outlooks, our beliefs have diverged irrecoverably. Ghosts. A paean to a distant memory. An ode to anguish.
You and I are gonna live forever? Now a question, not a statement of irrevocable certainty.
Let’s get down to the nitty gritty. Not that you want to hear it, but I need to vent.
We were guests at our friends Cotswolds Lake House. Amazing place. We’d had a fun day, five Parklife lads, chilling, reminiscing, cooking inordinate amounts of meat on the Big Green Egg.

I was drunk. He was sober. He doesn't drink any more. You can draw your own conclusions about why. You’ll be right. Anyway, I wasn’t that drunk. Everything I said made sense. I was loose-lipped. Emboldened.
What happened needed to happen, and it did. Cards on the table. His card, The Joker, mine the full deck of Illuminati: The Game of Conspiracy cards -  Collector’s Edition. Royal Flush, motherfucker.
Sorry, too aggressive. But the adrenaline is still coursing.

He thinks I’m crazy. Paranoid. That my default mode is to suggest everything is a psyop. Which isn’t far from the truth. I question, I doubt, I research, I want to - I need to zoom in on every Truth, every Lie, every Conspiracy. To understand it. From its core to its far reaching spectral tentacles. To analyse it. To expose it. To spread the Gospel.
I think he’s a normie. A sheep. I just can't understand how he can't want to see it. Why he won't see it. Why he refuses to engage. How can he not want to read ‘insert article here?’
He, like so many supposedly intelligent, kind, caring people with a thirst for knowledge responds to my rants with a blank stare and asks ‘But who are they?’
Wake Uuuuuuuuup!

Maybe they have woken up? Maybe it’s me who’s asleep. Get a hold of yourself. Have you learned nothing in your five (and ticking…) decades on the planet? Take a breath. Maybe I shouldn’t frame it as an argument? Maybe we’re both saying the same thing? Coming at it from different directions? Both scratching the same itch.

What if I flip it round in my head? Maybe it's not that he can't see it. Or won’t see it. It’s that he's already felt it. Intuited it. He’s living it. What I perceive to be a blank stare isn’t blank. It’s a mirror. Silently reflecting.

He understands that a solution can’t be found in never ending reams of research and by dedicating one’s very core to attempting to understand it. Or in 3am deep dives and four-hundred-and-sixty-two open and partially-read links to The Truth.
That’s the path to inaction.
The enlightened soul doesn't just think. It comprehends. It does.
When he asks ‘who are they?’

What if he’s not asking me to identify the members of the cabal, the exact mechanisms of the control grid humanity is facing. He knows that’s a futile task. A mug’s game. They cannot be defeated on their own terms. The deck is loaded. They’re beaten by not playing their game at all.

Supposing he’s tuned into something more primal, more base, more achievable. More real. He’s being the change. Living the freedom. Diving into the lake and swimming. Not burrowing into the rabbit hole and drowning.
Don’t fight it. Feel it.
The next morning I woke up early. Hungover. I opened the curtains and peered, bleary-eyed, out the window. An otherworldly orange glow.
And there he was.
Swimming in the lake.
Bills. Bills, bills and more bills.

Two punctures in a week. The same wheel. The first, a pothole. They’re a joke. I’m sure you know this. They’re everywhere. They’re seemingly contagious. Like a virus. In fact, perhaps not like a virus. But let’s not go there. At least I can prove potholes exist. Just look at my bloody tyre. The cure? A safe and effective one hundred and seventy quid new one.
Then, three days later, the red exclamation mark from hell appears on the dashboard.
‘Check tyre pressure’

You have got to be taking the piss. Sure enough, not a computer malfunction. A hiss. A nail in the bloody tyre. Fifty-seven miles of potholed tarmac this little wet-behind-the-ears Michelin has covered.
Anyway. Repairable. Thirty notes. Not another One-Seventy. Small wins.

Talking of road repairs, the Council tax went up. Again. Will they fix the potholes? Will they fuck. I’ll tell you what else went up…in fact I won’t…I’m boring you, sorry. Everything went up. Let’s just leave it at that. But unlike that annoying Sixties song, whatever it was, what goes up doesn’t bloody well come down. Ever.
Inflation is 3.1% apparently. My arse.
The no booze week I promised myself started with four cans of Punk IPA Monday. And spiralled downwards.

choices.label: End of the week
opts: Call the council about the potholes. Yes, actually call them. This time.
Cancel something. Direct debits, subscriptions, something. Take back a small corner of control.
Open a beer. You earned it. The bills aren’t going anywhere.

paras.t: Friday night. All six of us sitting down for dinner together. All of us home for the evening. Like the old days. No parties, no football practice. Family time. Roast chicken served with a rich pancetta-tarragon-mushroom-white bean stew rich in tomatoes and stock. Chianti.
The conversation a mix of college work, the latest memes, sport, Love Island, Christmas lists and thoughts on the current news/propaganda/psyops cycle.

I’d been trying to hook the kids into waking up/conspiracy rabbit holes (delete as you see fit) for years, with varying degrees of success. They existed in a comfortable niche between recognising that some (I’d like to think a lot, but some is far more realistic) of what I was educating/preaching/rambling on about (delete as you see fit) was true. In reality, a lot of the warnings that made sense on paper simply weren’t translated to their daily teenage lives. Yet…but you wait…

If I’m honest, naval-gazing and gloom-mongering about faked pandemics, neo-feudal panopticons and supra-governmental hidden layers of global control were probably less fun than gossiping about who’s dating who, the latest VAR outrage or regular online compulsive-shopping-disorder purchases.

We’d managed to keep the kids (kids, ha! Force of habit, two of them are grown men) at the dinner table after the chicken had been plucked clean of meat and the wishbone snapped with the lure of sticky toffee pudding, warming in the oven. They still argue over whose turn it is with the wishbone. I hope they always do.
Amy’s secret recipe condensed milk ice cream was out the freezer softening on the side and a pot of double cream was receiving lusty glances from Sam.

The conversation turned to Amy’s current bête noire, chemtrails. Amy’s older brother, Rupert had been down this conspiracy rabbit hole long before it was even a vaguely acceptable topic in polite society. She’d gone from sceptical but open-minded, to ‘it’s probable that covert weather modification experiments are happening on a small scale, but I’ve got better things to worry about’ to ‘the sky is a blanket of white every day and they want to kill us’.

Amy didn’t do the ‘conspiracy research’ (as the majority of people still perceive it) that I did. Not because she couldn’t, but because it made her sad. Sad that such evil could exist. She buried herself in her books, her yoga, her gardening and her homemaking instead. Every so often (Chianti) the anger burst through her sadness.
“If they’re not trying to kill us, what are they doing then?”
Here it was, the open invitation with a captive audience, to unleash my research, opinions and inner thoughts in a devastating, concise and brutal soliloquy.
‘I don’t know’ was all I could muster, and in a way this was more hard-hitting than thirty minutes of on-the-money truther-riffing.
The kids looked at one another, slightly bewildered.
Dad doesn’t know?

I rattled off a few ideas about what it might be, from ‘mostly harmless, mostly contrails’ at one end of the spectrum, to ‘nano-particulate release seeding the environment for 6G with humans as nodes in a network’ at the other.

But what seemed to really hit home in the eleven minutes before the sticky toffee pudding was piping hot and oozing, was the rather humbling revelation that, for all my podcast and article deep dives, I had no fucking clue what was going on. And that ‘chemtrails’ were front and centre of this uncertainty. I’d researched Stratospheric Aerosol Injection, ice supersaturation, manipulation of the ionosphere and solar geoengineering patents and projects. I knew that weather modification and potential military applications had been on the agenda since the 50’s. I was aware of Operation Popeye. I’d read Elana Freeland. I’d listened to Sabrina Wallace.
The most intellectually honest answer I could give was ‘I don’t know’. That I’d come to realise that I was an active (and probably textbook) victim of every psyop under the sun.
The kids asked a few chemtrail-based questions as they found room for a second portion of pudding, but didn’t stay at the table long after their bowls had had every drop of cream scraped out of them.
‘Put my mind at rest, Simon’ Amy implored as we started on the washing up. ‘They’re not trying to kill us, are they?’

‘Not yet’ was my instinctive but thoroughly unreassuring reply. ‘The only things I can say with a degree of confidence is that the world is being actively transitioned into a new paradigm. They’re hardly making a secret of it. Convid, the tokenisation of bloody forests, eight hundred zillion of global debt, you’ll own nothing and be happy…
Amy had had enough, already. ‘Shall we go and watch Location, Location, Location?’ she asked with a small sigh.
‘Yeah’ I replied. ‘Shall I get another bottle of red?’

choices.label: The washing up is done
opts: Open the second bottle. You’ve earned it. And the conversation’s not over — it’s just moved rooms.
Leave it. She doesn’t want to hear it. And maybe she’s right not to.
You should have said more. You should have said it better. You should have had an answer.

paras.t: My birthday party. Fifty-two today. Just the family. Twelve people. Three generations. One long table booked near the pizza oven in the local brewery taproom — The Gun Brewery. It's Peter's idea. My father-in-law. He insists we do something to celebrate. I'd have been happy to stay at home and cook. A couple of bottles of wine. An early night. Peter is still a social animal. I don't know how he does it, he's nearly ninety for Christ's sake. Still sharp as a tack. He's out for lunch most days with clients. I say clients with a pinch of salt. It's probably twenty minutes of his accounting expertise followed by a long Côtes du Rhône fuelled lunch and a snooze on the train on the way back from London, copy of The Times open on his lap.

Amy drives me there. Kids in the back. They no longer argue over who sits where, but I know Sam gets freaked out if he doesn't sit on the passenger side. A weird superstition he's never explained. We've a taxi home booked for 11 o'clock. A solid four hours of real ale drinking-time ahead.

We walk in through the vast modern glass doorways. Peter is performing his customary meet and greet service at the bar, insisting that everything goes on his tab. He's generous to a fault but he can't not be the accountant — has already checked the beer prices with mild dismay. Jenny is standing next to him, as funky and as beautiful as ever. Blue jeans, Superga trainers and a long bright red furry coat which makes her short white-grey bob look like a cutting edge salon creation rather than graceful aging. She's looking at the beer menu as if it's written in another language. She opts for a white wine, Peter already has a bottle of Côtes du Rhône on the go.

Amy's half-brother Jamie, large gin and tonic in hand, is at the bar too, trying as always to get a word in edgeways past his talkative social butterfly husband Graeme. Graeme, dapper as ever — Zara Man meets East End gangster with a cavalier flamboyance, an intentional slightly overplayed campness and a quiff Rockabilly-era Morrissey could've been modelled on — sips a Pepsi Max. He's the designated driver. As ever. He's not a huge drinker anyway, he appears to get high on theatrical story-telling and gossip alone.

The kids say their hellos, Uncle Jamie hugs the boys and showers 'his princesses' with kisses and flattery. He's lost weight recently. Not that he was overweight, just naturally a big unit. A man who could break a dining chair just by looking at it. Like Peter, Rupert and Jamie are both well over six foot but Rupert has his father's long limbs and lean body and Jamie is more solid. His diet? Fat jabs and gin-fuelled afternoons. He says he's done with big pharma after he suffered an adverse reaction to the Covid safe and effective. But they had him at weight loss without the treadmill.
I'm excited by the prospect of a real beer in a proper pub and focus on the serious work of perusing the drinks list with the boys.

I'm immediately drawn to Thousand Miler — an Old Ale promising raisin, fig and toffee, and at 4.5% a sensible starting point. Sam and George both opt for How's the Serenity — a New England style pale ale — cloudy, rounded, juicy with oodles of tropical fruit and hops. Amy is too polite to go straight to beer ordering and will exchange kisses, hugs and catch-ups whilst secretly craving a drink. I order her a pint of her Gun go-to beer — Scaramanga — extra pale, 3.9% with hints of lemon, grapefruit and mango.

The beers go on Peter's tab. Lots of 'cheers' and 'happy birthdays'. I take a large sip, subconsciously closing my eyes as I swallow my first mouthful. Heavenly. I can even kid myself about the health benefits as Gun Brewery beers are brewed with spring water drawn from deep below the wildflower meadows on their farm. I'll ignore the effects the beer/pizza combo will have on my blood glucose levels.
It is my birthday…

Sam and George head off to join Chloe and Emilia at the table, the youth clustering at one end. They're immediately and instinctively on their phones. I watch their Gen Z interactions, pointing at each other's screens with a background babble of text-speak OMGs and for-reals. Not antisocial I suppose. A new kind of social. Real-time documenting with a live commentary predominantly for themselves. The girls head off for selfies with the pizza oven, then in front of the large silver fermentation tanks of the brewery itself — proudly on display behind huge glass panels. Industrial chic meets Steampunk and rustic charm.
Put your tongues away for those selfies girls, you look like Only Fans cretins

George shows Sam something football-related on his phone — content he's made, or content he's watching — the line between the two is blurring. I overhear something about two million views — George's TikTok creator account went viral a few years ago and he earns a steady stream of near-passive income from it. I'm not convinced how creative it actually is, but it pays for his beers, Dominoes delivery, fuel and new trainers.

Rupert is the last to arrive, tall, slim, ginger-topped with quite a presence for someone so laconic. He's here alone tonight, his wife Cee has been called into work last minute as the other chef (Thai restaurant near Brighton) has called in sick. He's a Côtes du Rhône drinker like his father, but also partial to a lager. He doesn't really do craft ales, he looks at the chalkboard menu above the bar with a hint of disdain (I can almost hear him saying 'wanky' and 'pompous') as he tries to find the least pretentious option.
He orders a Numb Angel lager — wincing at the description —

A bright pale gold Munich Helles style lager, featuring a grain bill of Extra Pale & Munich for just a hint of maltiness. We brew it using a traditional bottom fermenting lager yeast & hop it principally with Czech Saaz, lending it an enticing florality to sit alongside the bread and malt aromas and flavours. A balanced bitterness leads to a refreshing and thirst quenching finish.
I imagine that grain bill really got his goat. He couldn't resist a little smile and an almost inaudible aaah as he took his first sip though.
We're all seated at the table now. Pizzas have been ordered. I keep mine simple — anchovies, black olives, capers.
You should've ordered the American Hot like the boys. What were you thinking not ordering something with pepperoni? You're going to have food envy aren't you? Perhaps we can share? It is my birthday.
Peter asks George and Sam what they've planned for their gap year.

George explains that he's still earning money from TikTok, posting football and music content with enough of his own creative input to prevent the AI moderator from flagging it and removing it for prohibited or copyrighted material. The table half-understands. I can see Peter's accountant brain trying to map it onto a traditional career structure and failing to do so.
Jenny asks 'But what's the actual job?'
'It's the modern version of making a TV programme or writing a book, I guess, but for social media, short-form and fun.'
For the vapid, dopamine-depleted, attention-deficient generation
Jamie asks 'But what happens when everyone's doing it?' Graeme, bluntly: 'Everyone is doing it.'

'What happens when AI is doing it and humans are relegated to simply being attention-farmed and commodified?' I ask, haughtily. I should've bitten my lip really, kept the tone lighter, but the two beer buzz took over.
'AI is already producing loads of content, but it needs the human touch too,' replies George, seemingly choosing to believe this delusional line of thinking.
'What about AI taking all the jobs?' asks Jenny.

I glance over at Rupert. He's biting his tongue. He's an old school conspiracy theorist who was listening to Alex Jones (the original one, not the modern imposter as he'd put it) talking about chemtrails (tracking flights on Flight Tracker and noting the planes he saw with suspicious trails that weren't on it) and warning about carbon credits long before it became trendy in 'resistance communities'. Years ago he'd have been on his high horse, preaching, causing a scene, apoplectic that no one could see what he was seeing. Everyone's a conspiracy theorist now and he seems content to bask in the afterglow of being right rather than saying I told you so.
'AI will take some menial jobs but create loads more,' George replies. 'Let me show you this.' He picks up his phone and scrolls through Instagram. 'Give me a minute…'

'Of course there will still be jobs,' Sam asserts, as if stating it as fact will make it true. 'The Government say they are creating millions of AI jobs,' he continues in normie mode, harnessing his mother's naivety and lack of compulsion to explore alternative takes beyond the headlines.

I can't believe he's falling for this shit. The Government reports don't stand up to any scrutiny at all. The headline figures are reported — AI-related jobs grow from 158,000 in 2024 to 3.9 million by 2035. Sounds enormous. 12% of the UK workforce. But read the actual report and the truth is revealed. It explicitly says it did not investigate the negative effects of AI technologies through the displacement of other occupations. They only modelled the upside. Jokers. And most of the 3.9 million aren't new jobs. They're existing jobs where the person now uses AI tools — a teacher who now uses AI in lesson planning counts. Mental note to chat to the boys about this… not now… don't start preaching Birthday Boy.
'Maybe it'll create more jobs?' Graeme chips in. 'That Nvidia guy seems to think so — tens of millions.'

'Sure, and Techno-Utopians like Musk sell us the dream of Universal High Income and robots wiping our arses on Mars whilst our Neuralink chip is switched to permanent ecstasy mode. I don't believe him either.'
'Why do you have to be so negative about everything Dad?' Emilia, who I assumed wasn't listening as she was buried in her socials, piped up.

'I'm not being negative, just realistic. It's their job to sell you a dream. Huang, the Nvidia guy, is using the past to predict the future. He says every tool expanded what one person can attempt. Which is true. But when one person and his AI can now attempt to do the job of fifty, what happens to the other forty-nine?'
I think she switched off after 'Huang'. I'm terrified for their future. They're happy to tune out. I'd have done the same as a teenager.

'Here it is,' George looks up from his phone. 'Twenty-eight future jobs that AI will create. One — AI Auditor — reviews AI for bias and accuracy. Two — Digital Twin Engineer — builds virtual replicas of public figures.'
'Hold on, these are jobs for humans?' (air quotes) 'AI will do both of those.' I interrupt.

'You're not going to read all twenty-eight now are you?' Amy asks. Well, it was posed as a question but came across more as a command. I suspect she knew I was ready to find a way of debunking every one of them.
'Can you send me the link Georgie?' I ask. If they were the top two jobs I dread to think what twenty-eight is.
'My round,' offers Jamie. 'What are we drinking?' he asks, just as the first of the pizzas arrive.
'Who's having the American Hot?' asks the hipster-waiter.
I want that one
'That's for me,' says Sam with his hand in the air. George ordered the same, but Sam has always let hunger get in the way of courtesy, and George has always been too soft, too kind, too submissive.
'Do you want a slice, Pa?'
'Go on then, I'll swap you.'
He knows.

Rupert has rather sensibly decided not to try and drive home after six pints. He and I are now chatting shit on the sofa with another beer. The kids headed to their rooms as soon as they got jumped out the taxi. Off to read the links I sent them no doubt.

I wish they’d look. Just one of them. A birthday gift. If one of them read it and said - I read about Working Futures. And the footnotes. I can see why you think it’s ridiculous Dad - an economic forecast for 2035, built on data from before the thing it was trying to predict existed.

They won’t read it and I won’t get a response like this as a present. Instead I got a five pack of black Selected Homme T-shirts (great for everyday wear, not too skinny, not too loose, long enough to tuck in but don’t look like a dress if worn untucked, low ‘slub’ design around the neck, 100% organic cotton, wash well. I should work for their marketing team).

Amy made the spare bed up for Rupert, a glass of water and some Alka Seltzer Plus on his bedside table, and headed off to bed herself. Rabbit hole avoidance. I’m sure she’ll manage to read for half an hour, despite the booze.
‘Your Dad was in good form tonight, Rupe. Kind of him to pick up the tab.’
‘Two bottles of red and revelling in his role as the patriarch.’
‘Revelling in being asleep in the car now. Jenny will be cursing him’.
‘Jenny will be worrying about AI taking the jobs. It baffles her, thinks it’s a glorified google that can make pictures of dancing cats’
‘Did you see that post that George was talking about’
‘No, I switched off. I zone out of conspiracy chat with Jamie and Graeme around. I don’t want a repeat of France.’
No one wants a repeat of France - the savage row that nearly broke up the family, I still don’t really know how it escalated
‘That was ten years ago. They’ve come round to your way of thinking now.’

‘Have they? Everyone thought I was mental. They get some of it now, they think I’m slightly less mental. But I’ve never had an apology. No one’s ever said you were right, Rupert. Know what I learned? Most people just don't want to know. Ignorance is bliss. And those that have started to wake up still don't want to do anything.’
‘At least there’s more awareness now. You can’t fight something if you don’t know it exists, well, refuse to accept it might even exist.’
‘I spent fifteen years trying to warn people. Rally the troops. Fight the oppression. Do something. I’ve given up, you know why?’
‘No.’

‘Whatever we do, it doesn't matter. I’ve been right about everything without changing anything. Actually not totally true. I’ve changed myself. Tried to add some doing to the knowing. The reality is, the only thing that will move the dial is the thing that never happens - mass non-compliance. Telling them as a collective to stick their rules up their arse.’
‘Stop paying tax, cut off their funding. Im all in. You first.’

‘Exactly. Tax is the perfect example. Everyone knows the system is rigged. Nobody stops paying tax. Not because they can't articulate why — because individual refusal is theatre. The bailiffs come for you specifically.’
‘What about these guys that withhold tax and put it in an account saying they don’t want to fund illegal wars?’
‘Apparently people do it and get left alone. Fancy trying it?’
‘You first.’
‘Talking of funding, the thing that might fuck them is debt. How much is the world in debt now?’
‘Bear with me…’
I google ‘world debt clock’
‘Over one-hundred-and-ten trillion dollars’ I say in a Dr Evil voice. ‘In fact that’s just government debt, Three-fifty trillion in total.’

‘At some point they’ll need a reset. Covid lockdowns kicked the can down the road for a bit. But there’s only so long they can keep hundred-million-pound notes in The Bank of England vaults to balance the books.’
‘They have hundred-million-pound notes?’

‘Yes, they’re called Titans. The entire monetary system balanced on pieces of paper that might as well have been Post-it notes stuck to the inside of a filing cabinet in Threadneedle Street. And people called me paranoid for keeping cash in the house.’
‘Another beer?’ I ask
‘Go on then. Do you fancy some of this? Homegrown’
Rupert pulls pre-rolled spliff from his pocket.
I haven’t smoked weed in years but I’m a fair few pints in now, so just go with the flow. We head outside to the deck in the rear garden, the temperature must be close to freezing.

‘The thing is, Simon, whichever way you look at it, a new financial system is just around the corner. Digital id, crypto, tokenisation. All baked in. Just depends if they press the button suddenly - a crisis that needs a solution - or just phase it in - boiling the frog.’

‘Even if we knew, Rupe, would it make any difference? The Epstein files proved that knowing changes nothing. Everybody knows. Nothing happens. Feels like they could announce pretty much anything and there’d be a forty-eight hours of social media uproar and then…well nothing. Back to paying the council tax and talking about the unseasonably warm weather.’

‘I spent twenty years trying to identify The Cabal. The Committee of the Three Hundred. The Illuminati. Whatever. I thought you had to identify the enemy to bring them down. Now? Not so sure. I mean, technocracy. It’s not even a conspiracy, is it? Not really. It's just... everyone rowing the same direction because that's where the money is. You don't need a room full of Bond villains. You just need a thousand committees and a profit motive. That’s harder to fight against. And a lot more mundane.’
‘I guess’

I was beginning to feel a bit light-headed. I couldn’t get the image out of my head of dozens of Dr Evils sitting in a boardroom, each stroking a white cat sitting purring on their lap, taking it in turns to utter more and more ludicrous, meaningless sums of money. Eighteen billion, trillion dollars. Nine hundred and ninety-nine billion, zillion dollars.’
‘You OK, Simon?’
‘Yeah, just a bit stoned. And thinking of Dr Evils.’
‘Sitting around a huge table stroking cats?’
‘Yeah. How did you know that?’
‘I was thinking of the same thing.’
We giggle. Then laugh at the fact we’re giggling. Uncontrollably.
‘Shhhh, we’ll wake Amy up’
We compose ourselves. But can’t look at one another.

‘Sometimes I think the Dr Evil characters in real life are offered up to us. Distractions. Pantomime villains like Klaus Schwab. People to boo and hiss at which the real work, the legislation, the preparation is carried out behind the scenes. I try and focus on the documents, the bills they sneak in whilst people are blindsided. It’s harder for someone to call you a conspiracy theorist (he says in baby voice, wiggling his fingers) if you bore them with documents. And I look at the motives of the characters driving the new financial paradigm narrative, who aren’t always in the spotlight.’
‘Narrative? Technocracy you mean?

‘Yes, which goes hand in hand with the transhuman agenda. Some of those guys are nuts. They've actually built a religion. Not metaphorically. Like, with tenets and a tax status - but they don’t want to worship God. They want to be God. Immortality through digital convergence.’

‘There’s that Canadian government PDF, the one about merging biology with tech — did you see that? It was just... on a website. Like a planning application. They said it'll change what it means to be human. Nobody noticed. And those that did just shrugged their shoulders. Hey, that’s cool. Satanic shit, man.’
‘You want Satanic? Read Max More. Wrote an essay praising Lucifer as the first free thinker.’
I start singing. In my head I sound just like Mick. I’m sure I don’t though ’Please allow me to introduce myself…
Rupert sings too. Feels like we’re properly harmonising, but it falls apart when we try and hit the high Whoo-hoos.
Olive and Wilf start barking.
‘They probably think there’s weird mammals in the garden.’
‘Not wrong are they?’
We look at each other, making more Whoo-hoos. We giggle like kids.

I lucked out with having him as a brother-in-law. He’s cool. Seems more at peace with himself than he was ten years ago. Wiser. Calmer. Like his anger has been tamed by growing runner beans and brassica. This is a good thing. I think.
We look at the time.
Nearly three in the morning.
Bedtime.
But what’s puzzling you is the nature of my game. Whoo-hoo.

I’d had a lie in of sorts after my beery, weedy late night. Up at nine, out the house by half-past. At the market an hour later. A slightly pointless meeting at noon which crammed fifteen minutes of content into two hours. Would’ve been better as a Teams call - at least I could’ve turned the camera off and scrolled through X, piping up with the odd comment every now and again to show I was tuned in.

I grabbed a spot of late lunch from the market - a gloriously fragrant Vietnamese pork belly Pho laced with star anise, holy basil and green chilli - and headed off home just as the winter gloom descended.

I got my usual enthusiastic greeting from the dogs - the same one I get whether I’ve been gone for ten minutes or ten hours. An equally warm one from Amy too - not quite as many licks though. She made me a welcome cup of tea whilst I freshened up and got into my tracksuit and slippers. Don’t laugh, I am fifty-two you know.

I sat at the kitchen table and watched Amy load the dishwasher. She had a system. I liked the system but didn’t copy it - which meant I was normally told to leave it to me. The glasses went on the top rack in a specific order that related to size, fragility, and some third variable I’d never been able to identify but suspected was related to emotions.
‘So, you and Rupert?’
‘What about me and Rupert?’
‘You were up until three.’
‘Two-thirty, wasn’t it?’
‘I heard you come to bed at quarter past three.’
I conceded the point by not answering it. The dishwasher tablet went in. Amy pressed the button that started the only cycle she used. Intensive 70 degrees. No Eco mode or Half Load for her.
‘He was on good form.’
‘You mean he brought some of his weed?’
‘I had a few puffs.’
‘I could smell it from the bedroom. I thought you didn’t like smoking anymore?’
‘I don’t really. But I’d had a few beers. No idea how Rupert smokes every day. I’d be fucked.’
‘What did you chat about? You’re the only one he bothers to talk to now about stuff.’
‘Can you blame him?’
‘No. Guess not. He used to love the confrontation, the challenge of proving people wrong. He’s mellowed.’

‘He’s definitely mellowed. He still reads, researches. He comes up with his oblique takes and zany theories. He still cares. But he’s tired. Jaded. I wouldn’t say his fire has gone out, but he’s been down the rabbit hole for decades, and where has it got him?’
‘Into arguments and 3am rabbit holes. Remind you of anyone?’ she asked rhetorically, eyebrows raised.
‘I’m starting to come round to his way of thinking. I was amazed when he didn’t come on the lockdown protests. But I now understand why he didn’t. What difference does it make?’
‘I thought you said it made a huge difference? Showed them how many saw through their bullshit. Made them take a few steps back.’
‘I did think that. And maybe it helped to an extent. But what was achieved in the bigger picture? More people have woken up…and done what exactly?’
‘You’ve always said you can’t fight an enemy that you don’t know exists.’

‘And now people know they exist, we do what? Sign petitions against digital ID? Moan on twitter? Vote our way out of it?’ I sneer condescendingly. ‘These things are set up so that the opposition is part of the design.’
Amy opened the pan drawer and studied the contents in deep thought. ‘Meaning what.’

‘Meaning you sign a petition to stop digital ID, and the petition goes to the people who designed digital ID, and they file it, and the filing is the system working exactly as intended. Your objection is a feature, not a bug. It makes the thing look democratic.’
‘So don’t sign petitions. You know I still do, it can’t hurt, can it? At least it’s doing something.’

‘It’s not about petitions specifically. It’s about the fact that every route — every obvious route — is part of the grid. Voting. Campaigning. Writing to your MP. Sharing articles. Waste of fucking time. All of it.’
‘All of it?’
‘All of the obvious routes, yeah.’
Amy selected a medium saucepan and our largest frying pan. I hadn’t asked what she was cooking yet. ‘So what’s the non-obvious route.’
‘That’s what I’m saying. I don’t know.’
‘So you and my brother sat up until three in the morning working out that you don’t know.’
‘We were working out the shape of the problem. You can’t find a solution if you don’t understand —’
‘Simon. At what point does working out the shape of the problem become the thing you do instead of doing something about the problem.’
‘What’s for dinner?’

There’s the rub. The answer? Possibly ten years ago. Possibly the moment I opened my first browser tab on Building 7 and felt the particular thrill of seeing something other people couldn’t see, which turned out to be more addictive than anything the seeing revealed.
‘Chicken cacciatore.’
‘Need some help?’ I knew she’d say no, this was her dish. But I asked anyway.
‘No, I’ve got it. You’ve had a long day.’ She smiled knowing that I knew she’d say that. ‘So nothing can be done? We’re fucked?’
‘We’re not fucked. And I’m not saying nothing can be done. I’m saying I haven’t found what can be done. Those are different things.’
‘They sound the same.’
‘They’re not the same.’

‘From here they sound the same. From here it sounds like everything is hopeless and everyone is controlled and every institution is captured and nothing any normal person does makes any difference. Which is — I mean, if that’s true, Simon, if that’s actually what you believe, then we might as well just — what? What do we do with that? Just give up? Shall we all just kill ourselves?’
‘No of course…’
‘Because that’s what it sounds like. Every time. It sounds like the world is ending and you’ve read enough articles to know exactly how, and the rest of us are idiots for carrying on.’
‘I’ve never called you an idiot.’

‘Well that’s how you make me feel sometimes. You describe a world where everything is meaningless and hopeless and we’re fucked. You keep telling the children that they’re going to grow up in a digital cage unless they wake up and fight. And now you can’t even explain how to go about fighting.’
A knock at the door.
It’s Kate, our next door neighbour.
‘Sorry to bother you guys. Do you have any Worcester sauce?’
‘Yes, I’m sure we do. Come in. Wine?’
‘I shouldn’t - but, oh, go on then.’
I open a bottle of red. Hair of the dog, fuck it.
