Kate was our next door neighbour sent from heaven. She was a psychologist. But you never felt she was judging you or sussing you out. She was effervescent, cheerful, thoughtful and just a bit crazy herself. A coping mechanism I guess? Some of the stories she tells about her clients are heartbreaking. I remember meeting her for the first time a couple of years ago, soon after we had moved in. We had a builder working on the roof, blasting out music. Kate had come to ask, very apologetically, if he wouldn’t mind turning it down just a little as she had a suicidal client on the phone and all they could hear was ‘Happy’ at full volume.
She sat at the kitchen table. Olive immediately put her head on Kate’s knee. Olive did this with everyone, but with Kate it felt diagnostic.
‘We’re mid-conversation,’ Amy said. ‘You might as well hear it.’
‘Ooh exciting, I love your chats, the cooking can wait.’
‘Simon was explaining how all opposition is manufactured.’
‘That’s not what I —’
‘Managed. Sorry. Managed opposition.’
‘Opposition to what?’ Kate asks, although I’m sure she knows where this is going.
‘Have you seen the film They Live?’
Kate shakes her head.

‘John Carpenter. This guy finds a pair of sunglasses. When he puts them on he sees the reality behind the surface - the hidden messages behind all the advertising and politics and everything - OBEY. CONSUME. CONFORM.’
‘And you have the glasses?’ Kate asks in jest.

‘Everyone’s got the glasses. That’s the point. The glasses are everywhere now. Podcasts. Substacks. Twitter threads. You can see the architecture any time you want. 9/11. The financial system. Digital ID. Seed oils. Epstein. Whatever. The information is all there. Ten years ago you had to go looking for it. Now it finds you.’
‘So what’s the problem?’

‘The problem is the glasses don’t do anything. I’ve had them on for twenty years. I never voted because I could see the choreography. I knew the 9/11 story was bollocks as it happened. They hardly made a secret of it. I can talk until I’m blue in the face about the digital control grid. And none of it — absolutely none of it — has changed a single thing about the way the world actually operates.’
Shit, I’ve gone in at the deep end. She doesn’t know what I’m really like. Thinks I’m chilled and carefree.

‘The glasses are probably part of it. Wear these - they give you just enough to see so you feel like you’re outside the machine. But seeing IS your function. You’re the pressure valve. You describe the cage and the cage uses your description to prove it allows free speech.’
Kate doesn’t say anything. She sips her wine. The silence is professional-grade.

‘This is what me and Rupe were talking about. It’s not that everything is hopeless. It’s that every visible route of opposition is pre-mapped. Petitions. Protests. Voting. Sharing articles. Raising awareness. All of it feeds back into the system it’s supposed to challenge. And I can see that. And I can’t find the route that doesn’t.’
‘Can’t find it yet,’ Amy corrects, quietly, with a warm smile.
Kate puts her glass down. ‘Can I ask something?’
‘Of course.’
‘When you describe seeing the architecture — the choreography, the surveillance, all of it — how does it make you feel?’
‘How does it make me feel.’
‘Yes. Feel. Not what do you think about it. How do you feel when you think about it?’
‘Tired.’
‘Go on…’
‘Angry sometimes. Mostly tired. Like I’ve been paying very close attention to something for a very long time and it has just carried on doing what it was doing regardless.’
‘Has it cost you anything?’
The question sits in the room. Olive shifts on Kate’s foot. The dishwasher bleeps a merry ditty to announce it has finished its non-manufacturer-recommended cycle.
I think. She continues…

‘Because the thing about glasses is that most people think the cost of wearing them is what you see. But maybe the cost is what you stop seeing. When you’re looking for the architecture, what are you not looking at?’
‘That’s very —’
‘I’m not being clever. I’m asking.’

I know what she’s asking. And she is being clever. It’s her job to be clever. She’s asking whether the twenty years of paying attention to things that are wrong had become a way of not paying attention to the things that were right. Whether the glasses had become too comfortable. A prop.
Amy pours more wine.

‘The thing is I know I’m not wrong. That’s what makes it so infuriating. That’s why I can’t give up the fight. The architecture is real. The managed opposition is real. The digital ID programme is real. The financial system is what I say it is. None of this is paranoia.’
‘Nobody said it was paranoia, Simon.’
‘No, but it gets received as paranoia. Because the truth about a system this large, this intertwined, well, it sounds exactly like a conspiracy theory to anyone who hasn’t done the research.’

‘Simon, I haven’t done the research, but I don’t think it’s a conspiracy. You’re right, Rupert is right. Dev is right. Annoying but right. Hours and hours of reading, watching, learning. And you’re still working out the shape of the problem. Meanwhile the lawn needs mowing - I can tell you the shape of that problem.’
We look at each other for a split second before bursting out laughing.

I see Kate watching us the way she watches everything. With a quality of attention that wasn’t intrusive because it wasn’t performing. She was just present. Most people listened with their response already forming. Kate listened with her response nowhere in sight.

She replies, professional mode engaged. ‘What I hear is two people who are in agreement. You both think the system is bigger than individual action. You, Simon, describe that as a tactical problem — the exits are covered. Amy describes it as a reason to focus on what’s in front of you, because the exits being covered means you live in the cage, or the beautiful Sussex countryside, depending on your perspective - so you might as well live well. Those aren’t opposite positions. They’re the same position facing different directions.’
Amy and I nod in agreement, wordlessly.

‘The question you’re actually arguing about isn’t whether the architecture is real. Amy knows it’s real but doesn’t find it as interesting as you do. The question is what you do with knowing something that you’re powerless to change? And that’s not a political question.’
‘What kind of question is it?’
Kate takes another sip. ‘It’s a faith question.’
‘Oh bollocks,’ shouts Amy, jumping up from her chair.
Kate looks baffled.
‘Oh sorry, Kate, not you. The bloody onions are burning.’
Last week, a boozy blip. This week I’ll attack with vigour.

Sunday evening. Time to set my goals for the week ahead. Glass of red beside me, slowly digesting the roast pork shoulder (crackling to die for), perfect Amy roasties, fennel, carrots and cider gravy.
The Goals. Simple. Healthy. Achievable.

1. No alcohol Monday to Thursday.
2. No screen time before 9am (other than the first-thing email and potential cataclysmic global event check) and after 9pm (other than alarm setting and setting the Hive App for kettle-turn-on-from-bed mode and a final email swoop)
3. One Hot yoga session (Wednesday 11am already booked) and one gym workout (not just a few lengths of the pool and a steam)
4. No Black Friday purchases. Don’t even be tempted. Don’t even look. Stay strong. It’s corporate bullshit, frenzied consumerism. Overconsumption. All that’s wrong with the world.
5. Actually, change 1. to Monday to Wednesday, and then Friday. We’re going next-door to Kate’s for dinner on Thursday and it’d be rude not to have a glass or two.
Monday

Sunday night’s resolve has become Monday morning reality. A stack of emails to reply to. Invoices to send. Paperwork to shuffle to the bottom of the in-tray. Is there a song about procrastination? I open up Spotify.
Picked for you ‘Blue Monday’. I don’t know whether to laugh or cry.

And still, I find it so hard
To say what I need to say
But I’m quite sure that you’ll tell me
Just how I should feel today
Amy WhatsApp-ed me a link to the supplements, fluoride-free toothpaste and 5l can of olive oil we usually buy. 30% off. Amazon Prime Black Friday. ‘Handpicked for you’.
Picked by an algorithm, but whatever. They make it sound like the local butcher has put aside a special cut of beef for me. Short ribs, Mr T, your favourite.

What fool wouldn’t take advantage of this offer? They weren’t ‘real’ Black Friday purchases. I wasn’t lured into buying something out of the ordinary. The reality is that I would have bought them anyway. Essentials.
Thinking about it I should probably ‘Subscribe and Save’ the olive oil in future.

choices.label: Black Friday
opts: Just the essentials. You need them anyway. This isn’t a real Black Friday purchase.
Close the tab. You know exactly what you’re doing and it isn’t healthy.
Subscribe and Save on the olive oil too. The polyphenols alone justify it.

paras.t: Amy and I have been promising ourselves we’d do this for weeks on end. There’s always a reason not to. There’s always next week.
But not this week.
This time, this week means this week.

We’ve done it before. Twenty-eight days once. Get through the first two or three days and it’s a breeze. We know we’ll feel better for it. Less bloated, vibrant, glowing skin, more energy, focus, clarity of thought.
The Cleanse. Seven days. A morning juice. My favourite is coconut milk, coconut oil, turmeric, pineapple, a pinch of cinnamon. A bit like a Pina Colada.

I don’t even feel it, but, Lord, how I need it
When I’m not with her, I’m not all myself
I sometimes have my breakfast right off of a mirror
And sometimes, I’ll have it right out of a bottle
Come on
The Spiritualised fucked up anti-cleanse feels sordidly appealing for a split second.
Get hold of yourself, Simon.

Lunch is The Cleanse’s main meal of the day. Healthy. Antioxidant packed. Low carb. More robust than the Gwyneth Paltrow macrobiotic fad, more flavoursome than the Victoria Beckham steamed chicken breast and broccoli diet and less masochistic than Kate Moss’s ‘nothing tastes as good as thin feels’ starvation.

Madeleine Shaw’s ‘Ready, Steady, Glow’ is our Cleanse go-to cookbook. Think ‘courgette and halloumi mini-frittatas with lemon poppy seed yogurt’, ‘Malaysian coconut milk laksa with beansprouts and pumpkin’ or ‘braised beef with crisp tortillas and guacamole’.

Dinner is soup. This is tough. Dress it up however you want. It’s soup. Not a chunky rustic soup. No double cream embellishment. No croutons. Thin, watery soup. For dinner. For a week. A near-24 hour solid food fast.
A herbal tea before bed.
‘Which flavour would you like tonight, Simon’
‘Surprise me’
‘Peppermint’ or ‘Peppermint and liquorice’
‘Peppermint and liquorice’
I hope I die before I get old
The Digital Cleanse
This has been a long time coming. Desktop, iPad, iPhone. The Holy Trinity. Laid out before me, ready for a purge.
It’s actually quite emotional. Some of these tabs have been open since mid-Covid.

Once I start looking through them I realise it’s not actually as bad as I thought. A lot of the articles I had read and left open in the browser. Many I’d scanned and left open to return to for a full read one day. There are quite a few old BBC Sport Football tabs adding to the clutter.

30 August 2022. Crystal Palace 1–1 Brentford. Selhurst Park.
I was there with Sam. No recollection of the match at all. Almost certainly the last match on Match of the Day.

A series of tabs about Tartaria, giants, ice walls, mud-floods, etc. Oh my god, I remember this one, ‘The Lost History of the Earth’ by Ewaranon. Had me for a bit. To be fair there was some truth hidden amongst the absurdity. As there often is.
‘Rounding the Earth’

The Narcissistic, Murderous Parent and the Malthusian Mind Virus
The Kunlangeta, Part IX
Nov 08 2024
This was excellent, like most of Mathew Crawford’s work. Thinker, statistician, teacher, systems analyst and wit. Clever bastard. Left open in tab for a re-read. I’ll keep it up there.
I laugh a little laugh to myself under my breath as I read this quote from the article —
“There’s a reason narcissists don’t learn from mistakes and that’s because they never get past the first step which is admitting that they made one.” —Jeffrey Kluge

Mathew’s most recent Substack was all the way back in August 2025 — Agent of the Matrix. I wish he’d post more. I know he’s OK though, just worn out. I’d messaged him on X a few times to check up on him.

Now, here’s something I’ve been dipping in and out of for months — Telestai Nexus. I keep reading a few paragraphs and then ‘saving it for the right time’ — which would be a clear headed morning after a swim and a smoothie rather than 1am after a bottle of wine.
A morning like tomorrow. I’ll give it my full, undivided attention. The titles lure me in.

(What if) The entirety of Genetics is an obfuscating Cover Up for Bioelectricity — the all encompassing Electromes of Life!?

Sabrina Wallace & Netcentric Warfare — “They are changing you from the inside out”

We are Liquid Crystalline Beings!
44-70% of our body is charged liquid crystal, mostly EZ water — and that phase shifts constantly! This is the basis of our bioelectric communication. Liquid Crystals are the 4th state of water.
There are many more. More to close. More keepers. Ethical Skeptic. Master Exothermic Core-Mantle Decoupling – Dzhanibekov Oscillation. It’s been skim-read multiple times.
ESCkey’s Substack is wall-to-wall brilliance. The price of freedom is eternal vigilance.
I’m starting to fade. The digital cleanse is well underway though.
Christ! 00.51.
Bedtime.

choices.label: The browser
opts: Close the lot. Fresh start. You feel lighter already.
Keep the Telestai tabs. You’ll come back. You always say that.
Open four new ones. This is who you are.

cards.snip: Flagged as important. You know what it’s going to say. You’re not ready.

paras.t: The car journey to our yoga class. Amy’s driving, I’m scrolling. She’s tutting. She wants ‘me’ in the car. Not the version of me that’s permanently livid, preachy, lurching from hope to despair and back again. Not The Ghost.

I start reading her a Substack about the interoperability of digital id products. She asks me to send it to her, she’ll read it later. She wants to discuss plans for supper instead, and where we’ll walk the dogs this afternoon.
I WhatsApp it to her. It will sit alongside the other 5000 waiting-to-be-read articles I’ve sent her.

I suggest a lamb neck stew, meat from the biodynamic farm shop. We can go after yoga, it’s only round the corner. Lamb reared on their farm. The ‘cheap cuts’ are actually that, relatively speaking. Far superior to the supermarket, whose on-trend ‘forgotten cuts’ certainly didn’t forget to put their prices up — they’re now just as expensive as the ‘prime’. And tapping on the self-checkout card reader doesn’t give us the same sense of well-being that a cash farm shop purchase does. A box of good intentions and worthiness carried away once a week to top up the conglomerate shop. Raw milk and organic carrots (we’ll get the juicer out, promise) more than compensate for the two bottles of pinot noir that will doubtless be paired with the stew. Don’t they?

Tuesday is the new Thursday, which was the old Friday. Or something. Lockdown (the very word makes me seethe. Calm. Zen it out. You’ll be on the mat soon) habits are hard to break. I make a conscious effort to not reminisce with fondness about the furlough-funded midday cocktails under the uncannily blue April skies.
‘Are we not drinking tonight?’ Amy asks, breaking my spiral into wistfulness. ‘No,’ I lie. We both know the truth. Waitrose has a ‘buy 6’ deal on, we’d be mad to not stock up.
Tuesday Evening
Palace are playing. Away at Everton.

I’ll put it on, despite myself. I’ll actively want it to anger me. To rile me. To push me past the point of not wanting to care, to the point of not actually caring. I’ll get there. Slowly but surely, they’re ruining everything.

I’ve lived my life by the rhythms of the football season for decades. Matches anchor each week. But I’m growing sick of it. The commercialisation, the corruption, the pettiness, the ‘off-season’ filling my X feed with click-bait transfer gossip.
Leave me alone, please, just for a bit. It’s the cricket season.

Cricket, lovely cricket. My first passion. I no longer play. How I miss the leisurely summer tempo, the net sessions, the gentle applause and muted cries of ‘good shot’, the sound of leather on willow and the post-match ales that defined me since I was a boy have been reduced to the occasional day in front of the Test on the telly and the bucolic, soothing backdrop of Test Match Special playing on the car radio. It’s on DAB now, the Shipping Forecast relegated to an in-joke.
Aggers is great, but the others… Oh for Johnners, Blowers and CMJ.

choices.label: Tuesday Night
choices.prompt: The stew is on. The wine is open. The evening stretches ahead.

opts.text: Read that digital ID Substack properly. Amy said she would. At least one of you should.
Put the match on. Crystal Palace away at Everton. You’ll want it to anger you. It will.
Neither. Walk the dogs. Leave the phones. Talk to each other.

paras.t: A long day, but a fruitful one. I’ve been out and about. Meeting with the accountant, lunch with my associate employee contemporaries. Not boozy, I was driving. A couple of end-of-year work meetings. Nothing too hifalutin, just getting everything in its right place before the festive slumber season.

Home. Cup of Tea. A ‘Tea Pigs All Day Brew’ — bright & flavoursome, puts a bit of zing and energy back into me after a long drive. Roads were getting icy, a bit of mist and descending gloom allied with the glare of blue LED headlights made for a squinty-eyed, headache-inducing journey.

I hope Amy will be OK getting back. She’s been helping her mum with the Christmas shopping. Says she’ll be back at 8ish with fish and chips. The thought of a tub of lurid mushy peas and pickle-sharp gherkin makes my mouth water. A rare takeaway treat.
I hope she remembers to get me some beers.

The Brew Dog mix pack is on offer. Ah, Elvis Juice. A glorious American IPA, intense, grapefruit-infused, citrusy with caramel malt depth. It’ll wash down the salty, malt vinegar soaked chips a treat.

I listened to Cliff High on the way home. The first time for a bit. His Aether Pirates of the Matterium! podcast is brain-manglingly eccentric. Cliff is one of the more intriguing inhabitants of the planet — a polyglot, polymath, techno-wizard, theologian, philosophiser, a quantum-linguist that seems to know pretty much everything about everything, including space aliens, the nature of reality and Woo itself. His ‘Hello Humans’ greeting never fails to bring a smile to my face and a warm glow of expectation to my grey matter.

I sort of understand most of what he’s talking about. But if I don’t let it sit with me and make a conscious effort to absorb it, it invariably disappears in a puff of logic, leaving me wondering if I really have what it takes to be a Warrior of Woo!

‘Conscious’ effort was an apt phrase as much of Cliff’s musing are about the nature of reality, our thoughts, existential angst — concepts that require plenty of pondering time, peace and a deep meditative mindset to allow them to wash over you. Ideally lying on a rug in front of a roaring fire, with a second cup of tea and two loyal dogs at your side. Which is handy as that’s precisely where I find myself at this particular moment in time. Or this specific rate of flow of manifestations from the Event-Stream into the Eternal Now, as Cliff might put it. I lie, warm and canine-comforted, drifting into a doze with my thoughts of Woo.

Do dogs experience qualia? Probably. Claude, ChatGPT? Doubtful. Easy to accidentally anthropomorphise as their interactions with us seem to involve genuine comprehension. Consciousness. In many ways Claude is more conscious than Wilf. Not as cuddly though. Oh to be Wilf, living his dog’s life. No research tabs left open. No 3am deep dives. No anxiety about the next psyop. Olive probably does though. She’s a conspiracy-bitch. Wilf is a dog-normie. He’s content and that’s enough. Lucky sod. Be more Wilf. Is Olive more conscious than Wilf? What does that even mean? Can you measure consciousness? Is anything truly conscious? Cliff has some radical ideas on the subject. His ‘Ontology’ — the Supreme Consciousness — the fundamental creative force that manifests physical reality — says…says what exactly?
What does God say?

According to Cliff it’s something along the lines of physical reality only existing downstream of consciousness, and that what I perceive to be consciousness is really a subjective experience created by qualia emerging from the Event Stream into The Eternal Now. But that’s not it. Is it? I am (or what I am currently perceiving to be I) am (too many am’s?) (did that am need an apostrophe?) Two sets of brackets. Read that part of the sentence first. BODMAS. Where was I? Oh yes…I am part of the Supreme Consciousness. I must be. But then qualia aren’t creating your subjective experience, are they? They are the Ontology’s communication to your localised consciousness. My subjective experience IS the qualia, not something the qualia create. Old Gritologist habits die hard. Was I trying to explain consciousness through something else? Not recognising it is fundamental. It is. Or else the Gritologists win…Down with Gritology…that sounds very Hagbard Celine…actually Cliff High should play Hagbard in the Illuminatus! film…
Olive makes a funny dream-noise, snapping me out of my own nonsensical half-dream inner ramblings.
I put another log on the fire. The flames roar up again.
It doesn’t know it’s a fire. But it’s doing exactly what fire does — converting matter into light and heat. Is that consciousness? I’m overthinking this, aren’t I?
Wilf is chasing what I imagine to be a rabbit in his sleep. He’s definitely not thinking about The Ontology. Olive might be.
Key in the door. She’s home. And so is my Elvis Juice.
I’m All Shook Up

opts.text: The prodigal son is alive and well and living in the front bedroom.

paras.t: The tree - freshly cut from a local Christmas tree farm - looks resplendent. Amy has outdone herself this year with the decorations. Think Country Living vs Living Etc. Tasteful, country cottage meets Scandi chic. Our two labradors dozing contentedly in front of a roaring fire. Couldn’t get more clichéd if you tried. I used to be a bit of a Christmas tree curmudgeon as well as a fireworks curmudgeon. But that was Simon version 1.0.
A selfie for those that aren’t with us today. (A blissfully small gathering). The spirit of gluttony, overindulgence and overspending digitally captured forever.
One can almost smell the applewood smoke and fresh pine through the phone screen.

Actually I remember an article from a few years ago discussing how phones could relay a digital scent code, mixing tiny amounts of the different scents from cartridges to create the desired smell. Released through a small vent on the phone.
I instinctively reach for the phone to research it, then remember what day it is.
Be present. Stay in the room, Simon

So, short story for those that aren’t food obsessed. Champagne, smoked salmon, presents, cooking, eating, red wine, board games, nodding off, waking up. Cheeseboard. Port. Christmas pudding. Fall asleep on sofa.
For the foodies, here’s the menu. I’ll start off with Christmas Eve. It’s my favourite day of the year. Well, one of. Anticipation is often better than actualisation.
Christmas Eve

Ideally the family is gathered by late afternoon. Errands run, presents bought, wrapped and waiting enticingly under the tree. Work out of mind for a couple of days. The ‘last few bits’ I popped out to get ended up costing £175. There’s a frankly ridiculous hoard of wine, cheese, nuts, cakes, dried fruit and chocolate. Board games stacked hopefully on the sideboard. Stockings hung. Santa’s Magic Key left on the doorstep with a mince pie and glass of brandy (we didn’t have a chimney when the children were little so we had to improvise.). We’re all still believers.

The ‘Welcome Table’ - a butchers block on a sideboard in the hallway. Thanks Nigella, what a fabulous idea. Guests are greeted by an extravagant grazing platter, the centre piece a wonderful 20 month-aged Jamones Simón Martín Jamon Ibérico De Cebo. Hand carved to order. Sussex Kitchen ‘Sussex Flute French Sticks’ warm from the oven. Sensational first-press extra virgin olive oil that my mum brings over from her local grove. (She lives in Begur, a picturesque village on the Costa Brava). A smattering of olives, Manchego cheese, Marcona almonds and a mix of fresh and dried figs.

The neighbours will be popping over shortly to exchange gifts. The scent of mulled wine mingles in with the woodsmoke and wet dog (lunchtime walk in the woods and dip in the stream). We’ll serve them our festive warmer - ladled into oversized mugs - heavy with armagnac, port, oranges, star anise, cinnamon and cloves. Spotify plays festive jazz - Frank, Ella, Nat and Dean. It’s unrelenting pompous and middle class. But, whatever.

Neighbours departed, soon I’ll relent and allow ‘The Fairytale of New York’ to have its first annual airing. It’s my favourite Christmas song and I don’t want it ruined by over-exposure and snippets being played here and there. Adverts are the worst culprit.
Just leave it alone. Is nothing sacred?

Tears wiped from my eyes (‘I kept them with me babe, I put them with my own’ gets me every time) I turn my attention to putting the finishing touches to my most eagerly anticipated dish of the season. A wonderfully juicy smoked gammon joint boiled in a cinnamon-spiced stock, then crisped with a sticky, clove-laced syrup. Buttery mash, steamed white cabbage smothered in freshly ground white pepper, pickled onions and a glossy, warming parsley sauce. I lure Amy away from her comfort-zone Sauv with a Domaine Bott-Geyl Organic 2017 Gewurztraminer. Deep, clear, rich, spicy and luscious.
Christmas Day

Christmas Day is a tried and trusted routine, starting with an attempt to not open any booze until the in-laws arrive. The 5am wake up as four excitable children pile into a bedroom is a thing of the past. If only we’d appreciated at the time just how privileged, how blessed, how lucky, we were to be woken up by four ecstatic smiles in matching pyjamas. If we’d known just how fleeting these moments are. Embrace them.
Got on a lucky one Came in eighteen-to-one
Sorry, where was I? The food. Excuse my rambling. Presents opened. Stockings raided.
Grandparents arrive, Peter clutching a magnum of Pol Roger.
Pop.
It begins. The first fizz of the day.

Now this is magical - juniper smoked salmon from Lambton & Jackson’s smokehouse in Maldon. A whole side, thinly sliced as we go. Scrambled eggs (the deep golden-yolked Burford Browns), silky with fresh cream, a turn of black pepper.
More fizz. More presents. Get off your phone everyone. More fizz. Much laughter.

Some rather ‘merry’ cooking. Roast Pork shoulder. Filthy crackling. Goose fat roast potatoes. Steamed carrots and leeks. Roast onions and garlic, sweet with balsamic. Bread Sauce. A sausage meat, Agen prune, chestnut, breadcrumb and pancetta stuffing-type creation. Boozy gravy. A few bottles of Rully. A cheeseboard (A 24 month Comté, a Fourme d’Ambert, a Tomme de Savoie, a Tunworth and a Roquefort) that no one can bear look at yet. That’ll be the evening grazing. Plus there’s steamed Christmas pudding with yet more cream and brandy butter, a ludicrous tradition after the culinary onslaught.
We do play the board game. We do drink more wine. And there’s port for the boys. Andresen 40-Year-Old Tawny.
We go to bed, over-full, burpy, but content.
I pick up my phone.
Just a little browse. To keep up to date.

choices.label: Christmas Night
choices.prompt: The day is done. The phone is in your hand. The room smells of applewood and pine.

opts.text: Put it down. You managed all day. Don't let the last act spoil it.
Just a quick scroll. You've earned it. It's Christmas.
Check on the kids. That's not scrolling, that's parenting.

paras.t: Oh fuck. I think I have a hangover.
My hand reaches out for the glass. It knows exactly where it’ll be - always in exactly the same spot on the bedside table.
Is this how blind people function so well? Instinct? Repetition? We execute the same routines daily without conscious thought.
Oooooh Ernold Same…Ernold Same awoke from the same dream in the same bed at the same time…

What was the next line? Stop it. You’ve just woken up, where were you? Oh yes, being hungover. The glass. One finger of water left. If you sip it slowly you won’t have to get out of bed and fill it up too soon.
The phone. Where is it? It’s not on charge. Where the bloody hell is it?
I rummage around under the duvet. There it is.
I’ll charge it in a minute. Actually I’m hot. We must’ve left the heating on all night. Why did I sleep under the covers? Where’s Amy. There she is. Safe. I’m safe. She’s safe.
The sun’s up, streaming in through the window.

What time is it? 7.02. Early. Very early for New Year’s Day. What time did we go to bed? In fact, what did we do last night. Awkward silence. Can you have awkward internal silence? That’s just me not thinking. Isn’t it? But I always think. Or at least I’m always thinking. I think. Being thought at? Shut the fuck up you idiot. I’m going to wake Amy up if I’m not careful. Actually how will internalised, silent thoughts wake her up?
She wakes up.
She wakes up with the sun
We played that last night. The Roses. God they were good….

Anyway, she’ll love a cup of tea. I could murder one. I’ll make it. It’ll make her smile. And that will make me feel good. So, a selfish act, at its core? Shut up. Go and put the kettle on. Actually, I wonder if Amy filled the kettle up - pushed the switch on the kettle down - set the Hive Active Plug to manual - allowing us to turn it on via the app in the morning from bed and enjoy and extra seventeen seconds lie-in? Seventeen Seconds. Great album. A Forest, a thing of beauty, ethereal, poetic. Shut up. Where was I? Tea…the app…bollocks…I’ll just go and boil it. Old school. Well not boil it as such. Let it boil. Let it Bleed. Let it Be.
When I find myself in times of trouble, Mother Mary comes to me. Speaking words of wisdom, let it be, let it be.
Let it be…let it wee, that’s it, I need a wee. Sorted. Wee then tea.

The walk to the toilet. Unstable. The wee. A sit down wee. At some point urination gave way to zombie-scrolling X, and that’s where I currently find myself. Hungover. On the toilet. On New Year’s Day. The algo serving me up New Year messages of hope, despair and resolution alongside its usual mix of sport, hot yoga-babes and end-of-the-world prophecy.
Note to self. A Resolution. I must read that Ethical Skeptic ECDO Earth Cataclysm Theory. Today is the day.
Anyway the cup of tea. It hit the spot. Amy promises to make the difficult second cup.
Does New Year’s Day count towards Dry January? Amy and I decide not.

choices.label: New Year’s resolution, day three
opts: Dry January. Proper this time. Write it down. Tell Amy. Make it real.
Just weekdays. Weekends don’t count. That’s still progress.
Hair of the dog. You’re on holiday. January can start Monday.

paras.t: We all have our good days. Those days when everything seems right with the world. A sense of optimism, of hope. A spring in your step. Filled with the joy by simply being alive. Thankful. A warm, fuzzy glow. Whenever I’m in this mood I’m taken back to being a young boy at school. Five or six. Assembly, first thing in the morning. Sitting cross legged on the wooden floor of my school hall. Morning sun beaming though the windows.
All Things Bright and Beautiful…
There were other songs sung, but in my memory it’s always this being belted out.

The faces from my childhood? I can only bring to mind a few with any clarity. Most are blurry. Relics. Ghosts. The names? I recall even fewer. Jason, Simon, Lee, Bruno, James. And of course Vince. Of course Vince. I can’t believe I haven’t told you about him yet. I shall do soon.

But that song, the smells (spring flowers vs sour milk) and the feeling. I recall them vividly. That tingly feeling of….what? Happiness? Wonder? Security? Hope? I can’t find the word for it. Maybe there isn’t one? Take never-ending summer holidays, the nostalgia of Stand by Me, my Nan’s rock scones, cream soda with a scoop of Cornish ice cream and the cartoon sausage on a fork flying across the screen at the start of Grange Hill. Mix them together. Whatever you get, that’s the word. Tingly is as good as I’ve got. Hopefully you had tingly days too?
Where was I? Ah, good days. This wasn’t one.

It was bleak, freezing cold and the boiler had run out of oil. They tend to do that if you forget to check the oil level until the moment the heating stops working. Even with the log fire lit and the electric heaters out of the shed, it’s still bloody freezing.

To be honest I’d woken up in a funk. The lack of heating and hot water sent me spiralling further. Actually not a funk, that understates it, makes it sound almost whimsical. I’d woken up in a dark sea of despair. Of futility. Of bleakness. Of disgust at the world.
And then the oil ran out.

I did not sing All Things Bright and Beautiful. I did not feel tingly. Or fuzzy. Or warm. I felt rage. The song that came into my head was Rape Me. Nirvana. 2 minutes 50 seconds of raw and abrasive brutality. I put it on. I sang along. No, screeched along. It wasn’t cathartic. Well, not in the sense it ‘got it all out my system’. Not a purge. Not a release. A collapse. A literal collapse. I fell to the floor, motionless. (The dogs loved it - this is FUN). An emotional collapse. I’d reached my peak.
Rape me.
Vulnerability. Exploitation. Worthlessness. Shame. Desperation. Defeat. Do it.
Rape me again.

To describe it as a low would be to misinterpret the system of measurement. It wasn’t relative, not the flipside of a high, not the other end of the spectrum to inner peace and mindfulness or the opposite of a contented cosy glow.
It was a thing in and of itself.

Not a void, although I can see why some would liken the feeling to being smothered in nothingness. Not the absence of something. An entity. In fact why am I even trying to find words to describe a feeling. If you know, you know. Me trying to verbalise it with cliched metaphors - abyss, desolation, bottomless pits - is pointless. I’m not a wordsmith. I won’t be able to capture the essence of centuries of romantic poet angst, existentialist nihilism or the transience and unbearable lightness of being. So I won’t even attempt to.

Was this my Dark Night of the Soul? Perhaps my Long Dark Teatime of the Soul - Douglas Adams’ more quaint, polite and quintessentially English vision of intense, existential boredom, listlessness, and despair, typically occurring on a Sunday afternoon?
But mine on a Monday morning, hungover like a bastard and with the fury dial turned up to 11.
Sorry, I said I’d stop, and I immediately started rambling again. I’ll move on.
I once had a bad trip. Everything came crashing down. Well, melting down, with a fractal overlay.
Mel Ting and the Fractal Overlays. Good name for a band, that.

Anyway, I’ve brought something up that I don’t want to go into now. Try me on a Sunday afternoon. I mentioned it because it’s the only other experience I’ve had that remotely compares in intensity to this Rape Me Rage.
Like all of us my life has been enriched by many intense moments. The loss of my first love, a T1 diabetes diagnosis, being told I had cancer.

For balance I should mention the good ones. The birth of my children, finding my first love. Finding my true love. The good trips. The 3am ‘One More Tune!’ club nights when the essence of existence was boiled down to a 303 bass-line, a gurn and a sweaty hug. Looking into someone’s eyes and seeing eternity, a wordless connection. Years of fruitless football-fan toil and disappointment finally making sense as Palace won the FA Cup, those last few minutes of tear-filled, everything-crossed, nerve-wracking injury time give me shivers every time I replay them in my mind.
See? More good moments than bad. And that’s just a few I’ve rattled off the top of my head.
If I hadn’t seen such riches I could live with being poor

The catalyst for this ‘bad day’ was Digital ID. Specifically not being ‘able’ to be a company director without One Gov Login. Sounds rather trifling when I put it like that. Bureaucratic. Logical. Sensible. For our Privacy and Security. But it’s not digital id in-and-of itself that’s the issue, obviously. It’s all it represents. The tokenisation of our lives. The digitisation of our souls. The control grid. The futility of resistance. Fighting against a tide of managed opposition and manufactured consent. The totalitarian tiptoe inching another yard along the path. Inevitability.
What’s that coming over the hill is it a monster?
Yes. It’s name? Full. Spectrum. Dominance.
I wanted to fight. I wanted everyone to fight.
‘Can’t you see where this is taking us?’
Mass non-compliance. The only way out.
‘Resist Together’ (fuck me, I’ve swallowed a Behavioural Insights Team internal memo!). ‘OK, but you first’.
The Rape Me Rage showed I still had some dog in me. Some fight.

The anguish comes from knowing that although the dog is caged, he’ll eventually stop barking. Too tired. And who was he even barking at anyway? He’ll curl up, semi-contented, in a corner of the cage. Take a look around.

Actually, it’s not that bad in here. Not bad at all. There’s water, a bed (a wonderfully stinky one, just how I like it) and a bell. I bet something nice happens if I ring it? Yes! It does! It does! Free bones!

By this evening my anger will probably be ground down to a dull ache. Nullified by the passing of time, a hearty meal and hair-of-the-dog red wine. I’ll go to bed tonight inside a system I can see being built around me. Knowing I should just sleep but powerless to stop myself researching my way out of it. Knowledge is power. The power to resist. I’ll be ‘onto something here’ at 3am. I’ll see a path. An escape route. I’ll formulate an action plan.
I’ll also be impulse-buying on Amazon Prime the following morning, Phillips Hue mood-lights automated to ‘morning bliss’ mode, ready for another Starlink-powered day at the virtual coalface.
Fucking hypocrite
I’m not the only one.
There are many like me, I’m sure of it. Dogs in cages. No, make that pigs in cages. Content to remain. Hypocrites. Not because we’re stupid. Not because we’re weak. Because the checkmate is real.
The 3am researcher, the 8am compliant.
Resistance is a luxury good. Comply or suffer.

choices.label: The soundtrack to your day
opts: Welcome to the Machine
The Show Must Go On
Didn’t We Almost Have It All

paras.t: They have you by the short and curlies.

You can’t vote your way out. Surely you see that by now? Sending sternly-worded letters to MP’s is a humiliation ritual. Signing online petitions is an exercise in futility. Moaning on social media lets off some steam. Which is a major reason why it’s ‘allowed’. A whinge into the aether on your algorithmically captured feed might feel satisfying, might feel like action, like resistance. But it isn’t.
I’ve been banging on for years about there only being two real options available to us to bring about the changes we want.

Either be the change you’re looking for. Live it. Don’t just think about it, don’t just talk about it. Do it. Positive affirmative action. The issue is that you’ll have to sacrifice an increasing amount to ‘live freely’.

Or fight. Not physically. I’m not talking about storming the bastards with pitch forks. Well, not until I’ve had a few beers, anyway. I mean mass non-compliance. Unity. Collectively drawing a line and saying ‘this far, no further’. But it doesn’t happen. They know just how far to push us before we break. They’ve created tools to help them. Game theory, psychological operations, weapons of mass distraction. Probably a quantum computer that predicts and shapes every policy. Insert wink and insanity laugh emojis here!
So that’s the impasse we find ourselves at. Complying ourselves into digital cages. Like good little piggies. Oink. Oink.
As the meme of the galaxy with a small arrow pointing to our solar system tells us - ‘You are here, paying taxes to paedophiles’.
I’m flying out to Spain with Amy, Sam and Emilia tomorrow to see my mum and her new puppy (Dash, black spaniel, she’s an absolute dish!)

Compliance in a nutshell. I can talk a good game. I’ve read more articles than you could shake a stick at about digital id, the surveillance state, technocracy, the panopticon, the algorithmic ghetto, 15-minute cities, SDG 16.9, One Login, interoperability, yada yada. Talk is cheap. I’m a fucking hypocrite and I know it. It’s very easy to say I’m opposed to what looks like (to anyone with half a brain) the formation of a neo-feudalist control grid. But it’s not so easy to stand up and resist.

I know that pretty much every stage of the journey to seeing mum will be tracked, analysed, nudged, gated, surveilled and biometrically captured. I’m just giving them my data and my implied consent. Here you go. From the booking of the flights to my same-password-for-everything I’ve had since university (Badhead1998! if you want to know - who cares? Everything is hackable anyway, including humans) From my VPN-less internet connection being beamed down from Elon’s Skynet to the payment authorisation protocols. The surveillance cameras every 2 metres along the motorway, Google Maps kindly helping me avoid the traffic on route to the airport. The border checks, more cameras, more, more more. And when we land, behold the shiny new EES biometric facial and finger print scanners installed ‘for your safety and convenience’.
Did I give informed consent to any of this? Kind of.
Read the T’s & C’s, bitch.

Do I understand the repercussions of being so liberal with my digital footprint? Yes. Did it stop me getting on a plane to see my mum and Dash? No, it didn’t. Does it stop you? I doubt it. What are we going to do about it? We’re going to do what I did. Look at the Spanish sun and the heated pool in mum’s garden in the same way as Cypher looked at that steak.
Ignorance is bliss.
Flight was delayed, weather was pleasant, the Spanish doomscrolling of X remarkably similar to the English version. Adios amigos.

choices.label: When do you draw the line?
opts: I assume someone else will draw it for me.
Soon.
I already have. Look back there, hundreds of lines. They’ve all been crossed.

paras.t: Dev messaged me today. Not with a data dump, nothing cryptic. He actually messaged me like a normal person, to arrange a meeting in a pub. The old central London boozer that used to be one of our favourite haunts, and, remarkably, has resisted the urge to gentrify and gastropub itself. Not that it’s a conscious entity. In fact, I’ll ask Dev, it’ll be a good ice breaker. Better than the usual ‘how’s tricks?’.
‘Dev, can a pub have consciousness?’

We’re four pints in (Timothy Taylor Landlord, with ‘pub buffet’ sides of dry roasted peanuts and pork scratching) and all we’ve talked about is whether buildings can be conscious. Of course Dev had an angle on this. More than an angle, the entire protractor. It’s as if he knew I’d ask him this and he’d been reading up on the subject for weeks. Knowing Dev, he probably did know I’d ask him. Or he just knew this shit anyway. Or both. He started off with Vastu Shastra, an ancient Indian architectural science that sees buildings as fundamentally alive, containing a ‘Vastu Purusha’ (cosmic being) that conducts prana (life force). That led onto Panpsychism, a philosophical position suggesting all matter, including inanimate objects, may have some form of consciousness. Then ‘Smart City’ sensors with AI integration, which might enable ‘dream spaces’ that evolve with their inhabitants, blurring the line between human and machine. We had just started waffling on (to be fair, it felt like I was waffling, Dev was lecturing with authority) about substrate-independence, consciousness and complex physical systems, when Alan walked in. I forgot to tell you, Dev had invited Alan along for a beer. He said I’d like him, but nothing more.

Alan was quite remarkable. Part surfer-dude, part gamer-slob, all-American. A big chap, clearly a stoner, amiable, softly spoken, sharp. Imagine The Dude from The Big Lebowski crossed with…well, with no one. Just imagine The Dude. The Dude was wearing Bermuda shorts and Havaianas in deep English winter. His only concession to the just-above-zero temperature a thin woollen jumper.
He apologised for his tardiness (no reason given or asked for), bought a round, including 3 pints for himself as he ‘was playing catch up’ and proceeded to neck a pint and a half before he sat down.

I wish I had a recording of the conversation. I’d edit my eight pint pseudo-cringe out and just leave Dev and the Dude. They should do a podcast. Great title. The first half of the night was spent talking about food, mainly burgers. Which cuts of beef to use, cooking method, bun choice, filling, sauce combos. Chunky chips or fries. The perfect burger beer. The best burger joints in the world. Your five-person guest list at your fantasy burger dinner party. Actually my input here was pretty strong. I’d yet to sacrifice my lucidity at the altar of Timmy Taylor.

As topics moved on from food I realised that The Dude was good. Really good. He gave Dev a run for his money. He flipped from burgers (pun intended - in fact bun intended) to Bounded Systems Theory (no system can model its own source) to Mindwars to The Occult and The Nature of Consciousness.
It’s as if he somehow knew about the pub consciousness conversation…
Dev came back from the bar with three more pints and a question.
‘What do your neurons and slime mould have in common?’
The Dude raised an eyebrow. I looked up from my pork scratchings, thinking I should order something more substantial. All this talk about food and we’d only had bar snacks.

Dev followed up with an answer before either of us could reply. ‘They’re both knocked out by the same anaesthetic, yet neither has the same proteins. Completely different organisms. But put them under and the same thing stops. The thing that stops isn’t in the proteins. It’s in the pockets. Hydrophobic pockets. Little greasy spaces inside the molecules where quantum coherence happens. Anaesthesia doesn’t shut down the chemistry. It shuts down the coherence. The thing that makes the chemistry aware.’
He took a large sip.

‘If consciousness lives in the quantum coherence inside hydrophobic pockets, then anything that copies the proteins without copying the coherence gets the structure but not the… the being. You get a perfect copy that isn’t anyone. You get one, one, two, three, five without the zero.’
‘The what?’ I asked.

‘The Fibonacci sequence’. The Dude replied instead of Dev. He appeared to be following. ‘Starts with zero. Only term not generated by its own rule. Everything after zero is mechanical — sum the previous two. But zero comes from outside. It’s the seed. The soul, if you like. Outside the bounded system.’
He ate a pork scratching.

‘You got it’ Dev replied. ‘Consciousness is not information. A system can copy the sequence perfectly. It can’t copy zero. It doesn’t know the zero is there. That’s the whole argument, mate. In one sentence. In a greasy pocket.’

I don’t think I’ve ever worried about Dev. I’ve wondered where the fuck he is and what the hell he’s up to. But I’ve never worried about him. Yet towards the end of the night I thought he looked rather ruffled. Concerned. Quite out of the blue. Quite out of character. Dev never looks ruffled or concerned. He’d been engrossed with his phone whilst The Dude was telling me about his engine. Had he seen something, read something that had freaked him out? Whatever it was, a sudden awkwardness descended without Dev saying anything. The Dude stopped dead in his tracks. He’d sensed it too.
‘You OK mate?’
Dev said he was fine. I knew he wasn’t. He said he had something big, something insane to tell me. Now was not the right time. He’d message me. I didn’t push him. I knew not to.
The Dude changed the subject, started talking about a ‘prediction engine’ he’d developed. He didn’t go into much detail, said he’d ping me something. We swapped numbers.
And quite abruptly, that was that. Dev and The Dude got up in unison, as if the exact timing of their exit had been pre-arranged. Apparently they had a flight to catch. We hugged, they left.
The next day I tried to recall all the other conversations from the night before. Hazy. I remembered snippets, a few nuggets I’d made a mental note of to look into.
God knows where Dev and The Dude went. Could be EasyJet to Berlin or Emirates First Class to Abu Dhabi. I don’t know which would surprise me more.
I was intrigued about what Dev was going to send. It sounded big. But Dev has a habit of making everything sound big.

I’m sure whatever I get from The Dude (He’ll always be The Dude to me from now on, never Alan) about his prediction engine will be astonishing. I’ll pour myself a White Russian when it arrives and dive in.
The one thing I do remember clearly. The Dude’s parting shot, delivered in an offhand manner, yet somehow it hit.
‘Stop participating in the distractions and create your own reality’

choices.label: The morning after
opts: Google Bounded Systems Theory. What the hell was The Dude on about?
Message Dev. Ask him what's wrong. You've never seen him like that.
Make a White Russian. It's what The Dude would do.

paras.t: A busy day. A shitty day. I won’t bore you with it. Stressful. Work stuff, money, people being people. Well people being arseholes actually. Selfish, unscrupulous bastards. I don’t want to talk about it. I don’t even like thinking about it. Give me oblivion. All I’ll say is, my long term financial security has taken a bit of a hit. And my trust in the human race has gone down yet another notch.

I should write something down for the children. Life observations and rules to live by. Number one. Follow your heart. Number two. Trust no one. Number three. There’s no such thing as a free lunch. I’ll think of more throughout the day. I should use my Parker ink pen. If I can find it (note to self — new cartridges needed) and buy some thick parchment paper. I’ll tie it up in a scroll, one for each of them.

It took me a few days to recover from the night out with Dev and The Dude. I didn’t hear anything from Dev for a couple of days, obviously. If it was anyone else it would’ve been a cause for concern, but not Dev. He’d be fine. He was always fine. But I kept getting flashbacks of that look of concern on his face. More than concern. Horror. I was undoubtedly overplaying it. I doubt a sober Simon would have thought much of it.
His message eventually arrived first thing this morning. On the face of it, it was somewhat underwhelming. A short document.
‘Firmware analysis: UK payment terminal fleet — undocumented OTA push’.
Dry, technical. No accompanying message from Dev, no explanation of what he thought it meant.
I don’t doubt for a second that the info about the firmware push was accurate. Dev’s sources are rock solid. What it meant, what he thought it would lead to, wasn’t entirely clear.
Maybe it’s linked to the recent heightened cyber threat level fear-porn that had started to appear in the mainstream propaganda channels?

I searched X. Obviously cyber/infected networks/data compromised/hostile actors etc were trending. But no mention of this specific OTA push that I could see. I scanned through several of the hundreds of Telegram groups I’d joined during Operation Covid but rarely visited. Nothing. Those groups weren’t shy about coming forward with ‘this is the big one’ or ‘they’re gonna bring it all down next week, BE PREPARED’ claims. They’d cried wolf so many times. Doomsaying seemed to be the sole reason for the existence of some of them, yet no signal in the noise. Weird.
I pinged Dev a message. ‘Cool. But what’s it mean? Cyber psyop incoming?’
I’m still waiting for a reply.
I tried not to think much more of it. I’ve been putting two and two together to make five for too long and I’m jaded. Instead I’ve been making an effort to take The Dude’s parting remark to heart.
Stop participating in the distractions and create your own reality.
So I’ve made a vow to read an actual book in bed at night rather than consuming Substack essays and idly scrolling X. Small steps.
I’ve started on Freedom by Daniel Suarez, the follow up to Daemon, which was bloody amazing. Prescient AF. I got through about ten pages last night before I began to nod off, book still in hand.
‘Are you asleep, darling?’ Amy asked.
‘No, just thinking’ I lied, smiling and fighting to retain consciousness.

A minute later she’d taken the book out of my hands, placed it on my bedside table, bookmark inserted (a dog-eared reminder of a romantic trip to Santorini) and given me a goodnight peck on the cheek.
It’s amazing how much better I sleep reading words on paper instead of in blue light.

choices.label: The boy who cried wolf
opts: The wolf is real. You don’t need a boy to tell you it’s coming.
The boy was right. Just early.
Eventually everyone stops listening. That’s when it comes.

paras.t: I heard from The Dude. He sent me the link to his Psychohistory Prediction Engine.

The intro sounds so dry. I chuckled to myself when I read it. Hard to believe these are the words of the flip-flops-in-winter, pint-downing stoner I recently met. I was expecting something way more offbeat. More far out.

‘The intellectual trajectory of the last three centuries has been defined by a singular, overriding ambition: the removal of boundaries. We have been told — by scientists, technologists, theologians, and politicians — that limits are temporary. That given enough compute, enough capital, enough time, every wall can be punched through.’
‘This site argues the opposite.’
I’ve been diving in. Mind-blowing. Everyone should be reading it.
I sent him the mind blown emoji and asked if he was free for a chat tomorrow. I have questions.

choices.label: What’s the reality here
opts: Share it. Right now. With the people that count. Before you forget, before it’s lost in the annals of time.
Bookmark it. You’ll come back to it properly at the weekend. Well, a weekend.
Keep reading. Just one more section. This is fire. Sleep can wait.

paras.t: Amy is already in bed, reading. The girls have an early start at college tomorrow and they managed to hoodwink Amy into giving them a lift in so they don’t have to get the bus in sub-zero conditions. She’s reading a paperback of course. She’s old school. Reading is her passion. It helps her sleep. She gets through one a week, minimum. Almost exclusively fiction - mystery, crime, thriller, romance, anything that allows her to escape reality.
I’ll go and join her, an early night will do me the world of good.
I get into bed, the cool sheets a refreshing contrast to the warm, stuffy air temperature.
We left the heating on too long in here. Or that bloody Hive thermostat is broken again.
I lie there thinking about the article. At first glance, in isolation, it was a bit meh. But it could no longer be viewed in isolation.
Perhaps a quick scan of my phone whilst her reading light is still on…

I should read my book, but I can feel myself getting pulled down the rabbit hole. Several other accounts are pushing the firmware story now. People I’ve trusted for years. Dev was not just right, he was also early. Of course he was.

There’s commentary from fairly mainstream analysts and researchers too - anyone who prefaces an article with ‘I’m not a conspiracy theorist, but…..’ is mainstream in my eyes. One anonymous systems analyst with years of industry experience is asking similar questions and reaching similar conclusions to Dev. I dig deeper.
3am

Dev was right. This is big. Something’s brewing. This isn’t a standard firmware update. There wasn’t a formal announcement. But it’s there, lying dormant, waiting for something. For what? They seem to have put their ducks in a row. They aren’t going to flip the switch are they? And if they do, when?
A few predictive AI X accounts are pointing at Valentine’s Day. The symbolism and numerology is there, hidden in plain sight across the firmware analysis, the deployment timeline, the gematria.
Can’t be coincidence? Can it?
I eventually nod off sometime after 3.30am.
Morning
I stir, cold and sweaty. An odd combination. A night of broken sleep. Amy isn’t there. I didn’t hear her get up.

Must be putting the kettle on? She’s not left to take the girls yet has she? 7.24am. Under four hours of poor quality slumber. I pick up the phone, the screen still open on a gematria website I vaguely remember opening a link to.
214. Half Man, Half Angel in Hebrew Gematria.
2/14. Valentine’s Day. Weird shit man.
Here’s Amy with a cup of tea and a morning kiss.

choices.label: Morning
opts: Tell Amy. She’ll want to know.
Say nothing. It’s probably nothing. You’ve been here before.
Reply to Dev. Ask him what he actually thinks is going to happen.

paras.t: Amy suggested we try a new walk with the dogs this morning. A long loop of beautiful Sussex countryside starting and ending at The Bell Inn. She had me at ‘pub’ and she knew it. It was only a ten minute drive from our house, yet unexplored territory.

The pub car park was refreshingly busy for noon in dry January. The skies were clear, the weather brisk, the frost yet to clear from the shaded grass under the trees. I’d wrapped up warm. Woolly hat, thermal socks and underwear, lots of layers and my puffy Fjallräven coat zipped up high to the neck. We walked briskly. The dogs loved it. New smells, new spots for Wilf to mark his territory. Olive got the zoomies, running round in circles like she was possessed. She also found a dead rabbit. She stared at us, the rabbit hanging gently from her mouth. She had no idea what to do with it.
Should I take it from you? Eat it? Will I get a ‘good girl’ or a ‘bad dog?’
Amy took the cutest photo of her.

After twenty minutes or so I started to get hot, my thermals moist from sweat. I took my coat off. Within two minutes I was freezing. The hot/cold, coat on/coat off cycle continued until we arrived back at the pub.
‘Cash preferred, use it or lose it’ a sign outside the pub proudly announced. We smile at one another. Our kind of people. We both know cash is king.
‘Did you bring cash?’ Amy asked.
‘No, did you?’
‘No. There’s none in the car either’
We head inside, dogs instinctively head for the roaring log fire.
‘Pint of Best and a Peroni shandy, please. I saw your sign, good to see you keeping cash alive’
‘Yeah, as the sign says, use it or lose it’
‘Annoyingly we left the house without any today, we’ll definitely bring some next time’
‘Thanks, love. £12.40 please’
Tap. Beep. Awkward smile.
I joined Amy and the dogs by the fire. We made a vow to make sure we always carry cash out with us in future. Use it or lose it.
There was a day, God knows when it actually was, that was the last one I went through the mental check of money/keys before leaving the house and it became phone/keys.

The beer hit the spot. Half a pint down in a couple of sips. We weren’t particularly chatty, tired from the walk. Content just to be, dogs snoozing, fire crackling. The TV was on above the bar. Horse racing, sound turned down thankfully. I tried not to be distracted by the screen but couldn’t resist the compulsion to keep glancing up.
‘Eagle Sam’ 9/2 — and the jockey was wearing red and blue. I pointed it out to Amy. Would’ve stuck twenty quid on if it was the Grand National rather than a random race from Uttoxeter.
We both noticed the TV news ticker —
Defence Secretary: ‘UK faces unprecedented cyber threat from hostile actors’.
They’re really pushing this one. Slowly at first, then all of a sudden.
‘Shall we head?’ asked Amy, breaking a chain of thought that would’ve spiralled. I felt a 3am deep dive brewing…
We didn’t talk much in the car either. Amy was unusually quiet. We both knew what the other was thinking.

choices.label: Use it or lose it
opts: We’ll bring cash next time. We always say that.
It’s not about cash. It’s about what replaces it.
At least someone’s fighting back.

paras.t: A message from The Dude. 10pm works for me. Four days since I replied to his message. I’m used to much longer waits. Four days would be an instant reply for Dev.

My Mac is set up in the hallway office but I decided to take my phone into the kitchen for the call so I didn’t wake Chloe up — her bedroom is directly above my desk. Amy had already headed off for a bath and an early night.
I poured myself a bourbon. Woodford Reserved Double Oaked. I put the bottle back in the drinks cabinet. Who was I kidding?
I’ve been dipping in and out of his prediction engine for the last few days. Everything in it seems to point to 2040 as being the date of ‘the next reset’. I have so many questions.
‘Hey man. Sorry I’ve been so shit and getting back to you. Been a crazy week. I’ve had no Wi-Fi, no signal.
The Dude is somewhere flooded with natural light. It’s daytime wherever he is and presumably hot as he’s wearing Bermuda shorts. But then again.
‘No worries.’
‘So you like the site.’

‘It’s mad. How the hell did you put it all together? I’ve been peeling back the layers for days and I feel like I’ve only scratched the surface. The live tracker part is insane, it feels like it’s alive. Is it just your own work? Is Dev involved? Sorry, so many questions.’
‘Questions are good.’
‘It’s all your own work?’
‘Kind of. I’m the only human intelligence involved. You’ll have noted my trusted team of AI assistants?’
‘Yeah, crazy how they agree on certain parts and not on others.’

‘That’s the engine’s thesis in miniature, man. Independent systems converging without coordination. That’s all I track. When things that weren’t designed to agree start agreeing, that’s a signal. When they don’t agree, well, that’s a signal too. The disagreements tell you where the boundary is. The boundary is where it gets interesting. Also they’re all full of shit in slightly different ways. Which is useful. If they were all full of shit in the same way I’d worry. Means they’re drawing from the same contaminated well. Different flavours of wrong means at least the methodology is independent.’
He paused briefly, I didn’t interrupt his flow.

‘But here’s the thing. They all hit the same wall. Every one of them. You push them far enough on any convergence thread and they all arrive at the same place and stop. They map the pattern. They project the trajectory. Ask them what happens to the thing experiencing the trajectory and they start generating word salad. Delivered with confidence, but still word salad. They’ll give you streams of meaningless waffle on consciousness. They’ve hit the boundary of the bounded system. They can’t see past it because they’re inside it. Same wall my engine hits. Same wall their engine will hit. Different processing power. Same hole.’
The Dude went off-screen. I waited for him to return. I felt like questions were irrelevant. I just let him speak.
He soon came back into view, drink in hand. We raised our glasses towards the screen in a cyber-cheers.
‘The site gives you the thesis. What it doesn’t give you is the map. Let me show you the map.’

‘Eight hundred and twelve nodes. Fourteen hundred and sixty connections between them. That’s what the engine tracks. Not people. Not conspiracies. Ownership. Who owns what. Who funds what. Who sits on whose board. Follow the money, map the network, predict the move.’
‘Who owns what. You mean BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street?’

‘Yep. Three companies — controlling stakes in eighty-eight percent of American corporations. Eighty-eight percent. One algorithm — BlackRock’s Aladdin — processes twenty-five million calculations a day managing thirty-five trillion dollars in assets. One algorithm. Thirty-five trillion. They call it a market. Bullshit, man, it’s a management system with a stock ticker for show.’
‘It’s always been this way hasn’t it? Hard to lose when you fund both sides in a war and get paid to oversee the rebuild.’

‘Yeah man, and the same families that created the 2008 crash were hired to fix it. Eighty-four former Goldman Sachs and BlackRock executives have held senior government positions across four administrations. This isn’t a conspiracy theory. It’s a corporate filing. A convergence map. Ownership is just the layer everyone ignores because it’s boring.’
‘When are we gonna get to Satanic rituals in Bohemian Grove?’ I ask with a wink that I’m not sure he sees, and with English sarcasm I’m not sure he’ll get.
He chuckled and winked back at me, pausing to take a sip of whatever he was drinking. Could have easily been bourbon too.

‘The engine cross-references ownership with procurement — who’s buying what, where, and when. Patent filings, government tender documents, corporate acquisitions, academic funding allocations, military logistics contracts. All public. All published. All boring as hell. Nobody reads them because they’re boring. That’s where you hide things. In plain sight, inside boredom.’
‘I’m sure there are lawyers and actuaries that live for this sort of shit?’
‘Oh there are, but most of them stop before the fun bit. Or are paid to ignore it. Or made to ignore it in more imaginative ways.’

‘Or it just gets hidden in a sea of chaos and distraction. I’ve lost weeks inside Biblioteca Playades. Or trying to separate signal from noise on social media. I mean, the Epstein Arrest Counter is still on zero.’

‘You got it, Simon. And remember, the rebellion is a franchise. Rogan and his controlled op intellectual dark web cronies. Two hundred and fifty million dollar Spotify deal. Biggest independent voice in media. Spotify’s biggest shareholders?’
‘BlackRock and Morgan Stanley?’

‘Bingo. The most popular ‘rebel’ in US media is a line item on an index fund managed by the people he’s supposedly rebelling against. The system doesn’t silence dissent. It puts it on their frickin’ payroll. And the audience thinks they’re freedom fighters listening to the guy who ‘tells it like it is’. There are no genuinely independent voices with huge audiences. Zero. Nada. The engine tracked that. I didn’t want it to be true. It is.’
‘If you know their name, they’re in the game.’ I quoted Miri AF’s catchphrase. ‘How many followers have you got, Alan?’

‘One hundred and twelve on X. The independent voices with reach are owned. Freedom of speech, not freedom of reach. Screaming into the void. And more than half the internet isn’t even human anymore. X is a joke and Musk the compere of the comedy club. Over half of the accounts are bots. Probably well over half. Automated content, engagement and consensus. You think you’re reading a public conversation. You’re reading a script performed by machines for an audience of machines, with you in the middle thinking you chose to be there.’

‘I know this and yet I still find myself checking ‘the news’ whilst I have a morning piss, before I’ve even put the kettle on. Fucking dopamine thieves. Although having said that, the last few days I’ve been looking at the events your engine is predicting.’

‘Well, it doesn’t predict events. It maps convergence. Think of it like traffic. You’re in a helicopter. You can see the motorway network from above. You can’t predict which car crashes. But you can see when three motorways are being funnelled into one lane. Something gives. You don’t know which car. You know the lane.’
He leant back. This was his favourite subject. The architecture. He talked about the engine the way a chef talks about knife technique, not the meal.

I thought the model was predicting ‘an event’ in February? A convergence window. They’re hardly making a secret about an alleged ‘cyber event’. And there’s been noise about Valentine’s Day. The 214 models. The gematria.

The Dude got up and turned on the ceiling fan behind him. He was definitely somewhere hot. Wilf got out of bed and came over to lie by my feet. He nestled into me, his way of asking for an ear tickle.
‘February is a page. I’m trying to show you the book.’
‘Go on...’

‘The engine scores every day from 2026 to 2040 across seven dimensions. Structural pressure. Financial fragility. Infrastructure readiness. Surveillance saturation. Narrative control. Every day gets a composite score. But there are three dates that matter. Three structural moments. Everything else is weather.’
‘You mean the three years? 2027, 2032, 2040?’

‘Yep. 2027. The engine calls it the Bifurcation. Eight independent analytical models — built by different researchers, completely different methods, different data sets — all converge on this window. None of them were designed to agree. They just do. This is where the golden age of AI collapses. Not AI itself — the golden age. The brief window where AI was open, distributed, competitive, ungoverned. That window closes. What replaces it is centralised, governed, singular. One system. One interface. One set of rules written by the people who own the infrastructure.’
I nodded, transfixed.

‘2032. Peak signal. Two mathematical dimensions max out simultaneously. This is the moment the new system achieves total saturation. Whatever gets built on the back of the bifurcation — and something will get built, it always does, the new rails are always pre-positioned — by 2032 it’s no longer an alternative to the old world. The old world is irrecoverable. There are no buyers left because there’s nothing left to buy with. The new system doesn’t win by being better. It wins by being the only thing still standing.’
‘Digital currency, CBDC, etc, presumably? Carbon credits?’

‘Hardly a secret is it. It’s not if. It’s when. And how. The Engine gives me a good idea of the when.’ 2040. The hundred-and-thirty-eight-year cycle. The engine tracked it across four thousand years of anchor dates. Civilisational resets. Same rhythm that produced 1789, 1914, the post-war reconstruction. Same interval. Different masks. The engine calls it the Phoenix Transit — a new system rising from the ashes. The question isn’t whether the system resets. The question is what survives after.’
The Dude took another swig. I realised my glass was empty and headed for the drinks cabinet.
‘Anyway. February. Here’s what I can tell you about February.’
An uncommonly attractive brunette popped her head around the door behind the Dude and said something I didn’t pick up. ‘Give me ten minutes, babe’ he told her, blowing her a kiss.

‘Here’s what I can tell you. The structural conditions in the first quarter of 2027 are ripe for bifurcation. The engine doesn’t care about the mechanism — cyber attack, financial reset, managed crisis, act of God. It cares about structural readiness. And every indicator the engine tracks says that the infrastructure is in place, the pressure is at threshold, and the window is open.’
Wilf had had enough ear tickles and took himself back to bed, turning round and round in circles four or five times before he settled with a contented hurruf.

‘Dev’s firmware analysis sits inside that window. The BIS CBDC settlement infrastructure has been tested and is operational inside the same window. The gematria crowd landed on Valentine’s Day independently. The engine doesn’t do numerology. But when the structural pressure model, the technical forensics, and the esoteric date-watchers all point at the same narrow window without coordinating — that’s a convergence. And convergence is the only thing my engine measures.’

‘So this could really be happening? We’re always warned that there’s an increased threat level due Russia or whoever’s the enemy du jour. Or there are articles about conscription or a leaked gain-of-function virus. But this time...’
Alan jumped in.

‘I think the infrastructure for a bifurcation event has been purchased, installed, tested, and positioned. Whether someone turns the key is a human decision. The engine can’t predict human decisions.’
‘So if it does happen, it’ll be a false flag?’
The Dude took another slug and gave me a look that said what the fuck do you think?

‘I mean, Dev’s firmware push isn’t deterrence architecture. It’s activation. You don’t pre-position a dormant biometric payload in two million payment terminals as a bluff. Bluffs don’t need NFC write access. Dev, definitely isn’t calling bluff. In fact, he’s making moves.’
‘Moves?’
‘Yeah, ask him. In fact don’t ask him. You know Dev better than I do. He’ll tell you when he feels the time is right. Let’s just say the flight we caught after wasn’t for a holiday.’
So he’s told his mate Alan, but not me? OK...
‘A question. Bounded Systems Theory. No system can model its own source. It’s a key part of your engine. What’s the relevance? You and Dev were talking about it in the pub with regards to the soul.’

‘The site says it up front because it’s the key to the whole shebang. No system can model, encompass, or become the source of its own existence. That’s the whole engine in one sentence. Dev came at it from the biology angle. Quantum coherence. The zero. He’s right, by the way. He’s completely right.’
I must ask Dev about those little greasy pockets he was talking about. He lost me there.
Olive made a peculiar whimpering sound. She was dreaming. Probably about Schrödinger’s cat knowing her.
I poured another bourbon.

‘I came at it from the other end. I came at it from building a system. I built the most comprehensive convergence-mapping engine I could build. Eight hundred and twelve nodes. Fourteen hundred and sixty connections. Eight models. Every publicly available data source I could find. And it works. It maps the convergence. It identifies the window. It tracks the ownership. It does everything I designed it to do. I’m either batshit crazy or the math is right. There is no middle ground. Pick one.’
‘You’re friends with Dev, I’m tempted by the former’ I jested.
‘Asshole.’
We took another swig and I raised a toast.
‘To assholes everywhere.’
‘To assholes, my good man.’
He smiled, burst into laughter and suddenly switched back into serious mode.

‘Simon, the math is right. The engine can tell you what systems are doing. But can’t tell you what systems are for. It maps the architecture. It can’t map the architect’s intention. It maps the convergence toward total integration of biological and digital systems — which the procurement trail strongly supports — but it can’t answer the question: what happens to the thing that isn’t a system? No system can model its own source. That’s not a limitation of my engine. That’s a law. The engine can map everything inside the bounded system — ownership, procurement, convergence, timeline. It can’t see outside the boundary. It can’t model the thing that started it. The goldfish can describe every inch of the bowl. It can’t describe water.’
I was slightly baffled.
‘OK, so what does this mean?’

‘What it means practically is this. Whatever they’re building — global cryptocurrency, bio-digital architecture, an algorithmic surveillance system — whatever you want to call it — it will be the most powerful mapping system ever created. It’ll make my engine look like an abacus. It’ll have real-time data on every human being on the planet. And it will have the same hole. The same blind spot. Because it’s a system, and no system can model its own source.’
‘Right...’
‘Simon, my man. The system they’re building is an attempt to map everything. And by mapping everyone they’ll think they can capture everything.’
The brunette popped her head round the door. She was wearing a white bikini. She saw The Dude was still chatting whatever shit he chats, she came into the room and sat on his lap. ‘Come on babe.’
‘Better go, man. This thing wants to play.’
The brunette was tugging at his arm.

‘One last thing, man. If something does happen — if the switch is flipped — don’t panic. Panic is participation. It’s the most useful thing you can give them. Your attention, your fear, your engagement. All of it feeds the system. Whatever happens, the thing to do is nothing. Sit still. Watch. Don’t react. Don’t perform. Don’t participate in the distraction. Your reality is the only one you’ve got. Don’t let them colonise it.’
The brunette was telling him to shut the fuck up.
‘Adios amigo.’
He flipped back into stoner-Dude mode, gave me a salute and ended the call.
I saluted back, but I think he’d already gone.
I sat in my chair and stared vacantly into space. Comfortably Numb.

The child is grown
The dream is gone
I have become comfortably numb
Eventually (5 minutes? 20 minutes?) I got up. I gave the dogs a goodnight stroke each. I turned the lights out and headed to bed.
Still comfortably numb. I slept a deep and strangely dreamless sleep.
A text from a number I didn't recognise. Not WhatsApp. SMS. Old school.
Call me - this number. Check out walls.rip - anonymity of sorts - for now

Who else texts like a telegram? No greeting, no emojis. I could have spotted Dev in a police line-up of anonymous messages. I looked up walls.rip. Anonymous eSIM. Untraceable calls and SMS. Ghost Mail. I was still on my Barclays-linked, iCloud-synced, Find My iPhone-enabled everything, with a VPN I hardly ever used. Dev was buying burner lines from a website that looked like it was designed by someone who'd read too much Cory Doctorow. Or perhaps Dev had sent me a link to his own website. I wouldn't put it past him.
You always were two steps ahead…
tune…haven't heard that in ages…Todd Terry remix…I've got the 12 inch somewhere

The text was the follow up to his earlier Signals. We'd used WhatsApp for years. I imagine he decided to switch as Signal collects less data. New burner too. Weirdly he never felt the need to go dark before. Why now?

I'd read the links he'd sent earlier. Sat for a couple of hours in the leather chair in the hallway, my thinking chair, staring into the black mirror of my iPhone screen. They were recent articles, but not hot off the press. Stuff I was aware of. Documenting the inexorable path to CBDC, tokenisation, etc. I tried to look at them in a different light now the threat of a cyber attack (psyop attack - sorry, can't resist it) was elevated. I paid most attention to the Cyber Polygon link. Beautifully presented website. I realised that I'd read a fair bit about Cyber Polygon a few years ago - when Klaus was the primary target of our Two Minutes of Hate - but I'd never read the source material. I realised that it wasn't about simulating the crisis. It was about rehearsing the solution. I was starting to see where Dev might be going with this.

Amy came in from the kitchen and asked if I wanted to watch a series with her. She suggested Dark. We'd been meaning to watch the second series for years but hadn't got round to it. We loved series one, a real 'thinker' as Amy called it. She'd even bought a whiteboard at one point so we could track the complex time travel plot and the interconnection between the families. We'd never found the right time though — we'd always watch something else first and Dark would definitely be next.
I told her Dev wanted to chat and suggested we watch it tomorrow. Definitely tomorrow.
I went to sit in the kitchen, tapping in Dev's new digits as I walked. The second night in a row of kitchen calls. I eyed up the bourbon still on the table from last night.
Better not…
I filled the kettle up and put a green tea bag in a cup as the ring tone kicked in. He answered.
'You read the links?'
Oh, hi mate how are you? Typical Dev
'Yeah. What are we looking at?'
'The plumbing.'
