'Helpful, Dev.'
'The firmware isn't the thing. The firmware is the last thing. Well the last thing before the thing. I've been looking at this wrong for weeks.'
'Looking at what wrong?'

'I thought the OTA push was the story. Dormant payload, biometric templates, NFC write access, BIS callback. That's what I sent you. That's what everyone's focused on. What does the payload do. When does it activate. Wrong questions.'
'What's the right question?'
'What's it for? What system does it serve? The firmware doesn't create anything. It connects to something. Something that's already built.'
'Go on.'

I could tell he was going to do that thing he does. The thing where he's been thinking about something for weeks and it comes out fully formed, like he's reading from a document written in his head. I've known him nearly forty years and I still can't tell if he rehearses this or if it's just how his brain works.

'The Digital Pound consultation closed six months ago. The BIS settled mBridge cross-border in 2024. Project Agorá — the Bank of England joined a tokenisation pilot with the BIS and six other central banks. All public. All published. All boring as fuck. Read by how many people outside the banking and conspiracy industries? Not many, I can assure you. Sure they'll have been referenced in articles about The Great Reset and The Great Taking. They're happy if ‘research communities’ are paralysed by fear and doubt, overwhelmed by chaos, locked in permanent debate instead of formulating action plans. Knowledge is only power if it's acted upon, otherwise it's a burden. I carried the burden for years.'
'So what's the action plan, buddy? I'm all ears.'
'I'll get to that. Be patient.'
'Pardon me for breathing, Your Worship.'

'Forgiven. Listen. The payment terminals have NFC write access to biometric templates. The ARC authentication layer is already in the airports. The Bank of England has run offline payment experiments with defence contractors. Thales. IDEMIA. The same firms that make military-grade secure elements and biometric passports. For a payment system that doesn't exist yet. Why does a currency that hasn't been built need to work when the internet's down? The rails are built Simon. Every piece of track is laid. Someone just hasn't turned the key yet.'
I poured the water over my herbal teabag. Rock and fucking roll.
'So the firmware is the key?'
'The firmware is the ignition. The car was built years ago.'
'The car? Where are we going?'
'If my calculations are correct, when this baby hits 88 miles per hour... you're gonna see some serious shit.'
'OK, Doc. So we're going the future?'

I could hear him grinning through the phone. The Back to the Future quotes were a language we'd spoken since the late eighties. My mum took us to see it at the Odeon in Streatham. We went to Pizza Hut afterwards. We loved constructing mountainous salads from the salad bar smothered in bacon bits. Well, 'bacon' bits. We've been talking to each other in film quotes for thirty odd years. Geeks.

'Basically, yeah. When they decide to juice the flux capacitor with 1.21 gigawatts, everything flips. Not gradually. Simultaneously. Every terminal that's received the firmware goes live. Hello digital pound. Biometrics at the ready. No more pilots, no consultations, no more bloody 500 page bloody PDFs. No transition.'
'Great Scott! They're gonna flip the switch overnight.'
'If I was a betting man…'
'If?'

'OK, I'll rephrase it. If someone would take the bet. The switch will be flipped. New system activated. How long it takes to transition to it and how we get there are the unknowns. But think. What'll happen if the lights go out. Emergency legislation. Think Coronavirus Act. Knocked up in four days. 340 pages. Look at the Civil Contingencies Act — a senior Minister can make law without Parliament if communications are disrupted. The Banking Act lets the Treasury restructure the financial system by statutory instrument. The digital pound consultation says personal data is protected ‘except for law enforcement under limited circumstances prescribed in law.’ Prescribed in law, Simon. Who writes the law when the internet's down?'

'So the cyber attack will be a false flag. No fucking prizes for guessing that. But I'd assumed it'd just be another psyop. A nothing-burger. Tomorrow's chip paper. Another inch or two of totalitarian tiptoe.'
'Whether someone flips the switch deliberately or not is kind of irrelevant. The new system is ready. The old one isn't coming back. The transition will be handled.'
'This is going to happen in the next few weeks? The Dude's engine suggests it might be in February. The numerology is more precise. Valentine's Day.'

'Simon, the convergence is real. Alan has detected a pattern. I've seen it from the technical side. The firmware is in place. No one's cracked the encryption on the time-lock on the activation window yet. Someone probably will, but if they do, what does it change? No one's going to stop it. The only question is whether they give us Soma or send us to Room 101.'
'Meaning?'

'Meaning when the old system goes down, they either starve you into compliance or feed you into it. The Great Taking or a, um, The Great Giving. Same difference in the long run. The ledger doesn't give two fucks if you're terrified or grateful. And neither do they. They just want the path of least resistance until everyone's on it.'
'Gun to the head, which way you going?'

'1984 has been memed to death. People are expecting that approach. That's David Rogers Webb's Great Taking. I think they're smarter than he gives them credit for. Starving people riot. Comfortable people comply. They don't need to take your stuff. They need to put your stuff on their ledger. If I'm running this I don't take your house. I tokenise it and tell you the mortgage is gone. You'd fucking thank me. At first.'
Tokenise the house? No mortgage? Don't mind if I do. Obviously a trap. But a seductive one…
'It's a trap,' I replied, with a passable Admiral Ackbar impersonation.

'No such thing as a free lunch. Fink calls it ‘repotting.’ Horticultural language for total asset capture. And we're the plants, mate. I'm not saying they'll do this in one hit. But they might. A debt jubilee. It's been discussed. Every debt instrument that exists gets retired when the system is reset. The debt doesn't disappear — it gets absorbed into the infrastructure, like pouring water into concrete. You can't see it anymore, but it's holding up the whole building. And now you're living in a building you don't control. They do. Of course. Whoever controls the ledger controls the rules.'

'Sounds plausible. But it won't happen overnight, surely? They'll need some chaos before the order. What should I do to survive the chaos? Stock up? Buy some gold coins? Surely a bit of extra foldin' won't hurt?'
'Maybe in the short term. But this isn't a cash problem. And it sure as hell won't have a cash solution. It's ledger migration, one way or another.'
'Surely I should get in some food? Stuff with a shelf life. I bet you've shipped in some foie gras and a few cases of La Tâche?'

'Don't take the piss. If I'm right about the managed part of this event they'll make sure everyone's fed. Give or take. They need everyone fed. Hungry people riot. Comfortable people comply. Anyway, you threw half the stuff you bought during Operation Covid away. If you really want to stock up, stock up on understanding what the fuck is happening. That's the only thing that might matter.'
'Easy for you to say.'
'Yeah. It is.'
'Meaning?'
'I'm walking the walk. I sold the London pad. Miami too. Alan's there now crossing the T's for me. I've got something up north. Off grid. 10 acres. Water from a well. Ey Up, lad.'
'You could bottle the water, Del Boy. Peckham Spring 2.0.'
'Well, Cumbrian Spring.'
'You're serious, aren't you?'
'Exchanged last week. I've got somewhere even more remote lined up too. I'm keeping that one under my hat for now.'
Obviously rural England is not enough for the international man of mystery.
'Fucking hell Dev.'

'I didn't sell because of the firmware. I sold because of everything before it. The firmware just confirmed what we already knew, mate. Fuck their Smart Cities. I probably can't hide, but I can sure as hell run.'
'When were you going to tell me?'
'Right now.'
'You're moving to Cumbria?'
'Already started. The flight after the pub wasn't a holiday.'
'I know. The Dude told me.'
'Of course he did.'
'So what is it? Survivalist compound? Tinfoil yurt?'
'Working farmstead. Solar. Battery. Land. Not a bunker. A life. Just not on their ledger.'
'Must be nice to have options.'
'Don't do that.'
'Do what Dev?'
'The money thing. It helps, sure. But I'd be doing this anyway.'
'I would too Dev. In an ideal world, of course. But I've got the kids, a mortgage, a business that needs me in Sussex, Amy's mum and dad need her, my dad…'
'I know.'
'You don't have any of that.'
'No. I don't. And that makes my choice easier. But you still have a choice, mate. The path of least resistance isn't always the one to walk down.'
'Yeah, I know you're right, but….'
'If you put your mind to it, you can accomplish anything.'
'OK, let's stop with the Back to the Future quotes.'
'Fuck off, we'll never stop. Why don't you come up? When I'm sorted. Bring whiskey.'
'If society hasn't collapsed by then.'
'If it has, we'll need whiskey. Listen mate. I've got to go. Think about it.'
'I will.'
'I know you'll think about it. I meant do it. Stop talking the talk.'
'Night Dev. Be careful up there.'
'Always am.'
'No you're not.'
'Love you bud.'
'You too fella.'

He actually did it. He's actually doing it. I've been reading about exit strategies and he's been executing one. I've been sharing articles about the Great Taking and he's been selling property. I've been sounding the alarm at dinner parties and he's been buying a farmstead. The gap between us isn't knowledge. It's never been knowledge. He'd do it from a tent. That's the thing. The farmstead will make it comfortable, but it doesn't make it happen. Dev would do it from a tent.
He said I still have a choice. I do. I know I do. But I also know what I'll choose. I'll choose this kitchen. I'll choose Amazon Prime. Watching Dark on Netflix. I'll choose compliance.
I rinsed the glass. I checked my blood sugar. 6.2, flat arrow. Steady. Stable. Comfortable.
Fitter, healthier and more productive…
I turned out the lights. I went to bed. Amy was asleep. I lay there and listened to her breathing. I tried not to think about ledgers and farmsteads and the distance between knowing and doing.
Concerned but powerless.

I've been down this path before. Amy and I packed the garage with dried pasta, tinned tomatoes, cannellini beans and bottled water during Convid. Withdrew a couple of grand in cash from the bank. Bought some physical gold and silver coins. We were told The Great Reset was coming. The New World Order. They were going to pull the plug. A false flag, a psyop. A global war, perhaps a cyber attack, another mutation that 'targeted the vaccinated’ or another novel virus - The Big One this time - something that, to paraphrase Bill Gates, will really get our attention.

We ended up taking half of the emergency food to the local tip as it had ‘expired’. Amy gets a bit squeamish about ‘best before’ dates. We’d gone from conversations about whether we would have to eat our dogs (I would, if it was a matter of life and death, Amy couldn’t and wouldn’t) if the global food chain collapsed, to dumping perfectly good food in landfill in the space of three years.

I’d researched what would really be needed if the lights went out and it was more than a few weeks worth of ragu bolognese, linguine and bottled water. The Prepper guides 'essentials' lists would keep Rambo going for years. Weaponry, first aid, water purification systems. The works.

I know Dev says not to worry about stocking up. But he's not right about everything. A few extra supplies can't hurt. Just in case. People I knew and trusted were recommending stocking up. Others were going further than just a recommendation, they were insistent that we all needed Armageddon supplies. I noted that many of the extreme alarmists had curated links to survival supplies websites (paid per click-through no doubt) and ‘A word from our sponsor’ (my favourite was the wonderfully-named ‘Sgt Prepper Shop’ interludes during their video posts. It was open season for shills.
So a few cases of tinned food. Some Evian. Those 5 litre tins of Cretan extra virgin olive oil on Amazon too. Great value. Packed full of polyphenols.

I also have this thing called Project Nomad installed on my Mac. Dev sent me the link last year. Seemed like an easy win. I haven’t dug into it fully, but it’s the kind of thing that Dev could quite easily have played an active role in building - a free open source node for media, archives and data - offline knowledge, local maps, AI and educational courses.

We’ve got some cash too. We were going to do this anyway so win/win. They seem to have been intentionally making it harder to get hold of cash in recent weeks - banks have reduced the withdrawal limit at cashpoints in lockstep and there’s a requirement to pre-book appointments for larger withdrawals. Appointments that never seem to be available. I haven’t seen a queue at a cashpoint for years. Not that there are many left. It’s all rather odd.
I wouldn't say there was a run on the banks, but people have been visibly taking out more cash. Even the normies. But there again they’d panic bought toilet roll and Marmite.

They don’t want us stocking up on cash. Why? Is this a reason to stock up? Or a distraction? If they really didn't want people withdrawing cash, cash simply wouldn't be in the news-cycle. They've been slowly getting rid of cash for years. Why the focus now? Fuck knows what’s going on. Fuck knows what’s ever going on.

That last bundle I withdrew in 2020 was long gone. A pint here, a plumber's bill there. Most of it was paid back into the bank and used to fund some crypto 'investments'. XRP skyrocketed. Then plummeted. The meme coins were a mug's game. I found that out the hard way. In those instances, what went up did come down. With a sickening thump.
Still, the gold coins safely hidden in the sock drawer are worth their weight in, well, gold. The value of which has increased steadily. That was a smart move. Very savvy.

choices.label: The garage
opts: Top up the stockpile properly. Prepper list. Do it right this time.
A bit of extra cash, some tins. Don’t go overboard.
Leave it. You’ve done this before. It’ll blow over.

paras.t: There was a meme doing the rounds a year or so ago. A video of this chap. I have no idea who he was. Rugged. Careworn. Probably late thirties. English James Dean vibes. Smoking a cigarette. Articulating the curse of awareness. All Nietzsche and objective ego. An appeal to others as intelligent as him. Who suffer like him. Those as edgy and paranoid as him. Not the others, not the fools.
It was so on the money. Too on the money. Contrived. Look how haggard knowing makes you. How unhappy it makes you. How alienated. How pointless knowing is.
Why has this come to mind again now?
It’s so achingly cool and perfectly sums up the plight of those who ‘have it all sussed out’.

But it’s not so cool when the mainstream catches up. When the fools finally awaken. Perhaps being two steps ahead is the point of the awareness? The ego is lured by its desire for a sense of superiority. Once a cause has been taken up by the conformists, you’re no longer a rebel. You’ve lost your cool.
But you got what you wanted didn’t you? You were proven right. The endless research vindicated. The conspiracy theorist slurs dismissed.
So why aren’t you happy? Was being the outsider actually what it was all about?
admit it, you loved the conspiracy slurs, you lived for them.
And here I am. Half-heartedly prepping for Armageddon we warned about, whilst the skilled TV watchers who spent years refusing to listen, run around in state of panic.

Everyone’s feed has been showing them the shortages, the queues, the fear. Mainstream, and all the flavours of alt-media in alignment. BBC showing queues at petrol stations going round the block. Sky interviewing shoppers incandescent with rage that Lidl had run out of bottled water. Grifters grifting. Barely a sheet of paper between laughable conspiracy theories and plausible analysis. Jenny Wilson on twitter thinks the conspiracy theorists should take a day off. But look through her feed (if indeed she exists as human) she also thought the unvaccinated should have been imprisoned and we came out of lockdown too soon.

The harsh truth is that I have no idea what’s going to come to pass over the coming day, weeks, months. Just look at the news cycle. Fear with a side order of placation and reassurance. Chaos, half-truths, conflicting reports. Stay calm, it’s under control, take sensible precautions, heightened threat levels, queues for petrol, reduced cash withdrawal limits, robust and resilient defence levels, markets crashing, markets stable. And the fact is, this sense of not knowing which way is up isn’t so different from the status quo. In fact it’s no different. We’ve been conditioned to accept chaos as the norm. Desensitised. Rabbits in the headlights.

My gut instinct is that the chances of this event being anything other than next weeks chip paper are slim. But whatever the extent of the problem, the solutions are baked in. Cyber attack. No cyber attack. Another lab leak. What difference?
The ludicrous thing is, part of me just thinks ‘bring it on’ - roll out v2 of the pandemic playbook. Give us another lockdown. Do something. You know the meme. Do something.

Flood it again. You know that meme too no doubt? The Chinese water torture is driving me crazy. I want them to overreach. Show their hand. Bring forth rebellion and non-compliance. But they’ll have a solution for that too. Checkmate all the way up.
Knowing - small tick.
Doing - even smaller tick.
Mattering - big red cross.

Anyway, the larder is stocked, the freezer full to capacity. I got a couple of bottles of Sipsmith gin whilst I was at it. A tenner off with Clubcard. Amy managed to get a couple of jerry cans of petrol and a hundred litres of heating oil. The wind up torch has been dug out of the shed.
The most token of token efforts.
Sgt Prepper would be rolling on the floor with laughter.

And then, as if by magic. Just before Valentine’s Day, they pull a different sort of massacre out of the playbook. Sorry to sound like that guy, but really? Two dead. Allegedly. Birmingham. Outside a primary school. Two young kids. Machete attack.

Guess what everyone is suddenly talking about? The cyber story hasn’t been debunked — it’s being buried under something the algorithm is hardwired to amplify. Grief, outrage, counter-outrage, the moderation debate, the vigil, the political statements.
The manipulation on all sides is painful to watch - the rage served to both camps, the bodies still warm and the engagement metrics already climbing.
The familiar disgust-exhaustion cycle. It’s painfully easy to see through and yet you can’t help but be drawn in, to feel the emotions. Despite yourself. Just as intended.
And the biggest horror? There’s nothing we can do about any of it.
Amy will be dismayed, disgusted, in floods of tears. Dev will ignore the noise and look for the signal. I suspect Rupert will assume it’s staged.
I wonder what @jennywilson89 will make of it?

Bloody February. Perpetual rain. White skies every day. Not cloudy. White. Not freezing, but certainly big coat weather. Too hot in the woolly hat. Too cold without it. The dogs don’t care. The muddier the better. Olive is obsessed with sticks at the moment. She’s a funny thing. Wilf thinks she’s weird. He’s old and wise. Sticks are for babies. Sniffing is where it’s at.
We’ve had log fires every night. Stews. Winter fuel. Red wine, but we’ve been trying to share a bottle rather than one each.

This evening we’ve got more of the same. A Friday that feels like a Wednesday. Just the two of us tonight, the children either at parties (Sam, George and Chloe) or with their boyfriend (Emilia). It’s only five o’clock but it feels much later. The dogs have been walked, the mud cleaned off them, dried off, and are enjoying their pre-dinner snooze. Six o’clock is their feeding time, regular as clockwork. They’ll get up from their beds at five-to and wander round the kitchen expectantly.
We’ve had a lamb shoulder slow cooking in the oven all afternoon. Moroccan style. Red onions, red peppers, chick peas, smoky with paprika and ras el hanout. One pot. Easy.
I scroll through the doom-feed whilst Amy goes for a soak in the bath. I put some music on Sonos. Panic seems particularly apt.
Could life ever be sane again?
I’ll wait until she’s back before opening the wine. Or shall I open the bottle and take her a glass for the bath? No. I’ll wait.

The level of cyber attack fear has been dialled down a notch or two. Attention has turned to the Birmingham murders. Two days since the event and still no official announcement about the suspect, other than police press conferences in which the public are asked to desist from speculation whilst enquiries are ongoing. I’m sure you can imagine the manner of delivery and intonation of Deputy Chief Constable Higgins? Obviously this request has ramped up speculation, gossip, theory and counter-theory.
There are multiple mainstream articles helping to diffuse the cyber threat too. Fewer social media posts showing tins of baked beans and toilet roll in garages.
As if to prove the point, Amy comes back from her bath and tells me about her chat with her Mum. All about the murders. Asking if Amy had the latest. What can be done to stop this happening?
‘She didn’t even mention the cyber attack today. Last week it was all she talked about.’
I snigger, in what I imagine was a quite annoying manner, uncertain what to say.
‘You think the threat has gone away?’

I open a bottle of red (a German Pinot Noir) whilst considering my reply. Any annoyance my snigger caused now forgotten about as she smiles that ‘about to have my first sip of wine of the day’ smile that I know so well.

‘Who knows? I’d question whether there was ever actually an elevated threat at all. I’m not saying there wasn’t one. There’s always one. It’s just that our attention was being drawn to it. There are attacks against companies, individuals, the state every day. Hackers blackmailing, terrorists making demands, modern warfare. Aspergers kids fucking about War Games style on AI in their bedrooms. Some are widely reported, others aren’t. And there have been cyber security conferences and cyber resilience training exercises for years. Nothing new.’
‘So why now?’

‘The million dollar question. Three possibilities as I see it. One. A genuine threat from a state or non-state actor that intelligence has uncovered and is trying to neutralise. Even a new AI model turning on us. Who knows? The governments and media hedge their bets in reporting it - switching from ‘raised levels’ and ‘sensible degree of preparedness’ to we got this but we need more resilience to continue to maintain stability and control. Resilience meaning funds and surveillance. There’s no attack. There’s more surveillance.’
keep it short, Simon, you’re losing her…
‘Two. There’s no threat over and above the norm. Outcome the same. Essential that there’s more funding and surveillance.’
I carry on talking whilst checking on the lamb. Achingly tender. We could eat it with a spoon.

‘Three. False Flag incoming. Systems will go down. Internet. Banking. The lights go out for a bit. Think Covid fear but with no Amazon Prime deliveries and heating for a week instead of the threat of a deadly plague. Order will be restored but the ‘something must be done’ to prevent this happening again. It could be worse next time. The playbook is already written - the buzzwords - robust - contingencies - digital - quantum - public-private partnerships - global unity against enemies of democracy. You get the picture.’
‘Gun to the head, which one?’

‘Probably two. I mean this is essentially the narrative of the daily social media scroll. Scare story. Nothing happens. Next. But each story changes the mood of the nation, our view of reality. Opens or close the Overton window a bit. Brings chaos, division, a distraction. People debate, argue, worry, demand solutions. And by fuck do they have the solution lined up and ready to roll.’
‘So why the cash and cannellini beans?’

‘Because…I don’t know. Does anyone? Hedging. You said gun to head. I went for the second option. The fact that we’ve now got the machete murders on the front pages makes me think I might be right. Who knows?’
‘What about Dev? You keep saying he thinks something will happen. The Valentine’s Day stuff.’

‘Dev knows what’s been put in place. The biometric payments. I mean it doesn’t take a genius to work out that new digital and financial systems are coming. But this is not about them coming at some unspecified point in the future. Dev thinks they go live this weekend. As he puts it - it’s not a prediction, it’s a fucking production schedule. But going live and being fully operational are two different things.’
‘So he thinks we’re going to start using fingerprints to pay for our shopping next week? That is so Dev.’

‘He thinks it’s the solution to a problem. The cyber attack equivalent of the vaccine rollout to end the pandemic. But they didn’t roll out the vaccines overnight. They made us wait. Ramped up the fear. Made people beg for their safe and effective freedom-giving juice.’
‘So we’ll be in lockdown again and the digital currency will be the thing that saves the day? Is that really going to happen?’

‘When you put it like that it sounds a bit ridiculous I guess. Who knows? I reckon it’s more likely that this just seeds the required solution in the public consciousness. Nudging us to accept it as necessary. Safe, secure, efficient, desirable. The new system is already turned on, we simply drift into it. Like landlines and mobiles. There wasn’t a grand ceremony and official Smartphone Day. It just happened. And now the thought of using a ring dial phone is ludicrous.’
‘So it’ll be fine then? I mean for this weekend. Our Valentine’s dinner.’
‘I guess. I mean, I don’t know. Probably.’
He did say stay close to home. I mean, we are anyway. So I won’t tell her. What difference will it make? It’ll only freak her out. And I want us to enjoy the Rully.

choices.label: Friday evening
opts: Long walk with the dogs. Just you, Olive, Wilf and the mud. Leave the phone at home.
Reply to Dev. You’ve been avoiding it. He sent two more messages today.
Open the Rully Rouge early. Start the Béarnaise. It’s Valentine’s tomorrow. Enjoy something.

turns.title: The Last Night at the Fair

paras.t: Valentine’s Day. We’re staying in. Always have done. Two courses in the local gastropub will set us back two hundred quid — a couple of pints, a bottle of red, probably two. I won’t be able to resist the cheeseboard. Drive there, taxi back, pick the car up in the morning. Rigmarole. Money better spent elsewhere.

Anyway we’re both decent cooks and love cooking together. We’re a good team. I’m meat and sauces. She’s veg and presentation. We rarely argue. We don’t get in each other’s way. We giggle. We’re silly together. It keeps us young and vibrant.

The flat iron from our local butcher is insanely good. The depth of flavour of a ribeye with the melting tenderness of a fillet. I’ll cook it on the griddle, charred on the outside, rare in the middle. Maybe veering towards medium rare to keep my darling happy. Compromise. It’ll rest on a huge slab of oak chopping board. Adds a rugged, rustic charm as a table centrepiece. A bugger to wash up though. Tomorrow morning’s problem. Triple cooked duck fat chips. Steamed spinach. Tomatoes roasted in olive oil with copious amounts of Maldon and black pepper. Just normal peppercorns freshly ground from our tall artisan-made mill. We used to spend three times as much on Tellicherry. Couldn’t taste the difference. I’ll start making the Béarnaise too early. It will be perfect. Simmering on a low heat waiting for its chip dipping, meat slathering fate. Buttery, glossy, thick, speckled with fresh tarragon and sharp with white wine vinegar. I’ll nurse it, stirring slowly. I won’t take my eye off it. Until I do. Then it’ll split. I’ll remain calm, seething inside. Unless I’ve been on the gin. Doesn’t suit me. Whoever called it Mother’s ruin was on the money. Anyway I’ll thicken it up with another egg yolk or an ice cube. It’ll be fine.
After the meal

It all went to plan. Even the bloody Béarnaise split. I managed to salvage it. The wine was delightful. Our ‘treat’ wine. Rully Rouge Premier Cru Clos du Chapitre, Jaeger-Defaix. God it’s good. Silky, pure, plenty of berry fruit, but with some guts too. And yes, we’ve just opened the third bottle.

The Kitchen Disco is now in full swing. Started off chilled. A bit of background jazz. Flowed seamlessly into some Café del Mar. The early José Padilla stuff of course. I’d planned to get the vinyl out tonight. I’m an avid collector. Well I was. I can’t remember the last time I bought an album. I still tell everyone how digital music is inferior to the analogue sound of vinyl LPs. The artwork. A more engaging listening experience. Warm and natural. Superior dynamic range. Full-album appreciation. Stories told over multiple tracks. Tactile. Real.
I can’t remember the last time I put one on the turntable.

So here we are sitting on stools by the kitchen island. We’ve been playing ‘song tag’ — Amy chooses first, then me, then back to Amy. Spotify Premium played on Sonos Play 5. Not cutting edge, but sounds good to me. We’re now at the dancey stage of proceedings. She chose Higher States of Consciousness. I replied with Smack My Bitch Up. Love The Prodigy. A romantic choice for Valentine’s Day! We’re now listening to Insomnia.
actually I’m starting to tire, the thought of sleep is beginning to appeal
I’ve got the Age of Love lined up next. Jam and Spoon Watch Out For Stella Mix, naturally. The thought of those hypnotic, otherworldly beats at the start makes my spine tingle.
‘It’s taking its time to play, what the fuck’s happening?’ Amy demands.
Starlink has been a bit hit and miss today, but most of these songs are all saved in our Spotify Library. This ain’t our first Sonos rodeo.
‘Wheel of death on the phone. Weird. I’m sure it was in a playlist in the Library? Sod it. I’ll get it out on vinyl. It’ll sound better too’
Bloody technology.

I rummage through the collection. I know it’s in here somewhere. I’d dumped the piles of vinyl in a random order on the shelf when we moved house three years ago (wait four, no five years ago. Where did all the time go?) and promised myself that I’d soon reorganise it into its usual orderly glory. Another entry to add to the list of things that never happened.

Found it. Eventually. I take it out of its sleeve, a million memories of top-off, wide-eyed, sweaty nights released with it. Onto the turntable it goes. The familiar plop as the spindle emerges through the hole. I hear my needle hit the groove (mental note, Stone Roses next).
Age of Love hits its angelic voices crescendo.
Remember we played together….
I’m dancing, eyes closed. My body in 2027. My mind in 1995. The dying years of The Before Times. Not that we knew it then. Tears well up in my eyes. My nostalgia spiral has started.
Time’s tide has smothered me. I can’t help but think of her.
I’m jolted back into the room as the final beats fade out. I head back to the turntable to load up the next track. It’s Amy’s turn really, but she won’t mind if I sneak on some Roses next.
As I flick through the collection, Amy leans over and shows me her phone. She’s been trying to send a WhatsApp but it won’t go through. She tries a text. Not sending either.
‘Try calling me?’. I suggest.
She clicks on Simon.
‘Nope. Nothing. Weird.’
I check my emails. Nothing received since just past nine.
‘Must be the start of the cyber attack’ I mock, whilst loading up She Bangs The Drums, tucking the vinyl under my arm to perform air quotes around cyber attack.
We laugh. Both of us silently wondering whether this actually could be the event.
I smile at Amy. It felt like a weak smile, not the confident, reassuring one I meant it to be.
She’s my Rock. My Love. My Everything.

How could it ever come to pass
She’ll be the first, she’ll be the last
To describe the way I feel
The way I feel

choices.label: Late night
opts: Keep fiddling with your phone.
Cuddle Amy and stroke her hair reassuringly.
Crash out.

paras.t:
Creaky noises make my skin creep
I need to get some sleep….
I can’t get no sleep

Where are you? In bed, check.
How do you feel? Neck’s sore. Note to self. I need new pillows. Mouth is dry.
I reach for my water. The glass is full. I take a big glug. It tickles my dry throat. I somehow manage not to spit it all out. I swallow it in stages.

What time is it? Actually what day is it? Feels early and maybe a Sunday. Reach for phone. It’s there, usual spot on the bedside table. You remembered to charge it before crashing out. First Brownie point of the day.
5.56am. Early doors.
And it’s Monday morning according to my phone, not Sunday.

I should check the girls’ location. Did they get back to Sophie’s after the party. Obviously Amy will have checked, but I should do my due diligence too. I turn to look at Amy. Deep sleep still. Away with the fairies, mumbling something about leaks. Or maybe it’s leeks? I’ll ask her when she wakes up. Doubt she’ll remember it. She’ll find it funny though. I look forward to seeing that smile.
I go to the ‘Find My’ App. Emilia — Last seen 7 hours ago. I swipe down to update. No change. Click on Chloe — same thing. 7 hours ago.
I remember the service being shit last night. Now I have three curves of full signal Wi-Fi reassurance. But Find My isn’t working.
I check to see if the internet is working. The BBC propaganda website first.
Nothing. I try something else…Crystal Palace blog…Nothing.
Fuck’s sake.
Is Starlink aligned? In fact, it’ll be easier to reboot the hub first. And I’ll put the kettle on whilst I’m at it.
Hub rebooted. Kettle on. Still no service.
X…just nothing. Insta….also nothing.
Weird.
Barclays App. ‘Closed for routine maintenance’
The Cyber Psyop, Day One.
Kettle’s boiled. Two mugs. Earl Grey and a spoon of sugar. Brown. Must be Demerara. Builders for me. I’m sweet enough already.

Back to the bedroom. The gentle clunk of mug on bedside table causes Amy to stir. Well, not gentle as such. Volume honed to perfection over the years — just loud enough to wake her with the knowledge that her tea hero has come to the rescue — not too loud as to be an annoyingly obvious ‘wake up and play’.
‘Morning’
‘Morning, darling. Cup of tea on the side for you.’
‘I know. My hero. I’ll make the difficult second cup.’
(It never gets old)
‘Bloody internet is still down’
‘Is it? Are the girls OK?’
‘Don’t know. I haven’t heard from them. Everything is down’
She jolts upright, reaching for the phone.
‘You’re right. Last seen 7 hours ago. Have you tried calling?’
I hadn’t.
‘No, I didn’t want to wake them’ I replied, half truthfully. ‘They’ll be fine’
‘What’s this, Simon?’
I got a Simon, something is amiss. She points at her phone. ‘100% — you’re fully charged.’
‘No, underneath that. The blue swirly logo — that app — ARC. What’s that? I don’t remember installing it.’
I look at my phone. I have the same logo, the same ARC app.
I click on it. It does nothing.
I look at Amy. She looks at me. I assume I have the same WTF look on my face that she does.
This is bizarre. I should message Dev. Wait, I can’t message Dev.

choices.label: ARC
opts: An app called ARC that does nothing. Weird.

paras.t: Amy left a half-drunk cup of tea on the kitchen worktop. It was highly unusual for her to start her day without kickstarting herself with at least three cups, often accompanied by a few rounds of Marmite on toast.

She was worried about the girls. She was always worried about the girls. They’d be fine, they were at Sophie’s, they were safe, the internet would be back up and running soon. It’d be much ado about nothing as it always is. Without all the ‘cyber attack’ warnings and ‘increased threat levels’ we’d have simply thought the internet was down. The difficult second and straightforward if I was making it third cups of tea would’ve been made and drunk.

This smacked of being an event, a happening, a ruse. Concocted. Implemented. Controlled. The ‘Story’ that the media would latch onto. ‘If it’s in the news it’s likely a ruse’. Stir up some panic, seed a bit of fear, ensure the algo-boosted X accounts throw in a splattering of ‘this is the big one’. BBC Verify, the arbiter of truth, setting everyone straight.
Some political bluster in the days to follow — ‘What we should do to make sure this cannot happen again?’

Answer — more robust verification processes, more control, more surveillance. Same as always. They’d definitely use the word ‘robust’, I’d stake my mortgage on it. And they’d definitely give more millions to Palantir or Oracle to guarantee this increased robustness.

Anyway, Amy didn’t finish her first cup. She panic-left the house within minutes of waking up to go and check on the girls, un-showered and in a tizz. I’d said they’d still be asleep. Probably for another five hours. If they’ve even gone to bed yet. We’d let them stay with Sophie on a Sunday night as they had a day off college today.
Amy rushed out. ‘Love you, I’ll be back soon’.
I put the kettle on to make myself a particularly challenging second cup and absentmindedly picked up my phone for the morning email/X/BBC headline check.

Nothing. Darkness. Of course. I knew there’d be nothing but somehow it still surprised me. The nimble-fingered unconscious info-sweep and instant dopamine hit is so engrained. I used to wake up and have a spliff when I was at University. My first contact with the world at large a perusal of The Sun (I know, I was young and liked the, err, sport section) on the tube to central London.
Nowadays the psyops start before I’ve even had a piss.
6.07am. The clock is the only thing that’s working on my phone. Well, that and the torch. All the apps open but state various versions of ‘service unavailable’.

I tried the Mac and the iPad too. Nothing. Reset the router a few more times. Starlink app opens OK — claims ‘Starlink is aligned’ — but also tells me it’s ‘Offline’ and the router is ‘unreachable’. Annoying. I had set aside the morning for sending out invoices to market traders, but this relied on Quickbooks Online, which was just hanging. Not even a courtesy ‘we’ll be back online soon’.

At least the power was on. Cup of tea number three and a couple of slices of toast. Real Patisserie ‘chewy brown’. Quite possibly the best loaf known to man. I buttered it whilst it was hot, the butter melting and collecting in the sourdough pools. A carby treat for my hangover.
Extra insulin needed, 12 units should do it.
Hardly scientific but an educated guess after years of carb-counting, trial and error.

Kate from next-door knocked. She was supposed to be on a video call with an overseas client. Early start for her. She was just checking if our internet was down too. I asked her in for a tea but she declined, wanting to go back next-door and get the Teams call to work.

I checked WhatsApp again. Lots of grey single ticks. No one was receiving my messages. I had one message from Vince. 1.01am. He’d obviously had issues too but it looks like it’s sorted in London now. Reassuring.

I sat in the beaten up leather armchair in the hallway. Slurping, crunching, chewing. No phone. Just me, my thoughts, a view of the plants in the courtyard outside the front door. The olive tree had wintered well. The magnolia looking as if it would soon blossom into its early Spring glory. The dogs settled at my feet. Peace.
I could get used to this. No phones. No constant connectivity.

I was just starting to nod off when I heard the sound of a key trying to fit into the front door lock. George was back. What the hell was he doing back just after six in the morning? Looked even more hungover than I felt. He’d been for a Valentine’s booze at the local with his mates and crashed on Thomas’s sofa. Couldn’t sleep, so decided to head home. Probably still over the limit. But it’s only a short drive down country lanes, I guess.

We confirmed to one another that the internet was fucked. (His words. Actually mine too, come to think of it.) He’d tried to call Amy but was getting either nothing, straight-to-voicemail or endless ringing with no answer.

‘Have you tried the TV’ he asked. I hadn’t thought of that. We turned it on. Just a black screen. Of course it is, we’d watched TV over the internet via an Amazon Fire TV Box for years. ‘Does this thing even have ‘normal’ TV?’ I asked George. He had no idea. He thought we did watch normal TV.
‘Cup of tea, Georgie?’
‘No thanks, I’m knackered. See you on the other side.’ He slunk off to his room.

turns.title: I am the God of Hellfire

paras.t: What the hell is that? The most God-awful noise. Ear piercing. The dogs bark in unison. Wilf, hackles up, deep and manly followed by a growl. Olive, bemused look on her face, higher pitched and more incessant.
George bursts back into the hallway, the door somehow staying on its hinges.
‘What the…?’
He shows me his phone. The source of the sound identified. The klaxon I assumed was only ever for Emergency Alert tests and scaremongering.
UK GOVERNMENT EMERGENCY ALERT

I skim read it in disbelief. Major cyber incident…UK financial and digital infrastructure…Emergency services…card and electronic banking payments have been suspended…and then at the bottom… from the same people who brought you The Plandemic…
STAY HOME. STAY CALM.
This is really happening.
We stand in stunned silence. I reach out to grab my phone, thinking for a moment I’d been pranked. But there it is. The same message. Phone still vibrating. An exclamation mark in a red triangle.
I read it again. More slowly this time. It still doesn’t fully sink in. All I can think of is Klaus Schwab, in full Dr Evil mode—
The COVID-19 crisis would be seen in this respect as a small disturbance in comparison to a major cyber attack.

And the ending. Stay Home. Stay Calm. Why no third instruction this time? Where was the ‘Save Lives’ or ‘Control the Virus’? Has the Nudge Unit had a rethink? They’re leaving us hanging, waiting for the final command. Probably some new behavioural game theory that’s being tested — condition your victims into expecting a trio of instructions, then, at a moment of heightened tension, deliver only two. Leave them expectant, confused, immobilised.
I feel like I’m at a crucial stage of a ‘choose your own adventure’ book. But the ‘turn to page sixty-five’ options are purely in my head.
‘Why do we need to stay home?’ asks George.
‘Good question. Crisis management I guess. They don’t want hordes of civilians panicking on the streets.’
‘Won’t telling people to stay calm have the opposite effect?’
It seems Georgie has learnt something on the way.
‘Good point. Especially when the ‘stay calm’ request comes via an unprecedented emergency alert.’
‘So do we stay calm?’
‘What’s on the cover of The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy?’
‘Eh?’
‘Oh for fuck’s sake, George, how many times have I told you to read it? Don’t Panic. In capitals.’
Banging at the door. Two teenage faces next to each other pushing their noses against the glass. It’s the girls. They’re back. Manic grins, eyes a mix of excitement and confusion.
I open the door and they pour in, unleashing a stream of Gen Z buzzwords - oh my days, what the hell?, OMG and other acronyms that I’m not down with the kids enough to understand.
‘Did you get it Dad?’ asks Emilia.
‘The alarm? Yeah.’ I’m aiming for reassuring fatherly meets effortless chill.
'Why did Mum come and get us so early? We had about two hours sleep’ Chloe asks grumpily. ‘What did she think was going to happen?’

I don’t bother to answer. It was largely rhetorical. Chloe knows full well than Amy would have been worried sick that she didn’t know they were safe. She was an obsessive ‘Find My’ track and tracer, message-me-when-you-get-homer.
‘I presume you girls have had no internet either?’
‘Not since, like midnight or something’. I decide not to call Emilia out on the ‘like’. Rarely a sentence goes by without one.

‘It’s so annoying’ Chloe shows me her phone. Instagram, SnapChat - both not updating. One of those bloody awful tongues-out, peace-fingered salutes selfies from a gaggle of scantily-clad girls at the pre-party the last Insta image and a message from Eddie on Snap, three kisses.
Eddie, eh? Who the hell is Eddie?
In comes Amy, noticeably less jittery now the girls have been rounded up. The dogs greet her like she’s been gone for months. They're loving this early morning kerfuffle.
‘Have you heard from Sam?’
‘No, not yet.’
‘Are you not worried?’
‘Well, not really, no more than normal. He’ll be fine. The internet is down, it’s not World War 3.’
‘I thought you’d be more, like, um, weird about this, Dad.’ Emilia clearly thought I’d be in a frenzy as one of my conspiracy predictions appeared to be coming true.

‘All that’s happened is the internet is down and the Government have sent an emergency bleep. Let’s not overreact, it’s probably nothing. No point jumping to conclusions or reacting with emotion. Let’s see what happens.’
‘I thought you’d have loads of theories, start talking about Hegelian dia-thingy and stuff.’
As if on cue, another ear-piercing klaxon sounds from everyone’s phone. Dogs barking, everyone reaching for their device. George is quickest on the draw.
‘Here’s another one. It’s different’

Remain calm. Remain indoors while situation is assessed. Initial reports indicate cyber attack limited to financial and digital infrastructure. Power, water, and essential services remain operational. Further guidance will follow.
‘Ten minutes later and they're doubling down on staying calm. Interesting.’ My mind is turning over nineteen to the dozen.
‘Cup of tea?’ asks Amy.
‘That’s the spirit’ I proclaim enthusiastically, with a slightly pompous patriotic fist-pump. ‘How very English. Stay Calm. Put the kettle on.’
We move to the kitchen. Kids in their usual seats at the table, Amy and I double-teaming the tea making.
‘Who wants eggy bread?’ Amy offers, pulling out her crowd pleaser. Sliced white bread, fried in eggs and butter topped with the unlikely-yet-delicious combo of marmite and Golden Syrup.
Three hungover ‘meees’ in unison. A ‘go on then’ from me. A blood sugar killer having already had early morning toast. But fuck it.
Despite the lack of internet connection, all three kids are glued to their phones, checking various apps, messaging services, email, refreshing, turning off and on.

‘This is so annoying’ Emilia grunts as she slams her phone down in anger. Moments after she does, the third klaxon of the day announces that the internet has been shut down as a precaution. We agree that an intentional switch off rather than a hack is good news. Of sorts.
‘If it hasn’t been hacked and it’s only turned off as a precaution, surely it’ll be back on soon?’ George asks optimistically. He’s undoubtedly thinking no internet, no TikTok, no income.

‘I guess so. How long can they shut the internet down for without riots? Mandatory digital ID. No problem. Epstein child torture. Whatever. No TikTok for forty-eight hours and Gen Z will be on the streets. Apoplectic cold turkeys.’

A text message cuts me off mid rant. It’s Sam. He’s fine. He’s at Mike’s. I send him a thumbs up. Amy raises an eyebrow. She’d have written a side of A4 demanding all the details, how he was feeling, what his plans are, etc, etc. He’d rather the emoji.

Eggy bread demolished, another round of teas drunk, we sit around the table wondering what to do. We’re all holding onto our phones, occasionally absent-mindedly scrolling through apps that don’t work. I’m torn between going back to bed, returning to the leather chair with a book or taking the dogs for a walk. I suggest the latter. We could all go when it warms up a little bit.
‘But they’ve told us to stay indoors’ protests Emilia. She’s a bit of a goody-two shoes when it comes to following instructions. Unless they’re from her parents.
‘Actually they’ve said stay local and stay indoors, which is a bit of a conflict. Anyway if I want to go to the woods with the dogs, I will. Twelve o’clock? Who’s in?
Twelve it is. In the meantime we retreat to our rooms to shower, take stock and nurse the Valentine’s hangovers. The unmade bed looks tempting..maybe a little lie down before a shower…
The Afternoon

The day is passing slowly. We’d been to the woods. They were eerily quiet. It’s only a two minute drive down a country lane to get to the parking spot where we start the walk so we weren’t able to get much of a feel for how busy the roads were. Everything looked normal, sounded normal. But there was an touch of uncertainty, a frisson of electricity in the air. Hard to describe, a bit like those days between Christmas and New Year when you’ve absolutely no idea what day of the week it is, with a hint of early Covid what the hell is going on thrown in for good measure.
And no internet.
Just UK Gov emergency pings giving us situation updates. It seems ‘partner nations’ have reported similar disruption according to the update we’d received at eleven.
Eleven. On the dot. In fact, all of them. On the dot. Hardly live updates…

‘Interesting choice of words.’ I’d pointed out to Amy. ‘Partner nations - meaning that ‘non-partner nations’ weren’t reporting similar disruption? Meaning they’re going to blame the attack on on a ‘hostile state’ - yes I used the quotation fingers, sorry, I know it’s annoying.
‘Like Chyna' Amy replied, she loved saying China in the Trump Chyna-virus voice.

‘There’ll be up there in the betting, for sure. Iran, North Korea, unidentified non-state actors, a terrorist cell. AI gone rogue. Not forgetting the odds-on favourite, good old false flag. I can see the meme now - horse race with an Irish commentator - ‘and it’s AI Gone Rogue, it’s lead being eaten into by North Korea. China being pushed along and looks beaten. AI Gone Rogue is coming back to them. Unidentified Non-State Actors is staying on gamely…but here comes False Flag, going very easily indeed, jockey Elon Thiel has a double handful. False Flag hits the front and wins going away.’
‘Twat’
We laughed. I think it was my jockey impressions and over-the-top Irish accent that made her call me a twat. She loved it really.

Telephone calls and texts had been a bit of a lucky dip. I’d tried Mum a few times, but had no luck getting through to Spain. Amy had heard from her Mum and Dad. They’d be the only ones panicking about us. Other texts received were just versions of ‘you getting this?’ or ‘what the fuck?’ I’d tried calling Dev a few times. Well more than a few. Not compulsively though. His original number and the new ‘walls’ burner, both dead.

The most interesting emergency alert, well, to me anyway, was the one received at two-thirty confirming that ARC - Autonomous Resilience Cloud Emergency application - has auto-installed on everyone’s phone. ‘No action required’ it noted. And ‘no authorisation given’ I noted. I’d spent about twenty minutes trying to think of a witty ARC acronym that I could text to Dev, but couldn’t think of a good enough one. It’d come to me.

At the moment ARC was simply an un-clickable app with pretty teal and white logo. No functionality. Presumably they’d send a message on it soon? I’d tried pressing it a few times throughout the day, but nothing had happened. It had installed itself on the home screen of my phone, relegating Barclays to page two. Perhaps I wouldn't be needing that for a bit? ‘Closed for routine maintenance’ it declared.
Routine, eh?
4.48pm text received from Dev. I’ll read it to you in full.
you seeing this

Even for Dev this is curt. Perverse even. Of course I’m fucking seeing it. Or is there something specific he’s hinting at? Wants me to validate a thought rather than telling me? Or is he just getting me to think? Testing me?
My reply, one graced with both capitalisation and question marks, unlike his.
Emergency messages? On the dot?
No reply yet. In fact no idea if it’s even been received.

Let’s be honest, the latter half of the day had been all about the wait for the PM Press Conference scheduled for 6pm. Covid vibes revisited. The nation awaits. Families would be huddled round the telly, just like the good old days.
Kate is going to join us. She says she doesn't want to watch it alone. I reckon she just wants to hear my sarcastic commentary. Hopefully that ARC acronym will come to me before then.

The tension was ramped up by the first ARC Emergency Update. Received at 5pm with a resounding ding, noticeably less forbidding that the emergency klaxon, and dressed up in a verging on neon teal. Less aggressive than the emergency red. Welcome to the future  - ‘we’ve got this’ vibes. Maybe I’m overthinking it?
It’s now just after half-five we’ve gathered on the sofa. BBC is simply showing ‘The Prime Minister will address the nation at 6pm’.
‘How come the TV is working on BBC now? Nothing earlier. No other channels though.’ George asks.
I hadn’t thought of that. ‘Probably some emergency override I imagine. I’ll ask Dev.’
‘If they can get BBC to work, surely they get ITV to work? Love Island is on.’ Chloe asks.
‘Oh my God, yeah.’ Emilia realises she’ll miss out on seeing some new contestants arrive on the Island, or some such garbage.
‘Oh my God, yeah.’ George repeats in a mockingly airhead tone.
‘Shut up George’ the girls reply in unison.
Some things never change.

6pm approaches, still the same message on screen. No sign of the PM yet. Will they roll out the same lectern? Will the PM be alone or joined by some trusty sidekicks? The cyber version of Chris Whitty with some fear-porn or a financial Patrick Vallance presenting some bogus statistics?
Next slide please…

choices.label: Six o'clock
opts: Kettle on. Telly on. The nation awaits.

turns.broadcastSrc: HM GOVERNMENT — PM ADDRESS — 18:00 GMT — 15 FEBRUARY 2027

paras.t: Good evening.

Yesterday, on Valentine’s Day, a little before midnight, a coordinated cyber attack struck the financial and digital infrastructure of the United Kingdom and twenty-two other nations. This has caused significant disruption to civilian systems in our nation and around the globe.

Here is what we know. I will not minimise it. The attack targeted the core transaction and record-keeping systems that underpin our banking, our public services, and much of our daily communication. Our security and intelligence services, working in close coordination with international partners, are engaged in a comprehensive response. I chaired COBRA at six o’clock this morning and have been in continuous session since.

Here is what I want you to understand. The damage is being assessed. The infrastructure is damaged, not destroyed. We are working — with every resource available to us — to restore normal service. Our current assessment is that this will take days, not weeks.

Let me be clear about what is not affected. Our electricity grid is operational. Our water supply is operational. Our gas network is operational. Our hospitals have power. Our emergency services are coordinating. No lives are in danger from the attack itself.

Many of you will have spent today unable to reach members of your family — unable to send emails, unable to use messaging apps, unable to refresh social media or stream the news the way you would on any other day. I know how difficult this is. I know how isolating it feels not to be able to reach a son or a daughter, a parent, a friend abroad.

These services have been restricted as a precaution while our cloud infrastructure is verified. They have not been damaged. We cannot leave them running while we are not yet certain they are safe. We expect to begin restoring them in stages from tomorrow morning, as verification work completes. Telephone calls and text messages remain operational throughout. If you need to reach someone urgently tonight, please use those.

Currently we are unable to access our bank accounts. Shops and businesses are unable to process our card payments. For this reason, for the next 24 hours retail, businesses and offices will be closed. A detailed plan for the opening of essential retail, including supermarkets, will be issued shortly.
Your savings are safe. Your deposits are protected. Nothing has been lost — only temporarily made inaccessible.

Schools were closed today and will remain closed for the remainder of the week. Hospitals remain open for emergencies only; all routine and non-urgent care has been postponed, also for the remainder of the week. All public transport services are suspended for the same period of time.
Our emergency services are operational. Our military and police forces will be visible, on the streets, to ensure the safety of every one of us.

The emergency communications platform on your phones — many of you will have already received alerts through it — is functioning as designed. It will continue to be your most reliable source of verified information in the coming days.

Part of this emergency communication system is ARC. You may have seen the app automatically installed on your devices throughout the course of the day. The ARC app adds an even more robust communication channel between Government and citizens.

I have spoken this afternoon with my counterparts across the affected nations. We are united — not only in our response, but in our resolve. This was an attack on all of us. It will be met by all of us.
In the meantime, I ask just three things of you.

First: for the next 24 hours, stay local, stay safe. Do not drive, unless it is a matter of life or death. This is not a lockdown, but a request. Look after each other. Check on your neighbours. Share what you have.
Second: do not fear. We will restore these systems. We will provide answers. And we will ensure that every family in this country is supported through this period. This period of days, not weeks.
Third: please continue to follow the guidance issued through ARC, the emergency alert system and on all BBC television and radio channels.

I will address the nation again at nine o’clock tomorrow morning with a full operational update. There will be detailed updates from my colleagues in the Cabinet and experts from the National Cyber Security Centre during this period.
There are dark days, challenging days, ahead. We face them with our unique British spirit. We face them together.
Good night. And be well.

paras.t: Good evening.
I said I would return at six with a progress report, and I am here with an encouraging update.

Forty-eight hours ago, our payment infrastructure was offline. Today, payment terminals are processing transactions across the country. Not all terminals. Not all cards. Not yet. But the trajectory is clear, and it is accelerating.

On your screen is a tracker that shows a regional breakdown of terminal restoration. Thirty-eight per cent of payment terminals are now operational, up from zero on Monday. Some of you will have used your card today. More of you will be able to tomorrow. These figures will be updated hourly and sent to you via ARC Emergency and Local ARC Updates. I will share these figures every evening until they are no longer needed.
The London Stock Exchange has confirmed that trading will resume tomorrow morning. This is a significant step. The markets are returning because the data underpinning them is intact and verified.

The network of essential retail outlets that opened yesterday has expanded today, as we said it would. Longer hours. More stores. More locations. From tomorrow morning, designated high street bank branches will open between ten and two for cash withdrawals — the list has been published through ARC and is available at your nearest Community Recovery Hub.

Our transport network is recovering. Limited rail services are running on key routes using manual signalling while our digital systems are verified. Transport for London has restored partial Tube and bus services. Fuel distribution continues at designated stations. The stay-local guidance remains in place, but we have broadened the definition of essential travel to include travel to work for those in critical roles, and travel to care for vulnerable relatives.

I want to say a word about the international picture. This attack struck twenty-three nations. I have spoken with fourteen heads of government in the last forty-eight hours. We are coordinating closely with our allies — sharing intelligence, sharing technical expertise, and learning from each other’s responses in real time. I have to be direct with you: not every country is recovering at the same pace. You will have seen reports of disorder in some cities overseas. That has not happened here, and I want to thank you for that. The calm and discipline shown by the British public over these three days has been, frankly, extraordinary. I spoke with the Japanese Prime Minister this morning, and he echoed that sentiment — our two nations, he said, have responded with a composure that others have not. We are sharing our technical recovery framework with partner nations who have requested it. The United Kingdom is among the first to begin restoring payment services. That is not luck. That is preparation, and it is resilience.

On communications. I know this has been one of the hardest parts of this week — not being able to message your family, to email, to connect in the ways we rely on. We said on Monday that we had restricted these services ourselves, as a precaution, while our cloud infrastructure was verified. That verification is progressing, and I can now set out the next steps. Email services are being restored this evening. For those of you with family overseas — and I know there are millions of you who have not been able to reach loved ones — international messaging services, including WhatsApp, will be restored from tomorrow morning. Domestic messaging services will follow as each platform completes verification with the National Cyber Security Centre. I know that is not fast enough. But the sequence matters, and we are moving as quickly as we safely can.

Schools will reopen on Monday. I confirm that without reservation. In the meantime, ARC Education went live this morning. Over two million households accessed educational content today. Your children’s schools are uploading lesson materials, reading lists, and video lessons through their local authority ARC channels. The streaming is fast, the materials are good, and your children’s teachers are working hard to keep them learning. I have been told by more than one parent that it is, and I quote, “better than lockdown.” ARC Education will continue until schools reopen.

The practical guidance on support during this period was published this afternoon through ARC, as the Chancellor committed to last evening. If you are in difficulty — if you cannot access food, medication, or essential supplies — your local Community Recovery Hub is there for you.

I want to say one more thing about the infrastructure that has made this recovery possible. The ARC authentication framework — the layer that sits beneath our payment systems, that has been powering your emergency alerts, that kept this channel open when everything else went dark — performed exactly as it was designed to. It is this framework that is enabling the restoration you are seeing on your screens tonight. It worked. And it will continue to work.
We expect the great majority of services to be restored by the weekend, with a return to normal schooling and work patterns from Monday and Tuesday of next week.
I will address you again tomorrow evening at six.
Be well.

paras.t: Good evening.

I was due to address you at six o’clock this evening. Shortly before that broadcast, at approximately half past five, financial systems across twenty-three nations experienced a further phase of disruption. The United Kingdom is one of those nations. I took the decision to delay this address so that I could instead chair an emergency COBRA session and speak to my counterparts in the affected nations. I wanted to come to you with information, not speculation.
Here is what we know.

The restoration of payment and banking services that had been progressing well over the past forty-eight hours has suffered a significant and unexpected setback. Our current assessment is that a second phase of the original attack was embedded within the systems themselves, and was triggered by the process of reconnection. The National Cyber Security Centre is working through the night to establish the full technical picture.

As a precaution, cloud services that were in the process of being restored have been taken back offline. This includes platforms and services that were cleared and returned to operation earlier today. I understand the frustration of that. But until we understand the nature of what we are dealing with, we cannot leave those systems running. The NCSC has made this recommendation and I have accepted it.

I know many of you experienced this directly this evening. In shops. At terminals. On your phones. I know many of you have seen messages on your banking applications using the word “permanently.” I want to address that. Those messages were generated automatically by systems detecting that their connection to verified records has been interrupted. They describe a technical condition at this moment in time. They are not a statement of fact about your money and they are not a prediction.
I must be straightforward with you.
I told you on Monday that we were looking at days, not weeks. Last night I told you we were on track. That schools would reopen on Monday. That businesses would follow.

I cannot confirm that timetable tonight. We are, in many respects, back to where we were at the start of this week. The progress we made was real. The systems that were restored were functioning. What happened this evening does not undo the work that was done — but it does change the picture, and I need my security and technical advisers to complete their assessment before I can set out a new timetable. I will not give you a timeline I cannot stand behind.
Here is what has not changed.
Our essential services are unaffected. Hospitals are open. Emergency services are responding. Power, water and gas supplies are secure. The emergency measures already in place remain in place.
Schools will not reopen on Monday as planned. ARC Education will continue and we will update parents as the position becomes clearer.

For the time being, all non-essential travel should stop. Stay local. Stay close to your families. Check on your neighbours, particularly those living alone. If you need help, your local Community Recovery Hub remains open.

ARC Emergency and ARC Local will continue to provide live updates through the night and into tomorrow. My colleagues and I will address you again at nine o’clock tomorrow morning with a full assessment of where we stand.
This is a setback. It is a serious one. But we have the infrastructure, the people and the resolve to deal with it. We dealt with the first shock. We will deal with this one.
Stay safe. Stay local.

paras.t: The screen holds for a moment after he finishes. The seal. The flag. Then black.
Amy doesn't say anything. She picks up her tea. It'll be cold by now. She drinks it anyway.

I don't know what I expected. Something. An admission, maybe. A flicker of honesty behind the rehearsed concern and the carefully modulated pauses. What we got was a man in a good suit reading someone else's words in front of someone else's flag, telling us that everything was under control in a way that made it abundantly clear that nothing was under control and that this was, in fact, the point.

The map was a nice touch. The national recovery hub map. Clean. Colour-coded. Teal dots for open hubs, gold for opening soon. It looked like a weather forecast. Friendly and reassuring and designed to make you feel that someone, somewhere, was across it. Three thousand and something. More by morning. The Prime Minister had gestured at it with the practised ease of a man who had never set foot in a community centre in his life.
I pick up my phone.
ARC Local. The app that didn't exist eight days ago and now runs half the country. Auto-detected location. It knows where I am. Of course it does.
The national map was abstract. A screensaver for the anxious. This is not abstract.
Mid & East Sussex Recovery Hubs.

There they are. My towns. Lewes. Uckfield. Crowborough. Haywards Heath. The dots scattered across the Weald like a rash. I zoom in. Burgess Hill. Heathfield. Battle. The familiar geography rendered in satellite green and ARC teal.

One hundred and one hubs open. One hundred and one church halls, leisure centres, school gyms and community rooms pressed into service as distribution points for a system that materialised fully formed, as if from nowhere, in less than a week. Target by 0800 tomorrow: one hundred and forty-three.
Brighton and Hove has twenty-two. Wealden has nineteen. Hastings sixteen. Even Rother, which struggles to keep a post office open, has eight.
I scroll east. Bexhill. Eastbourne. The coast peppered with dots. Each one a place I've driven past or walked through or cursed at for its one-way system. Each one now a node in something. A network.

Sixty more gold dots. Opening within 24 hours. Not being built. Being opened. Because they were already built. Or at least the infrastructure was. The registration points. The distribution routes. The capacity allocations. Kate said the clinic hub she's been volunteering at had cabling in the walls that wasn't connected to anything she recognised. Pre-installed. Waiting.
Amy leans over. She looks at the screen. She doesn't say anything for a while.
'That's a lot of dots.'
'One hundred and sixty-one by tomorrow morning. Just for our bit of Sussex.'
She processes this. Amy processes things differently to me. I catastrophise and connect. She absorbs and waits. When she's ready, she speaks. And when she speaks, she's usually right.
'How do they know where to put them?'
'The PM said local authorities and emergency—'

'No. How do they know. How do they know that Heathfield needs a hub and where to put it. How do they know the capacity for Wealden versus Rother. This isn't improvised, Simon. You don't colour-code an app in six days.'
I look at her.
She looks at the screen.
The dogs stir. Wilf does that thing where he repositions his entire body by moving one leg. Olive doesn't move at all but somehow ends up closer to the radiator.
'Dev would love this,' I say.
'Dev would already have it archived and annotated.'
She's not wrong.

I take a screenshot of the map. Lewes to Rye. One hundred and one dots of teal. Sixty dots of gold. A network that appeared like infrastructure always appears when it's been planned for years — suddenly, and all at once, and with a colour scheme.
I send it to Dev.
No message. Just the screenshot.
He'll know.

The night before money arrives. Tinned tomato soup, toast from frozen bread, tea. The fridge has insulin, butter, and half a lemon. Amy’s been at the hub all day. Simon watches BBC — the same three experts saying ‘unprecedented’ in slightly different configurations. He turns it off. Checks ARC Emergency instead. Reads the same information in a third of the time. Doesn’t notice the preference forming.
