paras.t: Two o’clock. Simon goes to Tesco. The queue starts in the car park. Not panicked — orderly, British, resigned. Soldiers in the car park directing traffic, high-vis over camo. Inside: shelves patchy but bread and milk and tins in decent supply. The beep. Simon holds his phone to the terminal. ARC EMERGENCY — PAYMENT CONFIRMED — BALANCE: £131.40. He’s bought bread, milk, eggs, pasta, tinned tomatoes, teabags, dog food, paracetamol, and a bottle of wine.

Amy leaves at 7am for the hub. Hamper distribution starts at 8. George is on Instagram — it came back yesterday afternoon. The crisis is the content. Everyone posting their Dark Month experience. Empty shelf photos. Hamper queue selfies. The algorithm doing what it always does. WhatsApp is alive. A text from Simon’s mum sent at 11pm on Valentine’s Day: ‘Hope you had a lovely evening darling xxx.’ Sent before the Event. Arriving now.

The first chapter that compresses time. EPM Week 2 refresh: another £200 drops into the phone. A push notification. Simon sees it, swipes it away, tells Amy over dinner. Already normalised. Six days from ‘the Chancellor has put money in your hands’ to swiping away the notification like a Deliveroo promo. The PM does a midweek address. Simon doesn’t watch it. He sees the ARC push summary while making coffee. Doesn’t turn the telly on.

Dev’s forensic dump arrives at 2am. The Signal channel goes from short probes to a wall of text. ARC timeline analysis. AIDA architecture matching a DARPA proposal from 2019. The FCA interoperability mandate. The procurement contracts. Amy comes downstairs. Reads it over Simon’s shoulder. Neither of them speaks for a while. Then Amy says something practical — ‘What are we supposed to do with this?’ Simon doesn’t have an answer.

The dead zone. Dev’s forensic dump is a week old. Simon has read it three times. He can’t verify it, can’t dismiss it, can’t act on it. Social media is fully operational. The conversation has moved from ‘what happened’ to ‘what’s next.’ Half of it matches what Dev sent him. The other half is conspiracy noise he can’t distinguish from the signal. Amy comes home from the hub: ‘You’re doing the thing again.’ ‘What thing?’

[STUB — Day 26–30. The language shifts. PM Week 3: 'The old system failed us.' Nobody says 'back to normal' anymore. Kate notices registration equipment at community centres. Cash nearly exhausted. BBC running 'what might the new system look like' segments. The country stops waiting to go back and starts waiting to go forward.]

[STUB — Day 31–35. The anticipation week. BBC speculation on new system. Hubs being fitted with registration equipment — Kate notices. Cash virtually gone. PM expected to address nation ‘within days.’ 23 nations confirm coordinated announcement. Schools ready to reopen within 48 hours. The build-up.]

[STUB — Day 35. HEAVY — centrepiece turn. PM prime time. International simulcast. Seven beats: old system broken → ARC survived → AIDA → THE DEBT JUBILEE → registration open → not temporary → 23 nations. Amy's eyes when the mortgage disappears. Street parties. Neighbours hugging. The gratitude is seismic, genuine, earned. Dev mesh: 'speech metadata. created 9 feb. six days before the attack.' Amy's inner voice: 'God help me, yes.']

[STUB — Day 36–37. Registered vs unregistered contrast. Amy's mum sends hamper photos. George: 'Mum, can I just register? I'm 19.' He does. 'Dad, it's just an app.' Simon finds out via AIDA notification. BritCoin first allocation: 10,000 BC/adult.]

[STUB — Day 38–42. Sam and Emilia registered by their mum. 'Your ex texted.' The knife that isn't AIDA — it's his ex-wife doing the right thing. Simon's rage/relief/grief. Mortgage showing £0.00. The horror of ease.]

[STUB — Day 49. Chloe in the kitchen doorway. 17. 'I'm literally the only person in my year who isn't registered.' She needs Simon's signature — under 18. The A-levels she's missing. Amy won't sign without Simon. AIDA learning platform genuinely excellent. Hub learning: worksheets.]

[STUB — Day 56. HEAVY. Kate from next door. Psychologist. Registered yesterday. Wine in the garden. 'I know what they're doing, Simon. The NLP in the speeches. The fear-reassurance cycle. I can see every stitch in the puppet strings.' She drinks. 'I registered anyway. Because seeing the strings doesn't make you less of a puppet. It just makes you a sad one.' Simon's mirror.]

[STUB — Day 63. Amy's brothers are holdouts. Rupert can't get his prescription. Jamie can't buy fuel. Amy's mum crying on the phone. Simon visits dad in care home — dad registered by institution, no consent. AIDA knows Simon through everyone else's data. Protest that evening: hundreds in a nation of 67 million. Police almost bored. 'Resistance is a luxury good.']

[STUB — Day 70. HEAVY — heart of the game. After the teenagers have gone upstairs. Dogs on the kitchen floor. Kettle boiling. Amy: 'Where's the mass, Simon?' The conversation. Not screaming — quiet, tired, honest. Dev on mesh: 'Don't do it.' AIDA: 'We're here when you're ready, Simon.' It used his name. 'We'll go tomorrow. Together.']
She said nothing. She played Northern Sky by Nick Drake. We hugged. We cried. We left for the Community Recovery Hub.

I never felt magic crazy as this
I never saw moons, knew the meaning of the sea
I never held emotion in the palm of my hand
Or felt sweet breezes in the top of a tree
But now you're here
Brighten my northern sky
Mid Morning
It was the discussion on everyone's lips. But ask the majority if they were registering you'd get a bemused look. What do you mean if?

On the face of it who could argue? Debts erased, £1000 per month (well 1000 Brits, same same), food hampers. And hampers they were. A far cry from ration books and make-do-and-mend. Fresh, healthy, tailored to your dietary requirements, customisable, delivered to your door. And free. And for what, registering on a 'new App'.
They simply couldn't be made to see the downside. Or they refused to acknowledge it. As Cypher said, 'ignorance is bliss'.
Some could see it, of course. We'd been on the protests. I'd say there were more there than there were for the Lockdown marches.
Amy could see it. Of course she could. Or perhaps she felt it — that would be more accurate. Some things she simply understood.
Very female. Very Amy. Not knowledge. Intuition.
I'd put in the hard yards. Hour upon hour of research and 'deep dives'. Over a decade's worth. I had a file on them and they sure as hell had a file on me. They had a file on everyone.
Why are they doing this? She simply couldn't comprehend evil. But she knew there was a 'they'.

She'd be in floods of tears if she saw a dead deer on the road. It's not fair that this beautiful creature must die. I would be upset, but that was the way of the world. I didn't have her empathy. Not many did.
This however, this was beyond her comprehension. I responded with rage. She responded with sadness. Infinite sadness.
I didn't know what to say, what to do. I knew what was going on. Well I thought I did. I used to think I did. I was having my doubts. What if this is just progress, what if it's just better.
Karma police, arrest this man

I'd bombarded her, everyone and anyone who'd listen, with my 'research'. Sent links to essays by investigative journalists, punchy truth movement YouTube videos. Shown them scientific papers. I had a bulging digital file of them. I had half-read paperbacks exposing the whole nine yards. I'd talked about neo-feudalism, transhumanism, satanism, spiritual warfare, prophecy of the Third Temple, eschatology, eugenics. The list goes on. And on. I'd even jokingly prepared a conspiracy-nutter style presentation on a whiteboard, joining the dots with string. Some listened. Some shrugged. Some stared blankly. Some laughed. Many asked who are 'they'?

I'd tell all my friends, but they'd never believe me
They'd think that I'd finally lost it completely

Yet here I was. Already AIDA registered. Clean, easy, quick. 1000 Brits in my wallet. Soon to be several thousand more once we've presented our statements at the 'Community Recovery Hub'. You couldn't make this shit up. But someone did. They did. Oh, plus the house. In our name. No mortgage.
Soon they'll call our names and ask 'papers, please?'

What else can I be?
All apologies

article.title: UK GOVERNMENT EMERGENCY ALERT
article.body:
A major cyber incident has affected UK financial and digital infrastructure. Emergency services are responding. Systems are contained but not yet restored.

IMMEDIATE ACTIONS:

- Remain in your current location unless it is unsafe to do so. Do not attempt to travel unless it is a medical emergency.

ESSENTIAL SERVICES:

Hospitals are operational for EMERGENCY ONLY - all routine appointments are postponed

Police, fire, and ambulance services remain operational. Call 999 for life-threatening emergencies ONLY.

Mobile telephone and text services will be intermittent.

REPEAT: Telephone or text message communication is EMERGENCY ONLY

Water, gas, and electricity supplies are being maintained. Intermittent outages may occur.

All card and electronic banking payments have been suspended whilst the network is being repaired.

Internet access will be slow or inaccessible today. It is anticipated that it will be restored within the next 24 hours.

Official updates will be issued via emergency message and through BBC television and radio channels

WHAT WE KNOW:

Financial infrastructure across the UK has been subject to a coordinated cyber attack. Initial assessment indicates systems are contained but not yet restored.

WHAT WE ARE DOING:

The full resources of the state are being deployed. The Prime Minister will soon address the nation with further information.

Do not attempt to contact government agencies unless your life is in danger. All available personnel are responding to this incident.

STAY HOME. STAY CALM.

UPDATES TO FOLLOW.
article.footer: Source: UK Cabinet Office Emergency Services

items.text: UK GOVERNMENT EMERGENCY ALERT

article.title: UK GOVERNMENT EMERGENCY ALERT
article.body:
A major cyber incident has affected UK financial and digital infrastructure. Emergency services are responding.

IMMEDIATE ACTIONS

Remain in your current location unless it is unsafe to do so. Do not attempt to travel unless it is a medical emergency.

ESSENTIAL SERVICES

Hospitals are operational for EMERGENCY ONLY — all routine appointments are postponed.

Police, fire, and ambulance services remain operational. Call 999 for life-threatening emergencies ONLY.

Mobile telephone and text services will be intermittent. Telephone or text message communication is EMERGENCY ONLY.

Water, gas, and electricity supplies are being maintained. Intermittent outages may occur.

All card and electronic banking payments have been suspended whilst the network is being repaired.

Internet access will be slow or inaccessible today. It is anticipated that it will be restored within the next 24 hours.

Official updates will be issued via emergency message and through BBC television and radio channels.

WHAT WE KNOW

Financial infrastructure across the UK has been subject to a coordinated cyber attack. Initial assessment indicates systems are contained but not yet restored.

WHAT WE ARE DOING

The full resources of the state are being deployed. The Prime Minister will soon address the nation with further information.

Do not attempt to contact government agencies unless your life is in danger. All available personnel are responding to this incident.

STAY HOME. STAY CALM.

UPDATES TO FOLLOW.
article.footer: Source: UK Cabinet Office Emergency Services

items.text: ARC — Transcript: PM Address to the Nation — 15 February 2027

article.title:
PM’s Address to the Nation
15 February 2027
article.date: 15 February 2027 — 18:00 GMT — Transcript via ARC Emergency
article.body:
Good evening.

Yesterday, on Valentine’s Day, a little before midnight, a coordinated cyber attack struck the financial and digital infrastructure of the United Kingdom and twenty-two other nations. This has caused significant disruption to civilian systems in our nation and around the globe.

Here is what we know. I will not minimise it. The attack targeted the core transaction and record-keeping systems that underpin our banking, our public services, and much of our daily communication. Our security and intelligence services, working in close coordination with international partners, are engaged in a comprehensive response. I chaired COBRA at six o’clock this morning and have been in continuous session since.

Here is what I want you to understand. The damage is being assessed. The infrastructure is damaged, not destroyed. We are working — with every resource available to us — to restore normal service. Our current assessment is that this will take days, not weeks.

Let me be clear about what is not affected. Our electricity grid is operational. Our water supply is operational. Our gas network is operational. Our hospitals have power. Our emergency services are coordinating. No lives are in danger from the attack itself.

Many of you will have spent today unable to reach members of your family — unable to send emails, unable to use messaging apps, unable to refresh social media or stream the news the way you would on any other day. I know how difficult this is. I know how isolating it feels not to be able to reach a son or a daughter, a parent, a friend abroad.

These services have been restricted as a precaution while our cloud infrastructure is verified. They have not been damaged. We cannot leave them running while we are not yet certain they are safe. We expect to begin restoring them in stages from tomorrow morning, as verification work completes. Telephone calls and text messages remain operational throughout. If you need to reach someone urgently tonight, please use those.

Currently we are unable to access our bank accounts. Shops and businesses are unable to process our card payments. For this reason, for the next 24 hours retail, businesses and offices will be closed. A detailed plan for the opening of essential retail, including supermarkets, will be issued shortly.

Your savings are safe. Your deposits are protected. Nothing has been lost — only temporarily made inaccessible.

Schools were closed today and will remain closed for the remainder of the week. Hospitals remain open for emergencies only; all routine and non-urgent care has been postponed, also for the remainder of the week. All public transport services are suspended for the same period of time.

Our emergency services are operational. Our military and police forces will be visible, on the streets, to ensure the safety of every one of us.

The emergency communications platform on your phones — many of you will have already received alerts through it — is functioning as designed. It will continue to be your most reliable source of verified information in the coming days.

Part of this emergency communication system is ARC. You may have seen the app automatically installed on your devices throughout the course of the day. The ARC app adds an even more robust communication channel between Government and citizens.

I have spoken this afternoon with my counterparts across the affected nations. We are united — not only in our response, but in our resolve. This was an attack on all of us. It will be met by all of us.

In the meantime, I ask just three things of you.

First: for the next 24 hours, stay local, stay safe. Do not drive, unless it is a matter of life or death. This is not a lockdown, but a request. Look after each other. Check on your neighbours. Share what you have.

Second: do not fear. We will restore these systems. We will provide answers. And we will ensure that every family in this country is supported through this period. This period of days, not weeks.

Third: please continue to follow the guidance issued through ARC, the emergency alert system and on all BBC television and radio channels.

I know that millions of British citizens are overseas tonight — on holiday, on business, visiting family. The Foreign Secretary is in direct contact with our embassies and high commissions worldwide. I will have more to say on this tomorrow. If you are overseas and have a working phone, you will have received an ARC Emergency notification with guidance for your location.

I will address the nation again at nine o’clock tomorrow morning with a full operational update. There will be detailed updates from my colleagues in the Cabinet and experts from the National Cyber Security Centre during this period.

There are dark days, challenging days, ahead. We face them with our unique British spirit. We face them together.

Good night. And be well.

items.text: ARC — Transcript: PM Morning Address to the Nation — 16 February 2027

article.title:
PM’s Morning Address to the Nation
16 February 2027
article.date: 16 February 2027 — 09:00 GMT — Transcript via ARC Emergency
article.body:
Good morning.

I am speaking to you from Downing Street.

Last night I asked you to stay local, to follow the guidance, and to look after each other. You have done so, and the country has had a calm and orderly night. I want to thank you for that, briefly, before we move on.

Here is where we are this morning.

Overnight there were a small number of isolated incidents which were quickly contained by police and military personnel. Power, water, gas, and emergency services have remained fully operational throughout. There has been no further attack, here or in any of the other affected nations. I have spoken with my counterparts this morning. The picture is consistent. The response is coordinated.

I want to be clearer than I think we have been so far about what is actually offline and why. The infrastructure has been damaged — that is what I told you last night and it remains true. The damage is to the security layer underneath our banking and payment systems. But most of the systems sitting on top of that layer — the apps you use, the card networks, the bank databases — have not been damaged in themselves. They have been paused while the security layer underneath is being rebuilt to a higher standard. Your bank’s database has not been emptied. Your records have not been lost. We will turn them back on, in sequence, as quickly as it is responsible to do so.

Restoration work has been underway since yesterday morning. The assessment we have completed overnight gives us confidence in the timeline I set out last night — days, not weeks. The Chancellor and the Director of Operations at the National Cyber Security Centre will set out the detail with me at six o’clock this evening, including the schedule for the first systems to come back online tomorrow.

In the meantime — and this is the practical part.

A network of designated pharmacies and food retailers is opening across the country this morning under restricted hours, on a cash-only basis. Please be patient with staff. Please take only what your household needs. Queues are expected.

From midday today, Community Recovery Hubs will open at community centres, libraries, leisure centres, and places of worship in every local authority area. These are not food distribution centres. They are warm, welcoming places — for anyone who needs help, information, a hot meal, or simply somebody to talk to. Particularly if you are alone, or elderly, or finding this period difficult, please use them. Please tell your neighbours about them. Their locations are being distributed through ARC Emergency this morning.

Schools, hospitals for routine appointments, and public transport remain as I set out last night.

Communications networks are running with delays. Telephone calls and text messages are working, but congested — please reserve them for essential contact. Email, messaging, and internet services remain offline as a precaution while our infrastructure is verified. ARC Emergency and BBC broadcast remain reliable.

To British citizens overseas. Emergency consular arrangements are now in place with twenty-three affected nations and with countries not directly affected by Sunday’s attack. The first emergency repatriation flights departed early this morning from airports in Spain, Portugal, Greece, Turkey, and Thailand. ARC Emergency notifications are reaching British nationals overseas directly — unlike our Cell Broadcast alerts, which operate through UK mobile towers, ARC operates at device level and can reach any British-registered phone with a signal anywhere in the world. Your embassy has specific guidance for your location. Do not travel to airports unless directed to do so.

I will speak to you again at six o’clock this evening, with the Chancellor and the National Cyber Security Centre.

Until this evening. Be well.

items.text: ARC — Transcript: Joint Address to the Nation — 16 February 2027

article.title:
Joint Address to the Nation
PM, Chancellor, NCSC
16 February 2027
article.date: 16 February 2027 — 18:00 GMT — Transcript via ARC Emergency
article.body:
THE PRIME MINISTER: Good evening.

I want to begin by saying that the country has had a calm and patient day. Two days into this disruption, the streets are orderly, hospitals are open, emergency services are responding normally, and the early signs from our restoration work are good. I am grateful for that patience, and I will not over-thank you for it. We have a job to do, and we are getting on with it.

I am joined this evening, as I said I would be, by the Chancellor of the Exchequer and by Paul Chichester, the Director of Operations at the National Cyber Security Centre. The Chancellor will set out the practical measures and the restoration timeline. Paul will explain, in plain terms, what has happened and what is being done. I will close.

Chancellor.

THE CHANCELLOR: Thank you, Prime Minister.

I am going to focus on three things this evening. The restoration plan and what to expect tomorrow. The practical arrangements for the days in between. And the support measures that are now in place.

On restoration. The 24-hour assessment window the Prime Minister announced last night has now concluded. The picture from that assessment is broadly positive. The disruption is at the authentication layer — the cryptographic system that verifies who is who when a card is presented at a terminal, or when you log in to your bank. The legacy cryptography that has underpinned that layer for thirty years has been compromised. The newer authentication framework — already deployed across UK payment infrastructure under regulation from last year — has not been. Our work since yesterday morning has been to verify each banking application, each card network, and each payment acquirer’s systems, and to bring them back online on the new framework, in sequence, as each is confirmed safe.

That work is moving on schedule. The largest UK card networks expect to begin processing transactions through tomorrow morning, with the major UK banks following through the day as their core systems complete verification. We expect to see meaningful progress through Wednesday and Thursday, and the great majority of the retail payment estate to be operational by the weekend. The Prime Minister will give a detailed restoration update tomorrow evening at six o’clock.

To be clear about what this means in practice tomorrow: some terminals at some retailers will accept some cards from some banks. Coverage will broaden through the day. If your card does not work at a particular terminal in the morning, please do not assume the system is broken — it may simply not yet have been restored. Cash will continue to be the most reliable payment method until coverage is widespread.

On the practical arrangements. From seven o’clock tomorrow morning, the network of designated retail outlets that opened this morning will expand significantly. More stores in more locations. Longer opening hours. Major supermarket chains, additional pharmacies, post offices, and selected hardware and home essentials stores will join the designated network. The full updated list is being distributed tonight through ARC Emergency, the BBC, and printed notices at every Community Recovery Hub. Cash payments only, until card coverage is restored. A household member may visit once per day.

The designated fuel network will continue, expanding to additional stations from tomorrow. Cash only, with rationing per vehicle. The list is being distributed alongside the retail list. Please use the designated stations, and please travel only if you need to.

From ten o’clock tomorrow morning, a designated network of high street bank branches will open between ten and two for cash withdrawals. Daily withdrawal limits will apply, and these will be communicated through ARC Emergency overnight. Please do not attempt to access online banking or mobile banking — these services are paused while restoration completes, and attempting to use them will not bring them back any sooner.

On support. Community Recovery Hubs are now open across every local authority area. They are warm, welcoming places — hot meals, hot drinks, a place to sit, somebody to talk to. They are particularly intended for those who are alone, those who are elderly, those without smartphones, those finding this period anxious. They are open today, they will be open tomorrow, and they will continue to be open for as long as is needed.

On wages, pensions, and benefits — I know this is a question on many minds. I will be straightforward with you. Your entitlements are protected. They are commitments of the Government and they will be honoured in full as our payment infrastructure is restored. I cannot promise that your usual payment will arrive in your account this week through the usual channels — that depends on the speed of restoration. What I can promise is that anyone in genuine difficulty in the meantime — anyone short of food, anyone short of essentials, anyone whose elderly parent or vulnerable neighbour is struggling — will be supported through the Community Recovery Hubs. Every hub has hot meals, hot drinks, volunteers and local authority staff trained to help, and information about what to do next. Detailed guidance for individual entitlements during this restoration period will be issued tomorrow afternoon, through ARC Emergency, the BBC, and at every hub. No one in this country needs to be hungry, cold, or alone tonight.

A business continuity package will be announced tomorrow at midday. The detailed guidance for employers, sole traders, and small businesses on how to handle this period will follow with it.

On schools. Schools are on schedule to reopen early next week. In the meantime, the Department for Education is working with local authorities to make educational content available through ARC from tomorrow morning. Your school will contact you directly with details.

For British nationals stranded overseas, the government will meet reasonable hotel and subsistence costs for the duration. These obligations will be settled government-to-government — no individual will be asked to pay upfront and seek reimbursement.

Prime Minister.

THE PRIME MINISTER: Thank you, Chancellor. Paul.

NCSC DIRECTOR OF OPERATIONS: Thank you, Prime Minister. I will be brief.

I want to explain, plainly, what happened and what we are doing about it.

The attack targeted the legacy public-key cryptography that has underpinned online banking and card payments for thirty years — the algorithms RSA, ECDSA, Diffie-Hellman. These standards have now been comprehensively compromised across the twenty-three affected nations. This was not a conventional ransomware attack. The malware was designed to undermine trust in the cryptography, not to encrypt or to steal.

That is why systems have been taken offline. What has been compromised is the authentication layer — the mathematical proof that, when a card is tapped at a terminal, the parties to the transaction are who they say they are.

I want to be precise about a question some of you will be asking. There is a newer authentication framework — known as ARC, mandated by the Financial Conduct Authority under Policy Statement twenty-six, four, and integrated across all UK payment infrastructure since 30 September last year. ARC operates at the device level, beneath the application layer, and uses post-quantum cryptographic standards. It has not been compromised by this attack. It is the framework on which this broadcast is reaching you — the ARC Emergency app runs on top of it. It is also the framework on which the wider banking and card payment systems sit. What we are now in the process of bringing back online is the application layer above the framework: each bank’s systems, each card network, each payment acquirer’s infrastructure — every one of which must be verified and restored on the new framework before transactions can flow.

In the hours following Sunday night’s attack, the National Cyber Security Centre issued an emergency directive, under Civil Contingencies Act authority, to UK cloud service providers and major communications platforms. The directive suspended all non-essential consumer internet services to prevent any lateral spread of the attack into other infrastructure. This is standard cyber-incident procedure — the same approach taken by United States agencies after the SolarWinds incident in 2020. As verification work completes, those services will be progressively restored.

In practical terms tonight: telephone calls and text messages remain operational but congested. Email, messaging applications, and social media remain suspended. Tomorrow morning we will begin phased restoration of email services, followed by messaging platforms later in the week. ARC Emergency and BBC broadcast remain reliable.

I will provide a further technical update tomorrow afternoon. Prime Minister.

THE PRIME MINISTER: Thank you, Paul. Thank you, Chancellor.

I will close briefly.

Two days ago, before any of us had heard of any of this, a coordinated attack was made on the financial infrastructure of twenty-three countries, including ours. Two days on, the lights are still on, the hospitals are still open, the streets are calm, and the work to restore our systems is moving on schedule. That is the picture. It is, broadly, a good one.

Tomorrow I expect the first systems to begin coming back. Coverage will be patchy in the morning and stronger by the evening. The Chancellor and I will speak to you again at six o’clock with a full update. I do not expect to need to keep you informed at this rhythm beyond this week, and I do not intend to keep you on the news any longer than necessary.

Until tomorrow evening, please continue with the three things I asked of you yesterday. Stay local. Stay safe. Look after each other.

Good night. And be well.

items.text: ARC — Transcript: PM Address to the Nation — 17 February 2027

article.title:
PM’s Address to the Nation
17 February 2027
article.date: 17 February 2027 — 18:00 GMT — Transcript via ARC Emergency
article.body:
Good evening.

I said I would return at six with a progress report, and I am here with an encouraging update.

Forty-eight hours ago, our payment infrastructure was offline. Today, payment terminals are processing transactions across the country. Not all terminals. Not all cards. Not yet. But the trajectory is clear, and it is accelerating.

On your screen is a tracker that shows a regional breakdown of terminal restoration. Thirty-eight per cent of payment terminals are now operational, up from zero on Monday. Some of you will have used your card today. More of you will be able to tomorrow. These figures will be updated hourly and sent to you via ARC Emergency and Local ARC Updates. I will share these figures every evening until they are no longer needed.

The London Stock Exchange has confirmed that trading will resume tomorrow morning. This is a significant step. The markets are returning because the data underpinning them is intact and verified.

The network of essential retail outlets that opened yesterday has expanded today, as we said it would. Longer hours. More stores. More locations. From tomorrow morning, designated high street bank branches will open between ten and two for cash withdrawals — the list has been published through ARC and is available at your nearest Community Recovery Hub.

Our transport network is recovering. Limited rail services are running on key routes using manual signalling while our digital systems are verified. Transport for London has restored partial Tube and bus services. Fuel distribution continues at designated stations. The stay-local guidance remains in place, but we have broadened the definition of essential travel to include travel to work for those in critical roles, and travel to care for vulnerable relatives.

I want to say a word about the international picture. This attack struck twenty-three nations. I have spoken with fourteen heads of government in the last forty-eight hours. We are coordinating closely with our allies — sharing intelligence, sharing technical expertise, and learning from each other’s responses in real time. I have to be direct with you: not every country is recovering at the same pace. You will have seen reports of disorder in some cities overseas. That has not happened here, and I want to thank you for that. The calm and discipline shown by the British public over these three days has been, frankly, extraordinary. I spoke with the Japanese Prime Minister this morning, and he echoed that sentiment — our two nations, he said, have responded with a composure that others have not. We are sharing our technical recovery framework with partner nations who have requested it. The United Kingdom is among the first to begin restoring payment services. That is not luck. That is preparation, and it is resilience.

Emergency repatriation flights have now operated from fourteen countries. Over forty thousand British nationals returned to the UK today, with further flights running through the night and into tomorrow. Cross-channel ferry services are running on emergency schedules. For those still overseas — your ARC notification will update with new flight schedules as they are confirmed.

On communications. I know this has been one of the hardest parts of this week — not being able to message your family, to email, to connect in the ways we rely on. We said on Monday that we had restricted these services ourselves, as a precaution, while our cloud infrastructure was verified. That verification is progressing, and I can now set out the next steps. Email services are being restored this evening. For those of you with family overseas — and I know there are millions of you who have not been able to reach loved ones — international messaging services, including WhatsApp, will be restored from tomorrow morning. Domestic messaging services will follow as each platform completes verification with the National Cyber Security Centre. I know that is not fast enough. But the sequence matters, and we are moving as quickly as we safely can.

Schools will reopen on Monday. I confirm that without reservation. In the meantime, ARC Education went live this morning. Over two million households accessed educational content today. Your children’s schools are uploading lesson materials, reading lists, and video lessons through their local authority ARC channels. The streaming is fast, the materials are good, and your children’s teachers are working hard to keep them learning. I have been told by more than one parent that it is, and I quote, “better than lockdown.” ARC Education will continue until schools reopen.

The practical guidance on support during this period was published this afternoon through ARC, as the Chancellor committed to last evening. If you are in difficulty — if you cannot access food, medication, or essential supplies — your local Community Recovery Hub is there for you.

I want to say one more thing about the infrastructure that has made this recovery possible. The ARC authentication framework — the layer that sits beneath our payment systems, that has been powering your emergency alerts, that kept this channel open when everything else went dark — performed exactly as it was designed to. It is this framework that is enabling the restoration you are seeing on your screens tonight. It worked. And it will continue to work.

We expect the great majority of services to be restored by the weekend, with a return to normal schooling and work patterns from Monday and Tuesday of next week.

I will address you again tomorrow evening at six.

Be well.

items.text: ARC — Transcript: PM Address to the Nation — 19 February 2027

article.title:
PM’s Address to the Nation
19 February 2027
article.date: 19 February 2027 — 21:00 GMT — Transcript via ARC Emergency
article.body:
Good evening.

I was due to address you at six o’clock this evening. Shortly before that broadcast, at approximately half past five, financial systems across twenty-three nations experienced a further phase of disruption. The United Kingdom is one of those nations. I took the decision to delay this address so that I could instead chair an emergency COBRA session and speak to my counterparts in the affected nations. I wanted to come to you with information, not speculation.

Here is what we know.

The restoration of payment and banking services that had been progressing well over the past forty-eight hours has suffered a significant and unexpected setback. Our current assessment is that a second phase of the original attack was embedded within the systems themselves, and was triggered by the process of reconnection. The National Cyber Security Centre is working through the night to establish the full technical picture.

As a precaution, cloud services that were in the process of being restored have been taken back offline. This includes platforms and services that were cleared and returned to operation earlier today. I understand the frustration of that. But until we understand the nature of what we are dealing with, we cannot leave those systems running. The NCSC has made this recommendation and I have accepted it.

I know many of you experienced this directly this evening. In shops. At terminals. On your phones. I know many of you have seen messages on your banking applications using the word “permanently.” I want to address that. Those messages were generated automatically by systems detecting that their connection to verified records has been interrupted. They describe a technical condition at this moment in time. They are not a statement of fact about your money and they are not a prediction.

I must be straightforward with you.

I told you on Monday that we were looking at days, not weeks. Last night I told you we were on track. That schools would reopen on Monday. That businesses would follow.

I cannot confirm that timetable tonight. We are, in many respects, back to where we were at the start of this week. The progress we made was real. The systems that were restored were functioning. What happened this evening does not undo the work that was done — but it does change the picture, and I need my security and technical advisers to complete their assessment before I can set out a new timetable. I will not give you a timeline I cannot stand behind.

Here is what has not changed.

Our essential services are unaffected. Hospitals are open. Emergency services are responding. Power, water and gas supplies are secure. The emergency measures already in place remain in place.

Schools will not reopen on Monday as planned. ARC Education will continue and we will update parents as the position becomes clearer.

Shops and supermarkets will not open tomorrow. All other businesses, hospitality and leisure venues remain closed until further notice. Your Community Recovery Hub will provide food and essential supplies.

For the time being, all non-essential travel should stop. Stay local. Stay close to your families. Check on your neighbours, particularly those living alone. If you need help, your local Community Recovery Hub remains open.

ARC Emergency and ARC Local will continue to provide live updates through the night and into tomorrow. My colleagues and I will address you again at nine o’clock tomorrow morning with a full assessment of where we stand.

This is a setback. It is a serious one. But we have the infrastructure, the people and the resolve to deal with it. We dealt with the first shock. We will deal with this one.

Stay safe. Stay local.

items.text: ARC — Transcript: PM Address to the Nation — 18 February 2027

article.title:
PM’s Address to the Nation
18 February 2027
article.date: 18 February 2027 — 18:00 GMT — Transcript via ARC Emergency
article.body:
Good evening. A short update tonight, because the picture is a good one.

Sixty-one per cent of payment terminals are now operational. Some regions are above seventy per cent. The numbers speak for themselves.

The London Stock Exchange reopened this morning. Trading was orderly. Designated bank branches opened for cash withdrawals as planned. These are the signs of a system that is recovering, and recovering well.

International messaging was restored this morning. I know that many of you have been able to reach family overseas today for the first time this week. The phased restoration of internet services, email, and domestic messaging is continuing, and the National Cyber Security Centre is clearing platforms as quickly and safely as it can.

Schools reopen on Monday. ARC Education continues until then.

We are now working with business and industry on a phased return to normal operations from Monday. Many businesses depend on cloud-hosted platforms and cannot fully reopen until those services are restored. The NCSC is prioritising the verification and restoration of business-critical cloud services over the weekend to support that reopening. A detailed sector-by-sector timetable will be published through ARC tomorrow.

We remain on track. The great majority of services will be restored by the weekend, with normal schooling and work patterns resuming from Monday.

I will address you again tomorrow evening at six.

Be well.

items.text: ARC — Transcript: Joint Address to the Nation — 20 Feb 2027

article.title:
Joint Address to the Nation
20 February 2027
article.date: 20 February 2027 — 09:00 GMT — Transcript via ARC Emergency
article.body:
THE PRIME MINISTER: Good morning.

I said last night that my colleagues and I would speak to you at nine o’clock this morning with a full assessment. I am joined by the Chancellor of the Exchequer and by Paul Chichester, the Director of Operations at the National Cyber Security Centre. I will set out the position. The Chancellor will address the financial and practical picture — including, directly, the questions I know many of you have been asking about wages, mortgages, and other financial obligations. Paul will explain the technical assessment his teams have completed overnight. I will close.

I told you last night that what happened was a setback. Overnight assessment tells us it is more than that.

What happened at half past five yesterday evening was not the same kind of event as Monday. Monday’s attack locked our systems. Yesterday’s attack damaged the records those systems held. I want to be precise about this, because precision matters and because you deserve it. The payment terminals that were restored, the card networks that were functioning, the bank systems that were coming back online — those restorations were real. They were working. What happened yesterday did not undo that work. It made the data underneath it unreliable.

I know that many of you spent the last three days believing this was nearly over. I know many of you made decisions on that basis — spent cash you were saving, made plans for Monday, told your children they’d be back at school. I am sorry that the timetable I gave you is no longer one I can stand behind.

But I want to be clear about two things before I hand to the Chancellor.

First: the essential infrastructure of this country is unaffected. Power, water, gas, hospitals, emergency services — all operational, all stable, all continuing. The military and civil contingency framework that has been supporting you since Monday remains in place and is not going anywhere.

Second: we are not starting again. The work done this week — the hubs, the retail network, the fuel distribution, the ARC communications framework — all of that holds. What has changed is the financial picture underneath it, and the Chancellor will address that now.

Chancellor.

THE CHANCELLOR: Thank you, Prime Minister.

I am going to speak plainly this morning, because I think you need me to, and because the situation requires it.

On Monday evening I told you your records were safe. On Tuesday evening I set out a restoration timetable. On Wednesday I showed you a tracker moving in the right direction. On Thursday I told you we were on track. All of that was true when I said it.

What happened yesterday evening has changed the picture. The second phase of this attack targeted the records themselves — the transaction histories, account balances, and financial data that sit behind your bank account, your mortgage, your pension, your savings. Our current assessment is that a significant proportion of these records, across the UK banking system and across the twenty-two other affected nations, have been corrupted. I want to be careful with my language. I am not telling you your money is gone. I am telling you that the digital records which describe your money — how much you have, what you owe, what you are owed — are currently unreliable, and we cannot yet confirm the extent to which they can be fully restored.

I know what that sentence means to you. I know what it means to wake up on a Saturday morning and hear the Chancellor of the Exchequer say that.

So let me tell you what we are doing about it, and I will start with the thing I think most of you are worried about right now.

Your obligations. Your mortgage. Your rent. Your gas bill. Your credit card. Your car finance. The direct debit that was supposed to go out on Monday and didn’t. The wages that didn’t arrive yesterday.

Here is the position. No payment can currently be processed through the UK banking system. That means no mortgage payment has been collected from you this week. No rent payment has left your account. No direct debit has been processed. No standing order has been executed. None of these are late. None of these are missed. They are, like everything else, frozen.

This morning I am issuing an emergency direction under the Civil Contingencies Act to every mortgage lender, landlord, utility provider, insurer, and credit provider operating in the United Kingdom. The direction is simple. No enforcement action. No penalty. No interest. No default. No arrears recording. No disconnection. No eviction proceedings. For the duration of this emergency, all financial obligations between individuals and institutions are suspended. This is not optional guidance. It is a legal direction, effective immediately, and it will remain in force until I revoke it.

I want to say that again, because I know some of you need to hear it twice. If you have a mortgage, you do not owe a payment this month. If you rent, your landlord cannot pursue you. If your energy bill was due, it is not due. If your car finance payment has not gone out, that is not a default. No record of non-payment will be made against any person for any obligation that could not be met during this period. You have not missed anything. The system that would process these payments does not currently exist.

On wages. I know that yesterday was payday for many of you, and that your wages did not arrive. I know that weekly-paid workers have now missed a full pay cycle. Employers cannot currently run payroll because the banking infrastructure that processes BACS payments is offline. HMRC’s PAYE systems are offline. The employer is not at fault. You are not at fault. The emergency payment infrastructure I will set out tomorrow is designed to put money directly into your hands — on your devices — regardless of whether your employer can currently process payroll. In the meantime, emergency cash provision is available at every Community Recovery Hub. No one in this country should go without income because the banking system is offline.

On pensions and benefits. The position I set out on Tuesday evening has not changed. State pension and benefit payments are commitments of the Government and will be honoured in full. For those whose payments were due this week and have not arrived, emergency provision is available at every Community Recovery Hub.

On the practical measures that come next. We are today accelerating the deployment of emergency payment infrastructure that does not depend on the legacy banking system. I expect to be able to set out the detail of this tomorrow, with payments beginning within forty-eight hours. This infrastructure will put money in your hands — on your devices — so that you can buy food, fuel, and essentials regardless of what happens to the banking system. It is being built on the ARC framework, which has been the one piece of infrastructure that has worked, without interruption, since Monday morning.

I know some of you are already asking what this means for your mortgage, your debts, your financial commitments in the longer term. It is the right question. It is not one I can answer this morning. When the full extent of the damage to financial records has been assessed, we will set out the position clearly. Until then, the direction I have issued today means that no obligation will be enforced and no penalty applied. That is enough for now.

Prime Minister.

THE PRIME MINISTER: Thank you, Chancellor. Paul.

NCSC DIRECTOR OF OPERATIONS: Thank you, Prime Minister. I will be brief and technical, because I think that is what is needed this morning.

Overnight, my teams have completed a preliminary assessment of yesterday’s event. I want to set out what we now understand.

Monday’s attack and yesterday’s event were two phases of a single operation. The first phase compromised the cryptographic layer — the authentication system that verifies identity when a card is used or a banking application is accessed. That phase was designed to be disruptive but recoverable. We recovered from it. You saw the recovery on your screens this week.

The second phase, which activated yesterday evening, targeted a different layer. It targeted the data itself — the records, the balances, the transaction histories. This phase was not designed to lock that data or to hold it to ransom. It was designed to overwrite it. The technical term is corruption rather than encryption. Encrypted data can be decrypted with the right key. Corrupted data has been replaced with meaningless information. The original data, in the affected systems, is not behind a locked door. It has been written over.

I want to be precise about what this means for restoration. The recovery work we completed this week — bringing card networks, banking applications, and payment terminals back online — was sound work and it was successful. But it was recovering the pipes. What flowed through those pipes — the data — has now been damaged at source. Reconnecting a pipe to a contaminated reservoir does not give you clean water. That is, in simplified terms, the position we are in.

Our assessment is that the two phases were designed as a sequence. The first phase created the conditions — took systems offline, triggered the recovery process. The second phase exploited the recovery itself — the process of reconnecting systems to central databases provided the activation pathway for the corruption payload. This is sophisticated. It is unprecedented in scale. And it confirms that we are dealing with a level of planning and capability that goes beyond anything we have previously attributed to any known threat actor.

I want to be clear about what is not affected. The ARC authentication framework, which operates at the device level using post-quantum cryptographic standards, has not been compromised. It was not targeted by either phase of the attack. The emergency communications infrastructure — ARC Emergency, ARC Local — remains fully operational. Power, water, gas, and transport control systems operate on separate networks and are unaffected.

My recommendation to the Prime Minister and Cabinet, which has been accepted, is that all legacy banking applications and cloud-hosted financial services remain offline until the full scope of the data corruption has been mapped. I understand the frustration of that recommendation. But reconnecting systems to data we cannot verify would cause more harm than the delay.

We will provide a further technical assessment on Monday morning.

Prime Minister.

THE PRIME MINISTER: Thank you, Paul. Thank you, Chancellor.

Let me close.

Five days ago this country woke up to something none of us had experienced before. For three of those days, the picture improved. Services returned. Terminals worked. I told you we were on track and I believed it.

Yesterday evening the picture changed again, and I know that the ground feels less steady this morning than it has all week. I know some of you are frightened. I know some of you are angry. I understand both.

Here is what I want you to hold on to. The infrastructure that has kept this country running since Monday — the hubs, the fuel network, the food distribution, the emergency services, the ARC communications system — none of that has been touched by yesterday’s event. It is all still there. It is all still working. And the emergency measures the Chancellor has just set out — the obligations freeze, the emergency payment infrastructure — are designed to carry us through whatever comes next, for as long as is needed.

This is no longer a matter of days. I will not give you a timeline I cannot stand behind. What I will give you is this: every resource of this Government, every capability of our security and technical services, and the coordinated effort of twenty-three nations is working on this. The Chancellor’s emergency payment infrastructure will be operational within forty-eight hours. When it is, money will be in your hands and food will be on your tables. That is my commitment, and I will keep it.

In the meantime, the same three things I have asked of you since Monday. Stay local. Stay safe. Look after each other. Your Community Recovery Hubs remain open — please use them, particularly if you are elderly, alone, or struggling. ARC Emergency remains your most reliable source of information.

We will address you again this evening at six with a further update.

Be well.

items.text: ARC — Transcript: PM Address to the Nation — 20 February 2027 (Evening)

article.title:
PM’s Address to the Nation
20 February 2027
article.date: 20 February 2027 — 18:00 GMT — Transcript via ARC Emergency
article.body:
Good evening.

This morning I sat in this room with the Chancellor and Paul Chichester and told you the truth about where we stand. I asked them to hold nothing back, and they didn’t. I know it was hard to hear. I know that for many of you today has been the worst day of this crisis — not because something new has happened, but because the hope you carried through the week is gone, and what’s left feels uncertain and frightening.

I’m not going to pretend otherwise. But I am going to tell you what has happened since this morning and what is coming.

The Chancellor’s emergency direction — the freeze on all mortgage payments, rent, bills, credit, and financial obligations — is now in force. It is law. No lender, no landlord, no utility company can pursue you for anything. That protection holds for as long as this emergency lasts, and I will not revoke it until I am certain you are ready.

On essential retail. I know that many of you are concerned about food and basic supplies. Local shops in some areas have remained open and I am grateful to every shopkeeper who has kept their doors open this week. Tomorrow afternoon, designated essential retailers — supermarkets, pharmacies, and fuel stations — will reopen. The Chancellor will set out the arrangements at midday.

Since this morning, Community Recovery Hubs have expanded across the country. I want to show you something.

Behind me is the current map of Community Recovery Hubs operating across the United Kingdom as of five o’clock this evening. There are more than three thousand open right now. By tomorrow morning that number will exceed five thousand. Every one of those points of light is a place you can walk to — a library, a community centre, a church hall, a school — where there are people ready to help. Hot food. Medical advice. Information. Somewhere warm.

Your regional hub map is being sent to your ARC Local right now. If you have someone nearby who is elderly, alone, or struggling — please check on them tonight and help them find their nearest hub tomorrow.

I want to say something about what I have seen today. I have seen volunteers who left their own homes — their own worries, their own kitchen drawers with the notes counted and recounted — to open a church hall at six in the morning for people they’ve never met. I have seen retired nurses walking into hubs and asking where to start. I have seen neighbours who didn’t know each other’s names on Monday cooking together on Saturday. That is not the Government. That is you. And it is the thing that no crisis can break.

On the wider picture. Several of our partner nations have today begun deploying their own emergency payment measures. We are not alone in this, and we are not behind. There are plans well advanced that will ensure no one in this country goes without.

I will address you again tomorrow with the Chancellor at midday with the full detail of the measures I have described tonight. The announcement will be broadcast live on BBC television and radio channels, and on ARC Emergency and ARC Local.

The same three things. Stay local. Stay safe. Look after each other.

Be well.

items.text: ARC — Transcript: Joint Address to the Nation — 21 February 2027

article.title:
Joint Address to the Nation
21 February 2027
article.date: 21 February 2027 — 12:00 GMT — Transcript via ARC Emergency
article.body:
THE PRIME MINISTER: Good afternoon.

Last night I told you that the Chancellor would address you today at midday with the full detail of the emergency measures we have been preparing. Before I hand to him, one thing.

Denmark and the Netherlands activated their own emergency payment systems yesterday. France and Canada begin this afternoon. Australia and Japan have announced measures for later this week. What the Chancellor is about to set out is consistent with what our partner nations are deploying. We are not alone in this.

Chancellor.

THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER: Thank you, Prime Minister.

I said on Saturday morning that I would set out the detail of our emergency payment infrastructure today. I said it would put money in your hands, on your devices, regardless of what has happened to the banking system. Here is that detail.

The Emergency Payment Module is live. As I speak, every ARC-enabled device in the United Kingdom is being credited with two hundred pounds. If your phone is beside you, check it now. You will see a notification from ARC Emergency. That money is yours.

Let me be precise about what this is and what it is not. It is not a loan. You will not be asked to repay it. It is not an advance on wages or benefits. It is an emergency allocation from this Government to you, directly. There is no application. There is no form. There is no means test. Every device receives the same amount.

I want to answer the questions I know you are asking.

How does it work. You use your phone exactly as you have always used it. You hold it to the payment terminal. You hear the beep. The transaction is confirmed. The amount is deducted from your EPM balance, which you can see at any time in ARC Emergency. The terminals are the same terminals you have always used. Every payment terminal in this country — in supermarkets, in pharmacies, in petrol stations, in corner shops, in pubs — has been ARC-enabled since September of last year under the Financial Conduct Authority’s interoperability mandate. The infrastructure is already there. We are using it.

Where can I spend it. Everywhere. Any terminal that accepted a contactless payment before this crisis will accept EPM today. From two o’clock this afternoon, major retailers will reopen — Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda, Morrisons, Waitrose, Aldi, Lidl, the Co-op. Boots and Superdrug will reopen for pharmacy services and essential items. Designated fuel stations are already operating and will continue. Your ARC Local app now contains a live map of open retailers and their operating hours in your area. Hours will vary — most major stores will operate from two o’clock until eight o’clock this evening, and from eight until eight from tomorrow onward.

What about my family’s phones. Every ARC-enabled device receives its own allocation. If your household has three phones, your household has received six hundred pounds. Children’s devices receive the same amount. I know this is imperfect — a single pensioner with one phone receives two hundred, while a family of four with four phones receives eight hundred. We chose speed and simplicity over precision. The Community Recovery Hubs exist to close that gap, and I will come to them in a moment.

What about prescriptions. Pharmacies reopening this afternoon will dispense NHS prescriptions. If you have a repeat prescription, bring your most recent packaging or a note of the medication name and dosage. Pharmacists are authorised to issue emergency supplies of regular medication for up to thirty days without a prescription, under the Emergency Supply provisions. If you are running low on essential medication, please go to your pharmacy this afternoon. Do not wait.

What happens when I run out. This is the first allocation, not the last. Further allocations will follow on a regular cycle. I will confirm the schedule and the amount by the end of this week. No one in this country will be left without the means to buy food and essentials. That is my commitment.

Is there a transaction limit. No. You can spend your balance in a single transaction or across as many as you wish. There is no minimum and no cap per purchase. When your balance reaches zero, it will be refreshed at the next allocation.

What will I see at the shops. Military personnel are present at major retail sites. They are there to help — to manage queues, to assist with logistics, to ensure deliveries reach the shelves. They are not there for security and they are not there for enforcement. They are squaddies helping stack shelves and carry boxes. If you see a uniform in the car park, that person is on your side.

On stock. I will be honest with you. Shelves will be patchy. Supply chains that rely on digital invoicing and automated ordering have been disrupted. Fresh produce will be limited. Bread, milk, eggs, tinned goods, rice, pasta, and frozen food are available in reasonable quantities at most major stores. The situation will improve daily as distribution recovers. Please buy what you need. Please do not buy more than you need.

On prices. Price controls are in effect under the Civil Contingencies Act for the duration of this emergency.

Now — for those without a smartphone. I know there are many of you, particularly among our older citizens, those in rural communities, and those whose phones were damaged, lost, or simply never owned. You have not been forgotten.

From tomorrow morning, Community Recovery Hubs across the country will begin distributing emergency food hampers. These are free. No identification is required. You walk in, you receive a hamper — tinned goods, rice, pasta, milk, tea, cooking oil, toiletries, batteries, candles. The basics. Hot food and drinks are available at most hubs now and will continue. If you have an older relative or a neighbour without a phone, please help them find their nearest hub.

On wages, pensions, and savings. I will address these in full on Wednesday once the NCSC has completed its data integrity assessment. For now, the position is unchanged — the obligations freeze protects you from any consequence of non-payment, and EPM provides the means to buy what you need. The bridge will hold.

Prime Minister.

THE PRIME MINISTER: Thank you, Chancellor.

One week ago the country woke up to something unprecedented. Five days ago we believed the worst was over. Two days ago we learned it was not. I will not dress that up.

But I want you to notice what just happened. The Chancellor has put money in your hands. Not next week. Not tomorrow. Now. The system he has described — the terminals, the hubs, the logistics, the payment infrastructure — was deployed in seven days by the men and women of the Treasury, the National Cyber Security Centre, the ARC programme, the armed forces, and thousands of local authority workers and volunteers across this country.

On the security situation. The National Cyber Security Centre continues to assess the full scope and origin of this attack. I have received a briefing this morning and I want to be straightforward with you. We have no intelligence to suggest a third phase is imminent. But we have not yet established the full capability of the actor responsible, and until we have, we must proceed with caution. That is why certain digital services remain restricted. That is why the measures the Chancellor has set out today are built on infrastructure that does not depend on the systems that were attacked.

These measures are not temporary. They are designed to hold for as long as they are needed. And they are designed to function whatever comes next.

This afternoon, go to the shops. Buy what you need for the week. If you have a neighbour who cannot get there, ask them what they need. If someone near you does not have a phone, walk them to the hub tomorrow morning.

This address has been broadcast live on BBC television and radio, and on ARC Emergency and ARC Local.

Stay local. Stay safe. Look after each other.

Be well.

items.text: PM’s Address to the Nation — Full Transcript

article.title: PM’s Address to the Nation — Full Transcript
article.body:
Five weeks ago, on a Sunday night, the lights went out.

For some of us it was the lights in our homes. For all of us it was more than this. Much more. The systems we relied upon to move our money, keep our records safe, that held the invisible architecture of daily life in place — they began to flicker. And then they went dark. And in that darkness, you did something remarkable.

You looked after each other.

I have spent these five weeks visiting communities across this country. I have sat in leisure centres, school gymnasiums and supermarket car parks. I have watched volunteers — strangers, neighbours, teenagers, pensioners — work together for the community and for one another, organising food distribution with nothing more than clipboards and goodwill. I have seen this country at its most bare and its most unified. And I have never been more proud to lead it.

But pride is not a plan. You deserve a plan, and I am here, today, to deliver that plan.

You deserve the truth. You have always deserved the truth. It pains me to say that prior to this egregious assault on our way of life, you have not always been given it. From this day onwards, that changes. That is my vow. And it is the vow of the leaders of every nation that stand together, as one, before you tonight. We will deliver the truth — openly, sincerely, and with integrity.

First, I must be clear about one thing. The system that failed us on the fourteenth of February will not be repaired — it cannot be repaired. Not slowly, not partially. The financial infrastructure that underpinned our economy — the databases, the transaction networks, the ledgers that recorded who owned what and who owed what — sustained damage beyond recovery. The experts we have consulted — and we have consulted every credible expert available — are unanimous.

We cannot go back. But we can, we must, and we will go forwards.

Because something survived.

Resilience. A resilience that lives within each and every one of us. A resilience we built together and that will last forever. The neighbours who checked on each other. The strangers who became friends in a queue. The teenagers who carried shopping for people they’d never met. You did not wait to be told. You did not wait for permission. You acted. We relied upon one another. And that reliance — that trust in each other — is the foundation everything else is built on.

But this is not all that survived.

In 2025, this government — alongside twenty-two partner nations — commissioned a programme. A resilience programme. A digital infrastructure designed not to replace the existing system, but to survive its failure. It was called the Autonomous Resilience Cloud — ARC. Of course you now recognise the name. It has been the backbone of the emergency information service on your phones these past five weeks. It was ARC that kept communication channels open. It was ARC that coordinated the hamper distribution. It was ARC that ensured your hospitals could still identify you and your children’s schools could still find you.

ARC was not a contingency. It was a conviction. A recognition that the systems we had inherited were fragile, centralised, and overdue for replacement. We hoped we would never need it. We were wrong to hope. We were right to build.

And built on the foundation of ARC is something new. Something we believe represents the most significant step forward in the relationship between citizen and state in the modern era.

Her name is AIDA.

AIDA — the Adaptive Intelligence for Domestic Assistance — is your personal recovery assistant. She is not a government database. She is not surveillance. She is a service — designed for us, accountable to us, and available to us all from tonight. AIDA will manage our recovery allocation. She will help us access healthcare, education, housing, employment. She will know what we need because we will tell her, and she will learn. She is built on transparency. Every decision she makes on our behalf is visible to us all. Every recommendation, we can refuse. She works for us. No longer us for them.

She managed the food — no one went hungry. She managed the power, and she kept the lights on.

Now I want to talk to you about what comes next. It impacts what we own and what we owe. This uncertainty has kept us awake these past five weeks.

I am here to tell you: tonight we will all sleep well.

As of eight o’clock this evening, His Majesty’s Treasury — in coordination with the Bank of England and twenty-two partner nations — has enacted a complete jubilee on personal debt. Your mortgage is cancelled. Your credit card balance is zero. Your student loan is cleared. Your overdraft is closed, at zero. This is not a freeze. This is not a deferral. The debt is gone. It does not exist. You owe nothing.

I will say that again, because I know you need to hear it twice.

You owe nothing. To anyone.

The old ledger is gone. The new one starts clean. BritCoin — our new digital allocation — will be credited to every registered household from midnight tonight. Ten thousand BritCoin per adult. Two thousand per child. A monthly allocation follows: fifteen hundred per adult, seven hundred and fifty per child. This is not furlough. This is not a loan. This is not temporary. This is the foundation of our new financial lives, and it begins tonight.

Registration is open now. It takes ninety seconds. You can do it from your phone, or you can visit your local Community Recovery Hub tomorrow morning. The process is simple because we built it to be simple. We have carried enough complexity.

What does registration mean? It means you are choosing to participate in both the National and the Global Recovery Programmes. It means AIDA can see each and every one of us — can allocate to us, can serve us, can protect us. Registration ensures that we can reach you. We can credit you. We can include you in the systems that will, from tonight, begin rebuilding our community, our country, our planet. Registration is not compulsory. But the recovery is real, and it is here, and it is here for all of us. No one should miss out. No one will miss out.

This is not a British project. It is global. This is not financial. It is human. This is not for the few. It is for us all.

Tonight, twenty-three nations are making this same announcement. The same jubilee. The same framework. The same commitment. From Washington to Berlin, from Tokyo to Canberra, from Delhi to São Paulo — the same words, the same promise, the same fresh start. This response was designed in five weeks, but built upon decades of planning, coordination, unity and trust.

The world you wake up to tomorrow will not look the same as the one you lost five weeks ago. It will look better. Not because the crisis was a gift — it was a catastrophe, and we grieve with every family that has suffered. But because the response to that catastrophe has given us permission to do what decades of politics could not: start again.

Tonight we register. Tomorrow we dream.

Our future is now.

items.text: Treasury Select Committee — Oral evidence: AI and financial infrastructure resilience

article.title: Oral Evidence: AI and Systemic Risk to Financial Infrastructure
article.body:
TREASURY SELECT COMMITTEE
Oral Evidence Session — AI and Systemic Risk to Financial Infrastructure
Thursday 21 January 2027

Witnesses: Carolyn Ainsworth, Deputy Director/Chief Engineer, National Cyber Security Centre; Nathanaël Benjamin, Executive Director, Financial Stability Strategy and Risk, Bank of England

Q214. Chair: Ms Ainsworth, can you describe in plain language what has changed in the past twelve months regarding the threat to UK payment infrastructure?

Ms Ainsworth: Certainly. Twelve months ago, the principal cyber threats to financial infrastructure were what we would term conventional — ransomware, denial of service, supply chain compromise. Sophisticated, but operating within known parameters. What has changed is the emergence of AI systems capable of identifying and exploiting vulnerabilities in critical software at a speed and scale that renders traditional patch cycles ineffective. To put it simply: the gap between a vulnerability being discovered and a vulnerability being exploited has, in certain scenarios, collapsed to near zero.

Q215. Chair: When you say 'AI systems' — are we talking about systems developed by hostile states?

Ms Ainsworth: We are talking about capabilities that now exist across multiple actors. The foundational research was conducted by Western AI laboratories for defensive purposes. Several of these systems were designated too sensitive for public release precisely because of their offensive potential. Our assessment is that equivalent capabilities are now available to a broader set of actors than we would wish. I am limited in what I can say in open session about specific attribution.

Q216. Ms Smith: Mr Benjamin, the Bank convened an emergency meeting with City institutions in November. Can you tell the Committee what prompted that?

Mr Benjamin: The meeting was convened following a classified briefing from NCSC on the results of an AI-assisted penetration assessment of UK payment clearing infrastructure. The assessment identified vulnerabilities in systems that had been subject to continuous human review for over a decade. Some of these vulnerabilities, if exploited in combination, could theoretically disrupt settlement and clearing across multiple payment schemes simultaneously. I want to stress that we have taken immediate steps to address the specific vulnerabilities identified.

Q217. Ms Smith: 'The specific vulnerabilities identified' — your phrasing implies there may be others.

Mr Benjamin: The nature of these AI-assisted assessments is that they reveal a landscape rather than individual points of failure. We are confident in the measures taken. We are less confident that any static assessment captures the full picture, given the pace at which these capabilities are evolving.

Q218. Mr Anderson: Ms Ainsworth, I want to return to something. You said the foundational research was conducted by Western laboratories 'for defensive purposes.' But the same capability that finds a vulnerability can exploit it. Is that correct?

Ms Ainsworth: That is correct.

Q219. Mr Anderson: So when we talk about keeping these systems out of the wrong hands — the distinction between right hands and wrong hands is not a technical distinction. It is a political one.

Ms Ainsworth: I would characterise it as an access and governance distinction. The capability itself is neutral. The question is who deploys it, under what authority, and with what safeguards.

Q220. Mr Anderson: And if those safeguards fail?

Ms Ainsworth: That is why we are here.

Q220a. Mr Anderson: Mr Benjamin, how many independent risk models currently operate across UK clearing and settlement infrastructure?

Mr Benjamin: I would need to confirm the precise number. However, I would note that the major clearing houses use a relatively small number of validated risk frameworks, several of which share common analytical foundations.

Q220b. Mr Anderson: 'Common analytical foundations.' You mean the same model.

Mr Benjamin: I mean that the pursuit of best practice naturally produces convergence in methodology. This is generally considered a strength.

Q220c. Mr Anderson: Until the methodology is wrong.

Mr Benjamin: That is why we stress-test.

Q220d. Mr Anderson: Against scenarios generated by the same methodology.

[Silence]

Chair: I think we should move on.

Q221. Chair: Mr Benjamin, one final question. If a coordinated attack of the type described in your classified briefing were to succeed — what is the Bank's assessment of recovery time?

Mr Benjamin: That depends on the scope and nature of the attack. For a targeted disruption of one or two payment schemes — days to weeks. For a broader event affecting clearing, settlement, and records infrastructure across multiple jurisdictions simultaneously — I would prefer not to speculate in open session.

Q222. Chair: That is noted. Thank you both. This evidence session is closed.

Committee note: The classified annex to this evidence session (Annex C) is available to Members on Privy Council terms. It is not available for public release. The Committee intends to return to this subject in its spring report.
